selection_reason: With no prior evidence, the first experiment should establish a strong baseline using the most principled full-pipeline configuration. I select config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) because: (1) multimodal is the core hypothesis of this study and is expected to outperform unimodal baselines; (2) multiprofile with transformer aggregation is the most expressive way to capture inter-profile relationships; (3) scgpt provides learned, biologically-informed RNA representations superior to linear PCA; (4) imagenet_vit_l is the strongest available image encoder. This experiment tests whether the full 'best-of-each-component' pipeline achieves high validation accuracy, giving me a reference point. Subsequent experiments can then ablate individual choices (e.g., swap to resnet50, avgpool, or concat vs. weighted) to identify which components drive performance. Expected relative cost: high (~75-85% of maximum), driven by the ViT-Large image encoder, transformer aggregation over multiple profiles, and scgpt fine-tuning. Accepting this cost upfront is justified because it is the configuration most likely to be near-optimal, and establishing a strong ceiling early allows efficient exploitation in the remaining 9 experiments.

Evidence: config_020 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat, multiprofile) achieved only 50.7% accuracy at 3.95 GPU hours — the most expensive setup in the space. With just one data point, the critical uncertainty is whether the large image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) is actually contributing meaningful signal or is simply adding cost without accuracy benefit. Question tested: config_006 is a clean single-variable change from config_020 (imagenet_vit_l → resnet50), isolating the image-encoder choice while holding RNA encoder (scgpt), aggregation (transformer), fusion (concat), and profile setting (multiprofile) constant. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It directly answers whether the dominant cost driver (vit_l) is worth its compute, which will shape all remaining 8 experiments; (2) if resnet50 matches or approaches 50.7%, every subsequent experiment becomes substantially cheaper, freeing budget for more informative searches; (3) if resnet50 is clearly worse, we confirm vit_l is essential and can focus remaining budget on other dimensions (RNA encoder, aggregation, fusion). Expected relative cost: moderate — roughly 2.5–3.0 GPU hours, about 25–35% cheaper than config_020, since resnet50 is significantly lighter than ViT-L while transformer aggregation and scgpt remain.

Evidence: config_020 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat) achieved the best accuracy (0.507) and is also cheaper (3.95 GPU hrs) than config_006 (resnet50 variant, 0.471, 9.06 GPU hrs), confirming that the ViT-L image encoder and scgpt RNA encoder with transformer aggregation are a strong combination. Uncertainty: we have only tested concat fusion so far; weighted fusion could better balance the two modalities' contributions, especially if one modality dominates. This experiment (config_019) changes only the fusion mechanism from concat to weighted while keeping the best-performing scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + transformer stack, providing a clean single-variable comparison to determine whether learned fusion weights improve over simple concatenation. It is the best next step because it directly exploits the strongest evidence with minimal additional risk, is likely to cost ~4 GPU hours (same architecture as config_020), and with 7 experiments remaining, confirming or refuting the fusion hypothesis early will guide whether to further explore aggregation/encoder variations or pivot to unimodal baselines.

Evidence: All three completed experiments used transformer aggregation, and the best result (config_019, acc=0.520) pairs scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted. We have no direct comparison of transformer vs avgpool aggregation, which is a major architectural choice affecting both accuracy and cost. Question: Does avgpool aggregation perform comparably to transformer when all other settings (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, multiprofile) are held constant? Why this is the best next experiment: config_016 isolates the aggregation variable against the current best, reducing uncertainty about whether the more expensive transformer is truly necessary. If avgpool matches transformer, we save significant GPU hours on all remaining experiments; if transformer is clearly superior, we confirm the investment. Expected cost: avgpool is a simpler aggregation than transformer, so this should be somewhat cheaper than config_019 (~2.86 GPU hours), likely around 2–2.5 GPU hours, making it a low-cost, high-information experiment.

The current best (config_016: scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, 0.542 acc) has established that weighted fusion and avgpool aggregation are optimal, and imagenet_vit_l outperforms resnet50. However, all four completed experiments use scgpt as the RNA encoder, leaving a critical uncertainty: whether scvi_n200 (a learned VAE encoder) can match or approach scgpt's performance within the same optimal architecture. config_045 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) directly tests this by pairing the only other learned RNA encoder with the best-known image encoder, aggregation, and fusion. If scvi_n200 is competitive, it may offer a cost advantage (smaller model than scgpt); if clearly inferior, it confirms scgpt as the definitive choice and lets us focus remaining budget on fine-tuning around the scgpt+imagenet_vit_l+avgpool+weighted core. This is the highest-information experiment for the remaining 5 slots because it resolves the RNA-encoder question under the already-validated optimal architecture. Expected relative cost: similar to or slightly below config_016 (~2.5–3.0 GPU hrs), since scvi_n200 is a smaller encoder than scgpt and avgpool is cheaper than transformer.

The dominant finding from 5 completed experiments is that scvi_n200 as RNA encoder produces a massive accuracy jump (config_045: 0.706) over scgpt (~0.47–0.54), making it the clear best encoder. Config_045 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) is the current best. The key remaining uncertainty is whether transformer aggregation can further improve upon avgpool when paired with scvi_n200's rich latent representations—scvi_n200 encodes profiles into a learned latent space where attention-based aggregation may capture cross-profile interactions that simple averaging misses. Config_024 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) is the most direct exploitation of the best configuration, testing the one architectural axis (aggregation) where evidence from scgpt experiments (avgpool slightly > transformer) may not transfer to the fundamentally different scvi_n200 latent space. This is the highest-value single experiment: if transformer helps, we get a new best; if not, we confirm avgpool is optimal and can focus remaining budget on other axes. Expected cost: ~5–6 GPU hours (transformer aggregation adds overhead over avgpool's 4.82 h baseline, but imagenet_vit_l and scvi_n200 are the same as config_045), which is moderate and justified by the potential accuracy gain.

Evidence: config_024 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) is the clear best at 0.725 acc, and weighted fusion has outperformed concat in all 3 prior comparisons (config_019 vs 020, config_016 vs 017-implied, config_045 vs 023-implied). The only untested variant in this top-performing family is config_018 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat). This experiment tests whether concat fusion could unexpectedly match or exceed weighted in the scvi_n200 regime, fully characterizing the best architecture family. If it confirms weighted > concat (as expected), we can confidently lock in config_024 as the family optimum and use the remaining 3 experiments to explore whether single-profile or other structural changes could push accuracy higher. Expected cost is moderate (~3.5–4 GPU hours), comparable to config_024's 3.60 GPU hours, since it uses the same encoders and transformer aggregation with only a fusion change.

The current best (config_024: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc 0.725) sits at the top of a 2×2 aggregation×fusion matrix for this encoder pair. Three of four cells are filled: transformer+weighted=0.725, transformer+concat=0.721, avgpool+weighted=0.706. The missing cell (avgpool+concat, config_023) will clarify whether fusion method interacts with aggregation strategy or whether the ~0.019 gap is driven purely by aggregation. If avgpool+concat lands near 0.70, it confirms transformer+weighted is the optimal pairing and we can lock in config_024 as the final answer with the remaining 2 experiments. If it lands closer to 0.72, it reveals that the architecture is more flexible than expected, opening a cheaper deployment path. This is the highest-information, lowest-risk experiment: it directly extends the strongest evidence (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l dominates all other encoder combos by ~0.18 accuracy), completes the design-space picture, and costs an estimated ~3–4 GPU hours (avgpool aggregation is lighter than transformer, similar to config_016's 2.94 h or config_045's 4.82 h). With only 2 experiments remaining after this, confirming or ruling out a simpler architecture before the final budget is the most efficient use of the slot.

Evidence: The scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile space is fully explored (all 4 aggregation/fusion combos tested), with config_024 (transformer+weighted) as the best at 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. The only major untested design axis for scvi_n200 is the image encoder. For scgpt, resnet50 was ~3-4 points worse than imagenet_vit_l, but the interaction with scvi_n200 is unknown. Question: Does config_007 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted) — the direct image-encoder swap of our best config — achieve comparable accuracy? This clarifies whether imagenet_vit_l is essential or whether resnet50 is a sufficient, potentially cheaper alternative. Rationale: With only 1 experiment remaining after this, testing the most impactful unexplored variable (image encoder) for the dominant RNA encoder is the highest-information experiment. If resnet50 is within ~1 point of vit_l, it confirms cost-effectiveness; if it lags significantly, it validates config_024 as the optimal choice. Expected cost: moderate, estimated ~3.5–5 GPU hours (resnet50 is architecturally lighter than ViT-L, though the scgpt comparison showed variable overhead; comparable to other scvi_n200 multiprofile runs at 3.6–4.8 hrs).

Evidence: The top 5 configurations all use scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, with the best being config_024 (transformer + weighted) at 0.725. All four aggregation×fusion combinations for scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l are now exhausted, so further gains require changing a fundamental component. The RNA encoder is the largest untested lever: scgpt performed far below scvi_n200 (~0.51 vs ~0.72), but pca_n2000 (a 2000-dim linear projection) is a fundamentally different representation that has never been tested in the multimodal multiprofile setting. Question: Does pca_n2000, combined with the best-known image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (transformer), and fusion (weighted), match or exceed scvi_n200's performance? This is the highest-information experiment for the final slot—if pca_n2000 is competitive, config_005 could push past 0.725; if not, it confirms scvi_n200 as the superior RNA encoder. Cost: pca_n2000 is a linear method (cheaper than scvi_n200's deep generative model), but transformer aggregation + imagenet_vit_l dominate the compute. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3–4 GPU hours, comparable to config_024 (3.60 h).

With no prior evidence, the key uncertainty is whether a well-designed multimodal, multiprofile configuration can establish a strong performance ceiling and inform which design axes (RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, fusion) matter most. config_010 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) is a balanced, near-optimal starting point: it combines both modalities (most likely to outperform single-modality), uses multiprofile with transformer aggregation (best for integrating multiple profiles), and uses weighted fusion (flexible modality combination). It avoids the most expensive choices (ViT-L, scGPT) to keep cost moderate (~2-3x a single-modality PCA baseline in GPU hours), preserving budget for 9 follow-up experiments that can test whether upgrading the image encoder to ViT-L or the RNA encoder to scGPT/scVI yields meaningful gains. This gives a strong reference accuracy and simultaneously tests the core hypothesis that multimodal + multiprofile + transformer aggregation is the right architectural backbone.

With only one completed experiment (config_010: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, transformer, weighted → 0.573 acc), evidence is very sparse. The most informative next step is to isolate a single design variable from the current best. Config_007 is identical to config_010 except fusion changes from weighted to concat, giving a clean A/B test of the fusion strategy while holding all other factors (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, transformer aggregation) constant. This clarifies whether weighted or concat fusion is the better mechanism for combining modality representations—a choice that will affect every subsequent multimodal experiment. If concat outperforms weighted, it opens a new promising direction; if weighted is confirmed, we can confidently fix that parameter and explore other axes (image encoder, RNA encoder, aggregation) in remaining experiments. Expected cost is comparable to config_010 (~6.5–7 GPU hours) since the architecture is identical, making this a low-risk, high-information experiment early in the budget.

The two completed experiments (config_010, config_007) establish that multimodal + multiprofile + pca_n2000 + resnet50 + transformer yields ~0.57-0.58 accuracy, with concat fusion slightly ahead on accuracy (0.5793 vs 0.5729). The largest untested design axis is the image encoder: upgrading from ResNet50 (~25M params) to ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L (~300M+ params) could substantially improve the visual representation and thus overall accuracy. config_004 is the direct, minimal-change extension of our best result (config_007) — same RNA encoder, aggregation, profile setting, and concat fusion — swapping only the image encoder. This isolates the effect of a stronger visual backbone and reduces uncertainty about whether the current accuracy ceiling is driven by limited image representation. Expected relative cost: ViT-L is roughly 1.5–2× more expensive than ResNet50, so I estimate ~9–11 GPU hours (vs ~6.7 for ResNet50 configs). This is a justified cost increase given the potential for a meaningful accuracy jump, and with 7 experiments remaining, confirming or refuting the value of a stronger image encoder is the highest-information experiment to run next.

The best result so far is config_004 (acc=0.5988) using pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, and concat fusion. The resnet50 comparison (config_007 concat vs config_010 weighted) showed concat edges out weighted on accuracy (0.579 vs 0.573) but weighted was better on F1 (0.573 vs 0.563), so the fusion choice is genuinely uncertain. Config_005 tests the same strong backbone (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer) with weighted fusion, directly clarifying whether weighted fusion can match or exceed the 0.599 accuracy with the better image encoder. This is the highest-value exploitation step: it refines the single most promising direction with minimal additional cost (~4.8 GPU hours, comparable to config_004 since only the fusion head changes). With 6 experiments remaining, locking down the optimal fusion before exploring alternative RNA encoders (scgpt, scvi) or aggregation strategies (avgpool) ensures subsequent experiments build on the strongest known base.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_004 (acc=0.5988) using pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat. All four completed experiments share pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, so the RNA encoder dimension is completely unexplored in the best-performing multimodal setup. The image encoder (vit_l > resnet50, ~2% gain) and fusion (concat > weighted with transformer, consistent across both image encoders) are well-established. Question: Does a learned RNA encoder (scgpt) improve over the linear PCA representation when combined with the strongest image encoder and aggregation/fusion stack? This is the largest remaining untested design axis that could yield a meaningful accuracy gain. Why this is the best next experiment: With 5 experiments left, testing the RNA encoder in the best-performing configuration (config_018: scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat) either opens a new exploitation path (if scgpt helps) or eliminates that dimension so remaining budget can focus on aggregation variants or other refinements. Expected relative cost: scgpt is a full transformer-based generative encoder, so this will be notably more expensive than config_004 (4.76 GPU hrs) — likely ~7–9 GPU hours — but it is the highest-information experiment available and justifiable given the potential accuracy upside.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_004 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) at 0.5988 acc. Image encoder (imagenet_vit_l > resnet50) and aggregation (transformer > avgpool, implied) are well-established. However, the RNA encoder dimension is under-explored: pca_n2000 works well, scgpt is clearly poor (0.5070), but scvi_n200 has never been tested in the multiprofile multimodal setting. Question: Does scvi_n200, a learned variational RNA encoder, outperform the linear pca_n2000 when paired with the best image encoder and aggregation? This is the single largest untested variable that could push accuracy above 0.599. Why this experiment: config_051 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) holds all known-best components fixed and swaps only the RNA encoder, giving a clean read on whether a richer RNA representation helps. If it matches or beats config_004, it opens a new promising axis; if it underperforms, we confirm pca_n2000 is optimal and can redirect remaining budget to other levers. Expected cost: ~4.5–5.0 GPU hours (transformer aggregation + ViT-L image encoder, comparable to config_004/005), keeping total well within budget.

Evidence: config_051 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat) achieved 0.7207 accuracy, far surpassing all other configurations. In every prior comparison of fusion types (configs 004 vs 005, 007 vs 010), concat outperformed weighted by ~1-2%. However, those comparisons used pca_n2000 or scgpt encoders, which produce very different feature spaces than scvi_n200's dense learned 200-dim embeddings. Question: Does the fusion preference hold with the much richer scvi_n200 representations, or does weighted fusion better balance the two modalities at this quality level? This experiment (config_045: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) is the single-parameter change from the current best, directly testing whether concat is truly optimal here. It is the best use of this slot because: (1) it is the lowest-risk, most informative next step—confirming or refuting the best architecture with minimal uncertainty; (2) if it confirms concat superiority, the remaining 2 experiments can target a different axis (e.g., avgpool aggregation or singleprofile); (3) if it surprisingly beats 0.7207, we immediately have a new best. Expected cost: ~4.6–4.7 GPU hours, essentially identical to config_051 since only the fusion operation changes (negligible compute impact).

Evidence: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted (config_045, 0.7250) is the clear best, with scvi_n200 dramatically outperforming pca_n2000 (~0.72 vs ~0.60) and imagenet_vit_l outperforming resnet50. The only untested architectural axis with this encoder pair is the aggregation method (avgpool vs. transformer). This experiment (config_042: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) tests whether avgpool aggregation can match or approach transformer's performance while keeping the proven best encoders and the slightly superior weighted fusion. If avgpool performs comparably, it confirms a simpler, cheaper architecture suffices; if transformer is clearly better, it validates sticking with config_045. This is the highest-value uncertainty to resolve with 2 experiments remaining, as it directly probes whether the current best can be matched more cheaply or whether transformer aggregation is essential. Expected cost: slightly lower than config_045 (~3.5–4.0 GPU hrs) since avgpool is a simpler aggregation than transformer.

Evidence: The best configuration found is config_045 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) at 0.7250 accuracy, with config_051 (same encoders, concat) at 0.7207 and config_042 (same encoders, avgpool + weighted) at 0.7062. This establishes a clear hierarchy: transformer > avgpool and weighted ≥ concat for the top encoder pair. Question: config_025 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat) is the last untested cell in the 2×2 aggregation×fusion matrix for the best-performing encoder combination. Testing it completes the matrix and confirms whether the observed monotonic improvements (transformer+weighted > transformer+concat > avgpool+weighted) hold for the remaining combination, or whether there is any unexpected interaction. Why this is the best use: With only 2 experiments remaining, I need to confirm that 0.7250 is indeed the ceiling for this architecture family before spending the final experiment. config_025 is the cheapest remaining test (~4.5–4.8 GPU hours, comparable to config_042 at 4.82) that directly addresses the key uncertainty. It is unlikely to exceed 0.7250 given the consistent ~0.019 transformer-avgpool gap and ~0.004 weighted-concat gap, but confirming this frees the last experiment for a broader architectural exploration (e.g., singleprofile or a different encoder pairing) rather than a redundant confirmation.

Evidence: The best configuration found is config_045 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, multiprofile) at 0.7250 accuracy. All four aggregation×fusion combinations for scvi_n200+imagenet_vit_l+multiprofile are exhausted. The image encoder (imagenet_vit_l vs resnet50) showed a large performance gap with pca_n2000 (~0.05-0.15), but it is untested whether scvi_n200's learned latent representations reduce dependence on the image encoder. Question: config_030 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted, multiprofile) tests whether the strongest RNA encoder combined with the best aggregation and fusion can partially compensate for the weaker image encoder, potentially yielding a competitive and cheaper model. Rationale: As the final experiment, this is the highest-expected-accuracy untested configuration in the proven multiprofile+scvi_n200+transformer+weighted family. It is the most logical single-variable extension of the best result. If it approaches 0.70+, it would confirm a cheaper viable alternative; if it falls well below, it firmly establishes imagenet_vit_l as essential. Expected cost: moderate (~4-5 GPU hours), slightly less than config_045 since resnet50 is smaller than ViT-L, making it a reasonable final experiment within the remaining budget.

With no prior evidence, the most informative first experiment is a strong multimodal configuration to establish a performance ceiling and reduce uncertainty about whether the full multimodal pipeline (RNA + image) with powerful encoders is viable. config_041 combines scgpt (a pre-trained generative RNA encoder likely to capture rich transcriptomic structure), imagenet_vit_l (the strongest available image encoder), transformer aggregation (most expressive for multiprofile integration), and concat fusion (a standard, well-understood fusion strategy). This tests the core hypothesis that multimodal fusion with strong encoders outperforms simpler alternatives. It is the most expensive configuration (scgpt + ViT-L + transformer + multiprofile + multimodal), so I estimate its relative cost as ~1.0× (the reference maximum). Establishing this upper bound early is critical: if it performs strongly, subsequent experiments can explore cheaper variants (resnet50, avgpool, scvi_n200) to find a cost-effective sweet spot; if it underperforms, we immediately know the architecture needs rethinking, saving budget from chasing an unproductive direction. With 9 experiments remaining, this single expensive anchor gives the most leverage for the rest of the search.

With only one completed experiment (config_041: scgpt + ViT-L + transformer + concat, acc=0.507, cost=3.95 GPU-hrs), evidence is very sparse. The most impactful uncertainty is whether the expensive scgpt RNA encoder is actually necessary or whether the cheaper scvi_n200 encoder (a 200-dim VAE) can match its performance. Config_013 isolates this single variable (scgpt→scvi_n200) while holding everything else constant (multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat). If scvi_n200 performs comparably, we save ~1-1.5 GPU-hrs per experiment across the remaining 8 runs, freeing budget for more exploratory trials. If it underperforms, we confirm scgpt's value and can focus optimization on other axes (fusion, aggregation, image encoder). This is the highest-information experiment at this stage because the RNA encoder choice affects every future multimodal configuration and carries the largest single cost differential. Expected relative cost: ~65-75% of config_041 (≈2.5-3 GPU-hrs), since scvi_n200 is substantially lighter than scgpt while ViT-L and transformer aggregation remain.

Evidence: config_013 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) achieved 0.721 accuracy, dramatically outperforming config_041 (scgpt variant) at 0.507, establishing scvi_n200 + ViT-L + transformer + multiprofile as the clearly superior architecture. Question: config_042 is the minimal extension of config_013, changing only the fusion from concat to weighted, testing whether learned weighted fusion can further improve over simple concatenation in this strong baseline. This isolates the fusion mechanism as the sole variable. Why best next: With 7 experiments remaining, exploiting the strongest signal (scvi_n200 + ViT-L + transformer) with a single clean ablation is the highest-information-per-cost step. It either yields a new best accuracy or confirms concat is sufficient, reducing uncertainty before testing larger architectural changes (e.g., image encoder or aggregation). Expected cost is similar to config_013 (~4.6 GPU hours) since only the fusion head changes, making it a fair and efficient comparison.

Evidence: The three completed experiments show that (1) scvi_n200 is far superior to scgpt as the RNA encoder (0.72 vs 0.51 accuracy), and (2) weighted fusion marginally edges out concat (0.725 vs 0.721) while being cheaper. All top configs use imagenet_vit_l, but the image-encoder axis has not been tested with the best RNA encoder. Question: Does resnet50 perform comparably to imagenet_vit_l when paired with scvi_n200 + transformer + weighted? This is the largest untested architectural axis and directly affects both accuracy and cost. Why this experiment: config_049 is a minimal, logical extension of the current best (config_042) with only the image encoder swapped. If resnet50 matches ViT-L, we unlock a family of cheaper configurations for the remaining 6 experiments; if it falls short, we confirm ViT-L is necessary and can focus remaining budget on finer-tuning around the ViT-L + scvi_n200 + weighted combination. Expected relative cost: resnet50 is substantially smaller than ViT-L, so this should train faster than config_042's 3.60 GPU hours, likely around 2.0–2.8 GPU hours, making it a cost-efficient exploration of a high-impact design choice.

The current best is config_042 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc / 3.60 GPU-hr. The key uncertainty is whether the transformer aggregation is meaningfully contributing over a simpler avgpool, since all top configs use transformer and no avgpool variant has been tested with the best RNA+image encoder pair. config_046 isolates exactly this variable (aggregation: transformer→avgpool) while holding the proven-best scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, and weighted fusion fixed. If avgpool matches within ~0.01, we confirm a cheaper architecture suffices, saving GPU hours for remaining experiments; if it drops substantially, we confirm transformer is essential and can focus remaining budget on other axes (e.g., singleprofile, alternative encoders). Expected relative cost: ~2.5–3.0 GPU hours (moderately cheaper than the 3.60 of config_042, since avgpool removes the transformer's self-attention layers over profiles). This is the best use of experiment 5 because it directly reduces uncertainty about the most expensive architectural component while keeping the highest-performing encoder/fusion combination intact.

Evidence: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted (config_042) is the current best at 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1 (3.60 GPU hrs). The RNA encoder is the largest performance lever (scgpt→0.507 vs scvi_n200→0.725, a 22-pt gap), but PCA_n2000 has never been tested in any multimodal setting. Question: Can the linear PCA_n2000 encoder approach scvi_n200's performance in the best-known architecture (transformer aggregation + weighted fusion + ViT-L image encoder)? Why this experiment: With 4 experiments remaining, reducing uncertainty about the RNA encoder is the highest-value move. If PCA matches scvi_n200, it confirms a cheaper, simpler alternative and frees remaining budget for fine-tuning other axes; if it falls well short, we confirm scvi_n200 is essential and can dedicate remaining runs to small refinements (e.g., single-profile variants or fusion tweaks) around the proven scvi_n200 stack. Expected relative cost: ~3–3.5 GPU hrs, slightly cheaper than config_042 since PCA replaces a trained neural encoder with a linear projection, while the ViT-L image branch and transformer aggregation dominate compute.

Evidence: The top three configs (0.725, 0.721, 0.713) all use scvi_n200 + transformer aggregation, confirming this as the dominant architecture. Within this sub-space, imagenet_vit_l + weighted is the best (0.725), but resnet50 showed a notably higher F1 (0.695 vs 0.685) suggesting more balanced predictions. Question: config_002 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) is the last untested multiprofile+transformer+scvi_n200 combination, testing whether concat fusion synergizes with resnet50's representation in a way that might close or exceed the 0.725 mark. Rationale: With 3 experiments remaining, completing this critical sub-space is the highest-value exploration; it has the highest expected accuracy among untested multiprofile configs (~0.71–0.72) and will clarify whether the small accuracy gap between image encoders is offset by fusion choice. Expected cost: ~6 GPU hours (comparable to config_049 with resnet50+transformer), making it moderately expensive but justified by its position in the most promising architectural family.

Evidence strongly favors scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + weighted fusion (config_042 at 0.7250 is the current best). The major untested design dimension is multiprofile vs. singleprofile: all 7 completed experiments used multiprofile with an aggregation step, so we have no data on whether the aggregation is genuinely adding signal or introducing noise. config_006 (singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted) directly tests this question with the best-performing encoders and fusion. If singleprofile matches or exceeds 0.725, it also reduces cost (no aggregation step, estimated ~2.5 GPU hours vs. ~3.6–4.7 for multiprofile+transformer). If it underperforms, it confirms multiprofile+transformer is essential, letting the final 2 experiments focus on multiprofile refinements. This is the highest-information experiment remaining given the budget.

The best configuration found is config_042 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy. All single-axis perturbations from this peak have been tested (concat→0.721, resnet50→0.713, avgpool→0.706), confirming a clear local optimum. The remaining untested configs with scvi_n200+imagenet_vit_l are config_015 (avgpool, concat), which retains the two strongest encoders while varying both aggregation and fusion. This is the closest untested neighbor to the current best and tests whether the transformer+weighted advantage is strictly necessary or whether a simpler pipeline with the same encoders could achieve comparable accuracy at lower cost. Expected relative cost: moderate (~4–5 GPU hours), slightly cheaper than config_042 (3.60) or config_046 (4.82) since it avoids the transformer aggregation. With only 1 experiment remaining after this, this choice maximizes the chance of either finding a marginal improvement or confirming config_042 as the final best, while keeping total GPU hours manageable.

The evidence strongly identifies scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted (config_042, acc=0.7250) as the best configuration, and no untested configuration replicates that exact combination. For this final experiment, I select config_029 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) as the most logical remaining test: it retains the best RNA encoder (scvi_n200) and the preferred weighted fusion, while testing whether the slightly weaker image encoder (resnet50) and simpler aggregation (avgpool) can still approach the top result. Based on config_049 (resnet50+transformer+weighted, acc=0.713) and config_046 (imagenet_vit_l+avgpool+weighted, acc=0.706), I expect config_029 to land around 0.69–0.71, unlikely to surpass 0.7250 but informative. Expected relative cost is moderate (~4–5 GPU hours), as resnet50 is cheaper than ViT-L and avgpool is cheaper than transformer aggregation. Since this is the last experiment and the best result (0.7250) is already secured, this choice minimizes additional GPU cost while providing a final data point on the scvi_n200+weighted axis with a cheaper backbone.

With no prior evidence, the most informative first experiment should establish a strong multimodal reference point while keeping cost manageable. config_009 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat) tests whether combining a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200) with a strong pretrained image encoder (ViT-L) via simple concatenation yields a competitive baseline. This clarifies: (1) whether multimodal fusion provides meaningful gains over what unimodal models would achieve (to be confirmed in a later experiment), (2) the performance ceiling for a single-profile setup, and (3) a reference accuracy to judge whether more complex aggregation (transformer/avgpool) or multiprofile strategies are worth the extra cost. I chose ViT-L over ResNet50 because for cellular image profiling, a large pretrained ViT is likely the dominant image feature source, and establishing this upper bound early guides whether cheaper image encoders are sufficient. Expected relative cost: medium-high (ViT-L is the primary cost driver; no transformer aggregation or multiprofile overhead, so it is cheaper than configs like 011/012/025 but more expensive than ResNet50-based configs like 001/010).

The sole completed experiment (config_009: multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieved 53.2% accuracy, a moderate baseline. The largest untested architectural lever is whether moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with an expressive aggregation (transformer) can meaningfully improve performance. config_012 keeps the exact same RNA encoder (scvi_n200), image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), and fusion strategy (concat) as the baseline, isolating the effect of multiprofile + transformer aggregation. Transformer aggregation is the most expressive way to combine multiple profile representations and is the natural 'upper bound' for multiprofile; if it does not beat the singleprofile baseline, I can rule out the entire multiprofile family and redirect remaining budget toward encoder swaps (scgpt) or fusion changes. If it does help, it opens a clear exploitation path (scgpt + transformer, weighted fusion, etc.). Expected relative cost: roughly 2× the 0.62 GPU-hour baseline (~1.2–1.5 GPU hours) due to multiprofile token processing and the transformer aggregation layer, which is a reasonable investment given 8 experiments remain and this is the single most informative architectural question at this stage.

Evidence: config_012 (multiprofile, transformer agg, scvi_n200, ViT-L, concat) achieved 0.721 acc at 4.65 GPU hrs, vastly outperforming config_009 (singleprofile, no agg, same encoders, concat) at 0.532 acc / 0.62 GPU hrs. The multiprofile+transformer combination is clearly the key driver. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether the transformer aggregation is essential or whether a cheaper avgpool aggregation over multiple profiles would capture most of the multiprofile benefit. This experiment (config_049) isolates that variable by swapping transformer→avgpool while holding all other settings identical to config_012 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, multiprofile, concat fusion). If avgpool reaches ~0.68–0.72, we confirm a much cheaper path to near-best accuracy, saving ~3+ GPU hrs per run and freeing budget for further refinement. If it drops substantially, we confirm transformer is critical and should focus remaining experiments on transformer-based variants (e.g., weighted fusion, different RNA encoders). Expected relative cost: moderate (~1.0–1.5 GPU hrs), roughly 1/3 to 1/4 of config_012's cost, since avgpool is far cheaper than a full transformer over profiles but still processes multiple profiles.

Evidence: Multiprofile with scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer/concat (config_012, acc=0.721) and avgpool/concat (config_049, acc=0.715) are the current best, both far above singleprofile (0.532). The RNA encoder dimension is completely unexplored—we've only tested scvi_n200. This experiment tests scgpt (a generative pre-trained RNA encoder) while holding all other proven-optimal components fixed (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, concat fusion). This is the highest-information-gain next step: if scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, it opens a new promising direction; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 as the right encoder and we can focus remaining budget on fusion and image-encoder variations. With 6 experiments still remaining after this, the risk of a negative result is manageable. Expected cost: comparable to config_012 (~4.5–5 GPU hours), as the dominant costs (ViT-L image processing, transformer aggregation over multiple profiles) are unchanged; scgpt's per-sample encoding cost is similar in magnitude to scvi_n200.

Evidence: The best result (config_012, acc=0.721) uses multimodal/multiprofile/scvi_n200/imagenet_vit_l/transformer/concat, and config_049 (avgpool/concat) is nearly identical at 0.715. scgpt underperforms scvi_n200 by ~20 points, and singleprofile is far worse. The dominant design choices (multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer) are well-supported. The key untested variable within this high-performing region is the fusion method: all top results use concat. Question: Does weighted fusion (learning modality-level importance) improve over simple concatenation when combined with the transformer aggregator? config_025 is the exact best configuration with only fusion changed from concat to weighted. This is the highest-value exploitation step: it directly extends the strongest evidence with a minimal, well-motivated change. Expected cost is comparable to config_012 (~4.6–4.8 GPU hours) since the transformer aggregation dominates training time and weighted fusion adds only a small parameter overhead over concat.

Evidence: The top-3 configs (0.725, 0.721, 0.715) all use scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile, differing only in aggregation (transformer vs avgpool) and fusion (weighted vs concat). We have transformer+concat (0.721), avgpool+concat (0.715), and transformer+weighted (0.725, current best). The missing cell is avgpool+weighted. This experiment (config_017) completes the 2×2 aggregation×fusion matrix, clarifying whether weighted fusion consistently improves over concat regardless of aggregation method, and whether avgpool+weighted could match or beat the current best. If it does, it would confirm a cheaper aggregation path (avgpool was 4.49 vs 4.65 for concat; weighted was 3.60 vs 4.65 for transformer+concat, suggesting avgpool+weighted may be ~3.5–4.0 GPU hours). This is the best use of experiment 6 because it directly resolves the remaining uncertainty within the proven-best encoder combination at moderate cost, and the result will guide whether to exploit transformer+weighted or pivot to avgpool+weighted for the final 4 experiments.

Evidence: The best config so far is config_025 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc. All four aggregation×fusion combos for scvi_n200+imagenet_vit_l have been tested, and scgpt was dramatically worse (0.507). The key unexplored dimension with the proven-best RNA encoder is the image encoder. This experiment tests config_034 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) to determine whether the lighter resnet50 backbone can match or approach ViT-L performance with the best aggregation/fusion pairing. If resnet50 is competitive, it saves substantial GPU hours for remaining experiments; if it is clearly inferior, it confirms ViT-L is essential and we can focus the last 3 experiments on other refinements. Expected relative cost: moderate (~2.5–3.5 GPU hours), likely slightly cheaper than config_025 (3.60 h) since resnet50 is smaller than ViT-L, making this an efficient probe of the image-encoder axis.

Evidence: All scvi_n200 + vit_l + multiprofile combinations (transformer/avgpool × weighted/concat) have been tested, with config_025 (transformer, weighted) as the best at 0.725. The remaining untested dimensions are the RNA encoder (pca_n2000, scgpt) and image encoder (resnet50). scgpt has already shown to be poor (0.507), and resnet50 underperformed vit_l (0.713 vs 0.725). This experiment tests pca_n2000 with the best aggregation/fusion setting (transformer + weighted) and the best image encoder (vit_l), directly probing whether a simpler linear RNA encoder can match the learned scvi_n200 encoder in the optimal multimodal pipeline. This is the best use of experiment 8 because: (1) it reduces uncertainty about the most important remaining design choice (RNA encoder) in the highest-performing configuration space, (2) if pca_n2000 performs comparably, it offers a significantly cheaper alternative for deployment, and (3) if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 is essential, allowing the final 2 experiments to focus on fine-tuning the resnet50/vit_l trade-off or accepting config_025 as the optimum. Expected relative cost: moderate (~3–4 GPU hours), slightly cheaper than config_025 (3.60 h) since PCA encoding is a fast linear projection versus scvi's iterative VAE training, while the ViT-L and transformer aggregation dominate runtime.

The current best is config_025 (acc 0.7250, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted). All single-component variants of this top configuration have been tested, and the remaining untested configs in the top-performing region (multiprofile + scvi_n200) all use resnet50. config_020 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) is the last untested combination in this region. Evidence suggests it will likely land around 0.710–0.718 (config_034 with resnet50+transformer+weighted scored 0.7131, and concat is slightly worse than weighted based on config_012 vs config_025), so it is unlikely to beat config_025 but will confirm the ceiling of the design space. This is the best use of experiment 9 because it closes the remaining uncertainty in the top region before the final experiment, ensuring we don't miss a marginal improvement. Expected cost: moderate (~3.5–4.5 GPU hours), comparable to config_025 (3.60) since it uses transformer aggregation but with the smaller resnet50 image encoder instead of ViT-L.

Evidence: The best configuration found is config_025 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.724989 accuracy. All four aggregation×fusion combinations for scvi_n200+imagenet_vit_l are now tested, confirming transformer+weighted as optimal. scvi_n200 is clearly superior to pca_n2000 and scgpt, and imagenet_vit_l slightly edges resnet50. Question: config_028 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) completes the remaining untested cell in the scvi_n200+resnet50 aggregation×fusion matrix, testing whether avgpool+weighted with the cheaper image encoder could be competitive. Why this is the best last experiment: It uses the proven-best RNA encoder and the better fusion method (weighted), providing a final data point on the resnet50 variant. It is unlikely to surpass config_025 but completes the design space with the top RNA encoder. Expected cost is moderate (~4.5 GPU hours, comparable to config_017 at 4.82 h), keeping total budget around ~42.5 GPU hours. Since no remaining configuration is likely to beat 0.724989, this moderate-cost experiment minimizes additional GPU hours while still yielding useful confirmation of the architecture ranking.

With no prior evidence, the key uncertainty is whether a multimodal, multiprofile pipeline outperforms simpler alternatives, and which component choices (encoder, aggregation, fusion) matter most. Config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) tests the core hypothesis that combining RNA and image modalities with multiple profiles yields strong accuracy, while using relatively simple, well-understood components (PCA for RNA, ResNet50 for image, average-pool aggregation, concatenation fusion). This establishes a solid performance baseline at moderate computational cost—roughly 1–1.5× a single-modality run, and significantly cheaper than ViT-L-based configs. If it performs well, subsequent experiments can systematically upgrade one component at a time (e.g., swap to ViT-L, scvi/scgpt encoders, or transformer aggregation) to identify the highest-accuracy configuration within the 10-experiment budget. If it underperforms, the result still clarifies whether multimodality or multiprofile aggregation is the bottleneck, directing exploration efficiently.

With only one completed experiment (config_004: multimodal/multiprofile/pca_n2000/resnet50/avgpool/concat → 61.9% acc, 36.42 GPU hrs), evidence is sparse and the priority is to identify the highest-leverage design axis. The image encoder is the most likely single source of large improvement: ResNet50 (~25M params) is substantially smaller and less expressive than an ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L (~300M+ params), so upgrading it should yield a meaningful accuracy gain if the image modality is informative. config_047 changes only the image encoder (resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l) while holding RNA encoder (pca_n2000), aggregation (avgpool), and fusion (concat) identical to the baseline, giving a clean single-variable comparison. This is the best use of experiment 2 because it reduces the largest uncertainty (whether a stronger image representation helps) before committing budget to more expensive combinations (e.g., transformer aggregation + ViT-L + scgpt). Expected relative cost: roughly 1.5–2× the baseline (~50–70 GPU hrs) due to the larger ViT-L backbone, which is justified by the expected accuracy gain and the information gained for all subsequent ViT-L-based experiments.

Evidence: Two completed experiments (config_004, config_047) share all settings except image encoder (ResNet50 vs ViT-L). config_047 (ViT-L, pca_n2000, avgpool, concat) leads with 0.6287 acc at a surprisingly low 4.54 GPU-hr cost. The ~1% accuracy gap is suggestive but based on a single comparison, and F1 actually dropped slightly, so the evidence is still thin. Question: config_001 is identical to config_047 except it uses weighted fusion instead of concat, directly testing whether a learned fusion weighting can improve on the current best while keeping the same cheap architecture. Why this is the best next step: It is a minimal, low-cost exploitation of the most promising configuration (expected cost ~4–5 GPU hrs, similar to config_047), reduces uncertainty about the fusion strategy without introducing multiple confounding changes, and preserves budget for later experiments to explore RNA encoders (scgpt/scvi_n200) and transformer aggregation. If weighted fusion helps, we gain a stronger base; if not, we rule it out cheaply and can pivot to larger architectural changes in experiments 4–10.

The best result so far is config_001 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.6352, F1=0.6183, 7.02 GPU hrs). All three completed experiments share the same RNA encoder (pca_n2000), so the impact of a learned RNA representation is completely untested. config_021 changes only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200 while keeping the best-performing image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (avgpool), and fusion (weighted) fixed, making it a clean single-variable ablation. This is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact design axis remaining: a variational autoencoder can capture nonlinear cell-state structure that PCA (linear) cannot, potentially improving the RNA branch's contribution to the fused representation. Expected cost is moderate (~8-12 GPU hrs), comparable to config_001 since scvi_n200 adds a small VAE forward pass but the dominant cost (ViT-L image encoding + multiprofile processing) is unchanged. With 6 experiments remaining, resolving whether a learned RNA encoder helps or hurts is critical before committing further budget to downstream refinements (e.g., transformer aggregation or scgpt).

Evidence: config_021 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) achieved the best accuracy (0.706) and F1 (0.667) at only 4.82 GPU hrs, a ~7% jump over the pca_n2000 baseline. The scvi_n200 RNA encoder + imagenet_vit_l + weighted fusion combination is clearly the strongest direction. Uncertainty: whether transformer aggregation can further improve over avgpool by better modeling inter-profile relationships in the multiprofile setting, especially with the richer scvi_n200 representations. This experiment (config_049) tests exactly that: it keeps all three best-performing components (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion) and swaps avgpool for transformer aggregation. It is the most direct and logical exploitation of the strongest signal found so far. Expected cost: transformer aggregation adds moderate overhead over avgpool; I estimate ~8–12 GPU hrs, still well within budget and far cheaper than the anomalous 36.42-hr resnet50 run. With 5 experiments remaining, this high-value exploitation step is the best use of experiment 5.

Evidence: The two strongest signals from 5 experiments are (1) scvi_n200 >> pca_n2000 for RNA encoding (+7.1% acc, config_021 vs config_001) and (2) transformer > avgpool for aggregation (+1.9% acc, config_049 vs config_021). The current best (config_049: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) achieves 0.7250 acc at only 3.60 GPU hrs. The key remaining uncertainty is whether scgpt could outperform scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder — both are learned encoders but with different architectures, and no scgpt+transformer+weighted combination has been tested yet. config_043 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is a clean A/B test against config_049, changing only the RNA encoder while holding all other parameters at their best-known values. If scgpt wins, we get a new best; if not, we confirm scvi_n200 is optimal and can focus remaining budget on finer-tuning other dimensions. Expected cost: similar to config_049 (~4–6 GPU hrs) since scgpt is a learned encoder of comparable complexity to scvi_n200, and the transformer aggregation + ViT-L image encoder are the same. This is the highest-information experiment available: it resolves the most impactful untested design choice while preserving all known best settings.

The current best (config_049: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc=0.725) strongly suggests that scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, and transformer aggregation are the key ingredients. However, the fusion mechanism (weighted vs concat) has only been tested with avgpool aggregation (where weighted narrowly beat concat: 0.635 vs 0.629). The interaction between transformer aggregation and concat fusion is completely untested. Config_009 is a single-variable change from the current best (weighted→concat), directly probing whether the transformer's learned token interactions might pair better with a simple concat than with a learned weighted sum. This is a high-value exploitation step: if concat matches or beats weighted, it confirms the ceiling of this architecture family; if weighted clearly wins, it locks in the best configuration and frees remaining budget for a different exploration axis. Expected cost is very similar to config_049 (~3.5–4.5 GPU hours), since the architecture (scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer) is identical and only the final fusion layer changes.

Evidence: The top-3 results (config_049: 0.725, config_009: 0.721, config_021: 0.706) all use scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile, with transformer aggregation and weighted fusion being the best combination. The 2×2 grid of (aggregation × fusion) for this encoder pair is nearly complete—only avgpool+concat (config_020) remains untested. Question: Does avgpool+concat close the gap to transformer+weighted, or does it confirm that transformer aggregation is the critical factor? Why this experiment: It is the cheapest remaining way to fully characterize the best encoder family (~4–5 GPU hours, comparable to config_021 at 4.82 and config_009 at 4.65), reducing uncertainty before the final two experiments. Given that transformer already outperforms avgpool by ~0.019 and weighted slightly edges concat, config_020 is unlikely to beat 0.725, but completing the grid gives high-confidence evidence that config_049 is the optimum in this design space, allowing the remaining budget to be spent on a targeted exploration (e.g., singleprofile ablation) rather than redundant testing. Expected relative cost: low, roughly 4–5 GPU hours, consistent with other vit_l + scvi_n200 multiprofile runs.

Evidence: The top-4 configurations all use scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile, with transformer+weighted (config_049, 0.725) as the best. All four aggregation×fusion combinations for that exact encoder pair have been tested. The remaining uncertainty is whether the transformer+weighted advantage is specific to imagenet_vit_l or generalizable across image encoders. This experiment (config_013: scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted) tests that interaction directly. It is the best use of experiment 9 because: (1) it is the highest-expected-accuracy untested configuration that extends the proven best architecture family, (2) it is cost-effective—resnet50 is substantially cheaper than imagenet_vit_l, so expected training cost is ~3–5 GPU hours (low relative to the 68.41 already spent), and (3) if it confirms the transformer+weighted boost is encoder-agnostic, it validates our ceiling estimate for the final experiment; if it underperforms significantly, it confirms imagenet_vit_l is essential and we can be confident 0.725 is near the practical maximum, making the last experiment a confirmation rather than a gamble.

Evidence: The top-5 configs all use scvi_n200 + multiprofile, with transformer aggregation and weighted fusion yielding the best accuracy (config_049: 0.724989). Notably, config_013 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted) achieved the highest F1 of any experiment (0.694524) despite slightly lower accuracy (0.713087), suggesting resnet50 captures complementary spatial features. Question: Does the resnet50 + transformer combination with concat fusion (rather than weighted) unlock a different accuracy/F1 tradeoff that could approach or exceed 0.725? This is the only untested multiprofile scvi_n200 configuration combining transformer aggregation with resnet50 and concat fusion. Rationale: As the final experiment, this is the most logical exploitation of the proven scvi_n200 + transformer family while testing the one unexplored image-encoder/fusion pairing that showed the strongest F1 signal. Expected cost is moderate (~5-6 GPU hours), comparable to config_013 (6.22) and config_009 (4.65), keeping total budget reasonable.

With no prior evidence, the first experiment must establish a strong multimodal baseline and reduce uncertainty about the most impactful design choices. config_008 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, transformer, weighted) tests the core hypothesis that combining RNA and image features with multiprofile transformer aggregation yields strong accuracy. It uses pca_n2000 (moderate-cost, 2000-dim linear representation) and resnet50 (solid but cheaper than ViT-L) to keep cost manageable while the transformer aggregation is the key expressive component being validated. If this performs well, it justifies investing in more expensive encoders (scgpt, ViT-L) in later experiments; if it underperforms, it signals that simpler aggregation or different encoders may suffice. Expected relative cost: moderate-to-high — transformer aggregation and multiprofile processing add overhead, but avoiding ViT-L and scgpt keeps it well below the most expensive configurations (e.g., config_041/035).

With only one completed experiment (config_008: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, transformer, weighted → 0.573 acc, 6.61 GPU-hrs), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality is actually contributing to performance or whether the RNA signal alone suffices. config_029 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, transformer) isolates this by removing the image encoder while keeping the same RNA encoder and transformer aggregation, making it a clean ablation. If RNA-only approaches or exceeds 0.573, the search can pivot toward cheaper unimodal or simpler multimodal configs; if it falls well short, multimodal fusion is confirmed as essential and I can focus remaining budget on optimizing image encoder and fusion strategy. Expected relative cost: roughly 3–4 GPU hours (no image encoder, but retains transformer aggregation and multiprofile processing), about half of config_008, preserving budget for subsequent experiments.

Evidence: config_008 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, transformer, weighted) is our best at 0.5729 acc but costs 6.61 GPU hrs, largely due to transformer aggregation. The RNA-only baseline (0.5191) confirms multimodal adds ~5% value. Question: Is the expensive transformer aggregation actually necessary, or does simple average pooling (avgpool) capture most of the multiprofile information at a fraction of the cost? This experiment (config_007) is a clean single-variable ablation of config_008 (transformer→avgpool, everything else identical), directly testing whether the ~4+ GPU hr premium of the transformer is justified. If avgpool matches or nearly matches 0.5729, we unlock much cheaper multimodal configs for the remaining 7 experiments, preserving budget for exploring image encoders and RNA encoders. If it falls short, we confirm transformer aggregation is critical and can confidently invest remaining budget in transformer-based variants. Expected cost: ~2–3 GPU hrs (roughly 40–50% of config_008), making it a high-information, low-cost experiment that reduces uncertainty about the most expensive architectural component before committing further budget.

Evidence: config_007 (avgpool + weighted fusion, pca_n2000, resnet50) achieved the best accuracy (0.639), and avgpool clearly outperforms transformer aggregation (0.639 vs 0.573 in config_008). The fusion method (weighted vs concat) is an untested design axis within the best-known architecture. This experiment tests whether concat fusion can match or exceed weighted fusion while keeping all other hyperparameters at their proven-best values (multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool). It is the most targeted, low-uncertainty next step: a single-variable change from the current best. If concat improves accuracy, it opens a new direction; if not, we confirm weighted fusion is optimal and can pivot to testing stronger image encoders (ViT-L) or learned RNA encoders. Expected cost: similar to config_007 (~10-11 GPU hours), since the architecture is identical except for the fusion operation (concat vs weighted average), making it a moderate-cost experiment relative to the budget.

Evidence: config_007 (pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the best at 0.639 acc, clearly outperforming transformer aggregation (0.573) and concat fusion (0.619). Multimodal strongly beats RNA-only (0.639 vs 0.519). The main untested lever within the proven avgpool+weighted recipe is the image encoder: upgrading from ResNet50 to ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L could yield a meaningful accuracy gain since image features are a key multimodal signal. Question: Does a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) push accuracy above 0.639 while keeping the cheap, proven avgpool+weighted pipeline? This is a single-variable extension of the best config, making results interpretable. Cost: ViT-L is ~300M params vs ResNet50's ~25M, so I estimate ~18–25 GPU hours—moderately more expensive than config_007 (10.6) but far cheaper than the concat-fusion configs (~36). With 5 experiments remaining, this is the highest-value exploitation step: it tests the most impactful unexplored axis (image encoder quality) within the already-validated architecture, and a positive result would set up further refinement (e.g., RNA encoder upgrade) in subsequent runs.

The top-3 experiments (config_007: 0.639, config_026: 0.635, config_002: 0.619) all share avgpool aggregation + weighted/concat fusion + multiprofile, establishing that this architecture is the clear winner over transformer aggregation (0.573) and rna_only (0.519). The one major unexplored variable within this winning architecture is the RNA encoder: all top results use pca_n2000. Config_009 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable swap from the best config (config_007), testing whether a learned variational RNA representation can outperform PCA while keeping the proven avgpool+weighted+resnet50 backbone. This is the highest-information experiment: if scvi_n200 improves accuracy, it opens a promising exploitation path for the remaining 4 experiments (e.g., pairing scvi with other image encoders); if it does not, PCA is confirmed as sufficient and we can focus remaining budget on fine-tuning other axes. Expected cost is similar to config_007 (~10–12 GPU hours) since the downstream architecture is identical and scvi_n200 produces the same 200-dim representation dimensionality.

The best result so far is config_009 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.6776, 5.90 GPU hrs). The key evidence is: (1) scvi_n200 substantially outperforms pca_n2000 (~4% gain), (2) avgpool beats transformer aggregation, and (3) weighted fusion beats concat. The main remaining uncertainty is whether imagenet_vit_l can match or exceed resnet50 as the image encoder in the scvi_n200 context. With pca_n2000, the two image encoders were nearly tied (0.6390 vs 0.6352), and imagenet_vit_l was cheaper (7.02 vs 10.60 GPU hrs). config_034 tests this exact swap while keeping all other settings at their proven-best values. If it matches or beats config_009, we get a cheaper top configuration; if it falls short, we confirm resnet50 is optimal and can direct the remaining 2 experiments toward other levers (e.g., singleprofile or scgpt). Expected relative cost: moderate, roughly 6–8 GPU hours (comparable to config_026's 7.02 hrs, since it uses imagenet_vit_l with avgpool+weighted fusion, avoiding the expensive concat pathway).

The current best (config_034, acc=0.706) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, and all evidence points to these being the optimal choices for each dimension. However, scgpt as an RNA encoder has never been tested in any multimodal setting. Config_012 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is the direct logical extension: it swaps only the RNA encoder to scgpt while keeping all other proven-best components. This tests whether scgpt's richer learned representations could surpass scvi_n200's 0.706 accuracy. If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, we gain a new best; if not, we confirm scvi_n200 is optimal and can use the final experiment for a minor refinement (e.g., config_032 to check transformer aggregation). This is the highest-information experiment remaining because it explores the last untested major design axis. Expected cost is moderate (~6-8 GPU hours), slightly higher than config_034 (4.82) due to scgpt's larger model size, but well within budget.

Evidence: config_034 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) is the clear best at 0.706 accuracy. Across all comparisons, avgpool has outperformed transformer (e.g., 0.639 vs 0.573 with pca_n2000+resnet50), but that gap was measured with PCA embeddings. scvi_n200 produces learned, richer representations that may benefit more from attention-based (transformer) aggregation to selectively weight profile interactions. Question: Can transformer aggregation with the strongest encoder pair (scvi_n200 + vit_l) close or surpass the avgpool result? Why this experiment: It is the single most informative untested variation of the best configuration—only the aggregation method changes. If it beats 0.706, it meaningfully improves the final answer; if it does not, it confirms avgpool is optimal and the remaining experiment can be spent on a longer-shot alternative (e.g., singleprofile). Expected relative cost: moderate, roughly 7–9 GPU hours (transformer adds attention computation over avgpool's 4.82 h, but vit_l and scvi_n200 are already in the pipeline), which is acceptable given the high information value.

The strongest evidence across 9 experiments points to scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer aggregation + multiprofile as the optimal architecture, with config_032 (weighted fusion) achieving 0.7250. The only untested variant of this proven-optimal combination is config_036, which swaps weighted fusion for concat. While weighted has generally outperformed concat (config_007 vs config_002), the interaction between transformer-generated contextual representations and concat fusion is untested and could yield a different inductive bias for the final classifier. As the final experiment, this is the highest-probability candidate to either beat 0.7250 or confirm config_032 as the best. Expected cost is similar to config_032 (~3.6 GPU hours) since the architecture is identical and only the fusion operation changes, bringing total budget to ~82.5 GPU hours.

With no prior experiments, the most critical uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion (RNA + image) provides a meaningful accuracy gain over single-modality approaches, and which encoder pairings are viable. config_004 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) directly tests this core hypothesis with a balanced, moderate-cost setup: scvi_n200 captures learned biological structure in the RNA space (more informative than PCA for downstream fusion), resnet50 is a well-established and relatively cheap image backbone, singleprofile keeps training cost low, and concat is the simplest fusion strategy to establish a baseline. This experiment will (1) confirm whether the multimodal pipeline yields a usable accuracy signal, (2) provide a reference point to later compare against RNA-only or image-only baselines, and (3) inform whether upgrading to multiprofile, transformer aggregation, or ViT-L is worthwhile in subsequent experiments. Expected relative cost: moderate — lower than multiprofile + transformer + ViT-L configurations but higher than PCA + resnet50 singleprofile setups, making it an efficient first probe of the search space.

Evidence: We have only one data point (config_004: multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat → acc 0.536, 0.56 GPU hrs). This is moderate and we don't yet know which design axis is most limiting. Question: config_031 is a clean single-variable ablation of config_004, swapping only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l while keeping scvi_n200, singleprofile, and concat fusion identical. This directly tests whether a stronger, pre-trained vision transformer encoder meaningfully improves multimodal accuracy over a standard CNN. Why this is the best next step: the image encoder is likely the largest single lever for cellular profiling performance (ViT-L captures richer spatial/morphological features than ResNet-50), and isolating this variable gives us a clear signal to guide the remaining 7 experiments. If it substantially improves over 0.536, we can exploit the ViT-L direction; if not, we redirect effort toward RNA encoder or multiprofile aggregation. Expected relative cost: moderate — imagenet_vit_l is roughly 2-3× the compute of resnet50, but with no aggregation overhead (singleprofile), total training should be around 1.0–1.5 GPU hours, well within budget.

Evidence: Both completed experiments (config_004, config_031) are multimodal singleprofile with scvi_n200 and concat fusion, achieving ~53.2-53.6% accuracy. The image encoder choice (resnet50 vs vit_l) shows negligible difference, so that axis is largely resolved. The major unexplored axis is multiprofile aggregation, which could substantially change how cellular profiles are combined. This experiment (config_011) is the minimal logical extension of our best result (config_004): it adds multiprofile with avgpool aggregation while keeping scvi_n200, resnet50, and concat fusion fixed, isolating the effect of profile aggregation. This is the best use of experiment 3 because resolving whether multiprofile helps (and by how much) will determine whether to invest remaining budget in multiprofile+transformer variants or stay in singleprofile space. Expected cost: ~0.7-0.8 GPU hours (multiprofile data loading and avgpool aggregation add moderate overhead over the 0.56h singleprofile baseline, but avgpool is far cheaper than transformer aggregation).

Evidence: config_011 (multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.632 accuracy, a ~10% jump over singleprofile baselines (~0.53), establishing multiprofile as the dominant design choice. The singleprofile image-encoder swap (resnet50→ViT, config_004 vs 031) showed negligible difference, but that was in a weaker regime; in multiprofile, stronger per-profile image representations may matter more when aggregating across profiles. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l improve accuracy in the multiprofile setting while keeping all other variables (scvi_n200, avgpool, concat) fixed? This isolates the image-encoder contribution. Why this experiment: It is the cleanest single-variable extension of our best result, directly testing the most natural next improvement. If it helps, we have a clear path to push accuracy higher; if not, we rule out the image encoder and pivot to aggregation (transformer) or fusion (weighted) in subsequent experiments. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_011's 7.27 GPU hrs—ViT-L adds per-image overhead across multiple profiles, so I estimate ~8.5–9.5 GPU hrs, which is acceptable given 6 experiments remain and the potential accuracy gain justifies the spend.

Evidence: config_051 (multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is our clear best at 0.715 acc, far exceeding singleprofile configs (~0.53) and the resnet50 multiprofile variant (0.632). The key winning factors are multiprofile + ViT-L image encoder + avgpool aggregation. Question: Can a transformer-based aggregation of multiple profiles outperform simple average pooling by capturing non-linear inter-profile interactions? This experiment (config_003) isolates that single variable—changing only aggregation from avgpool to transformer while keeping the proven scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, and concat fusion—making it the cleanest logical extension of our best result. Why now: With 5 experiments remaining, exploiting the strongest direction is justified; transformer aggregation is the most likely architectural upgrade to push accuracy above 0.715. Expected relative cost: moderately higher than config_051 (4.49 GPU hrs) due to the transformer attention layers over profiles, likely ~6–8 GPU hours, which is affordable within our remaining budget.

The current best is config_003 (acc 0.721, F1 0.681) using scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer aggregation + concat fusion in multiprofile mode. The single most direct untested variation in this proven architecture is swapping concat for weighted fusion (config_035). All other dimensions (RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, profile setting) are held at their best-known values, isolating the fusion mechanism as the variable. This is low-risk exploitation: if weighted fusion helps, we get a new best; if not, we confirm concat is optimal for this architecture and can pivot to exploring alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scgpt in config_008) in remaining budget. Expected cost is similar to config_003 (~4.6 GPU hours) since the architecture is identical and weighted fusion is a lightweight linear combination, making this a moderate-cost experiment that directly targets the top of the accuracy landscape.

The current best (config_035: scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) achieves 0.725 accuracy. All six completed experiments use scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder, so the RNA encoder choice is the most important untested variable in the best-performing architecture context. config_044 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) directly tests whether a different learned RNA representation (scgpt, a generative model vs. scvi's variational model) can improve on 0.725 while keeping the proven-best image encoder, aggregation, and fusion. This is the highest-information experiment: if scgpt wins, we've found a new best and can exploit it in remaining experiments; if it loses, we confirm scvi_n200 is optimal and can focus remaining budget on minor refinements. Expected cost is moderate (~4-6 GPU hours), comparable to config_003 (4.65 h) and config_035 (3.60 h), since scgpt and scvi_n200 are both learned encoders of similar scale paired with ViT-L and transformer aggregation.

The current best (config_035: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted; acc=0.7250) uses all empirically validated winning components. The only remaining untested configuration in the scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile space is config_036 (avgpool, weighted). Testing it completes the 2×2 grid of aggregation×fusion for this encoder pair and directly clarifies whether the modest transformer-over-avgpool gain seen in config_003 vs config_051 (0.7207 vs 0.7150) holds under weighted fusion, or whether avgpool+weighted is a near-equivalent, cheaper alternative. This is the best use of experiment 8 because: (1) it exploits the strongest evidence (scvi_n200 + vit_l + multiprofile is clearly the winning combination, with scgpt performing catastrophically at 0.52), (2) it reduces residual uncertainty about whether transformer aggregation is truly necessary or if a cheaper avgpool suffices, and (3) it is relatively low-cost (avgpool is cheaper than transformer; expected ~3.0–3.5 GPU hours vs 3.60 for config_035), preserving budget for the final 2 experiments. If config_036 matches config_035 within noise, we confirm the plateau and can spend remaining budget on a cheap confirmation; if it lags, we lock in config_035 as optimal with high confidence.

Evidence: The top-4 configs all use multimodal + multiprofile + imagenet_vit_l, with the best being config_035 (scvi_n200 + transformer + weighted, acc=0.725). scvi_n200 has dominated as the RNA encoder, but PCA_n2000 has never been paired with the proven-best image/aggregation/fusion stack (VIT_L + transformer + weighted). Uncertainty: It is unclear whether a simpler linear encoder (PCA) could match or slightly exceed the learned VAE (scvi) in this high-capacity multimodal setting, possibly by reducing overfitting on the RNA branch. This experiment (config_024) directly tests that question by swapping only the RNA encoder in the best-performing pipeline. It is the best use of experiment 9 because it is the single highest-information test remaining: if PCA matches scvi, we confirm a cheaper alternative; if it falls short, we confirm scvi_n200 is essential and can spend the final experiment on a minor perturbation of config_035. Expected cost: PCA_n2000 avoids VAE training, so this should be moderately cheaper than config_035 (3.60 GPU hrs), estimated around 2.5–3.2 GPU hrs, keeping total budget well within range.

Evidence: The best configuration found is config_035 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) at 0.7250 accuracy. The data clearly shows scvi_n200 >> pca_n2000/scgpt for RNA, imagenet_vit_l > resnet50 for image, and multiprofile >> singleprofile. No untested configuration replicates the full optimal combination. Among untested configs, config_022 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) has the highest expected accuracy (~0.64-0.66) because it retains the best RNA encoder, best aggregation, and best fusion—only the image encoder is downgraded. This experiment tests whether the transformer+weighted aggregation/fusion combination generalizes across image encoders, confirming that the imagenet_vit_l encoder is the primary driver of the performance gap (config_011 with resnet50+avgpool+concat gave 0.6315, and the encoder swap to imagenet_vit_l contributed ~0.09 of the total gain to 0.725). As the final experiment, it cannot beat config_035 but provides the strongest confirmation of the design hierarchy. Expected cost: moderate-to-high (~5-7 GPU hours) due to multiprofile processing with transformer aggregation, comparable to config_011 (7.27) but potentially lower since transformer aggregation over resnet50 features may be less expensive than avgpool over the same.

With no prior evidence, the most important question is whether a multimodal fusion of RNA and image features provides a meaningful accuracy advantage over single-modality baselines, and what a reasonable 'strong default' performance looks like. config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is chosen because: (1) it tests the core multimodal hypothesis with two well-established, pretrained representations (PCA for RNA, ViT-L for images) that require no additional encoder training; (2) avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion are the simplest, lowest-risk choices, reducing the chance of a poor result due to architectural complexity; (3) it serves as a strong baseline against which I can later compare learned RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt), transformer aggregation, and concat fusion.
