Expected relative cost: medium — ViT-L forward passes dominate, but the absence of a transformer aggregation layer and a learned RNA encoder keeps training time well below the most expensive configs (e.g., those with transformer + scgpt). This leaves ample GPU budget for the remaining 9 experiments to explore more complex variants.

Evidence: config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) achieved 0.635 acc / 0.618 F1 at 7.02 GPU hours. With only one data point, the most critical uncertainty is whether the expensive ViT-L image encoder is actually necessary or whether a cheaper ResNet50 backbone would yield comparable accuracy. Question tested: config_036 changes exactly one variable from config_004 (imagenet_vit_l → resnet50), holding all other settings identical (pca_n2000, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile, multimodal). This clean ablation isolates the image-encoder effect. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) If ResNet50 matches or nearly matches ViT-L accuracy, every subsequent multimodal experiment becomes ~40-50% cheaper, freeing GPU budget for more informative experiments within the 8 remaining slots. (2) If ResNet50 is clearly worse, we confirm ViT-L is essential and can focus remaining budget on RNA-encoder and aggregation choices. (3) The cost/accuracy tradeoff of the image backbone is the highest-leverage design decision for the rest of the search because it affects the cost of all future multimodal runs. Expected relative cost: ~3-4 GPU hours (roughly 50-55% of config_004's 7.02), since ResNet50 (~25M params) is substantially smaller than ViT-L (~300M params) while the RNA and aggregation pipelines remain the same.

Both completed experiments (config_004, config_036) used avgpool aggregation and achieved ~0.635–0.639 accuracy. The only difference between them was the image encoder (resnet50 slightly better), which is a small gap. The largest untested design dimension for multiprofile settings is the aggregation method: transformer aggregation can model inter-profile dependencies that avgpool discards. config_013 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while keeping the otherwise-best settings (pca_n2000, resnet50, weighted fusion), making it a clean single-variable test. This is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact choice: if transformer aggregation helps, it could unlock meaningful accuracy gains across many downstream configs; if it doesn't, we confirm avgpool suffices and can focus remaining budget on other axes (RNA encoder, fusion). Expected cost: transformer attention over multiple profiles adds overhead on top of config_036's 10.60 GPU-hr baseline, so I estimate ~13–15 GPU hours—moderately more expensive but justified by the potential accuracy lift and the information gained for the remaining 6 experiments.

Evidence: All three completed experiments used pca_n2000 (linear) as the RNA encoder, with the best result being 0.639 (config_036: resnet50, avgpool, weighted). Transformer aggregation was clearly worse (0.573), confirming avgpool is the right choice. The image encoder (vit_l vs resnet50) made negligible difference (~0.004), suggesting the RNA representation is the more likely bottleneck. Question: Will a learned non-linear RNA encoder (scvi_n200, a VAE trained on single-cell data) improve over linear PCA while keeping the proven resnet50/avgpool/weighted architecture? Why this experiment: It isolates the single most unexplored high-impact dimension (RNA encoder) within the best-performing architectural shell, reducing uncertainty about whether non-linear RNA features can push accuracy above 0.639. Expected cost: moderate — scvi_n200 adds a small VAE training overhead compared to PCA, so I estimate ~11–12 GPU hours, comparable to config_036 (10.6). This is a focused exploitation of the best-known architecture with one targeted variable change, making it the highest-information experiment for the remaining 6 slots.

The strongest evidence so far is that scvi_n200 dramatically outperforms pca_n2000 for RNA encoding (0.6776 vs ~0.635-0.639), and avgpool aggregation is clearly superior to transformer (0.635-0.678 vs 0.573). The best configuration (config_038: scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted) achieved 0.6776 at a modest 5.90 GPU hours. The key remaining uncertainty is whether the larger imagenet_vit_l image encoder can further boost performance when paired with the superior scvi_n200 RNA encoder. config_001 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) is the most direct exploitation of the winning direction, testing only the image encoder swap. With pca_n2000, ViT-L and ResNet50 were nearly tied (0.635 vs 0.639), but with a stronger RNA branch, the richer image features from ViT-L may provide a larger complementary signal. Expected cost is moderate (~7-8 GPU hours), comparable to config_004, since ViT-L is the main cost driver and scvi_n200 is cheaper than pca_n2000. This is the highest-value next experiment: it either confirms resnet50 is sufficient (saving budget) or reveals a new best configuration to build upon in the remaining 5 experiments.

Evidence: config_001 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) is the clear best at 0.706 acc, and scvi_n200 consistently outperforms pca_n2000 (~4-7% gap) while imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 with scvi_n200. Transformer aggregation showed a large penalty (config_013: 0.573 vs config_036: 0.639), so avgpool is well-supported. The only untested dimension within this best-performing region is the fusion method (we've only seen 'weighted'). This experiment tests whether concat fusion can match or exceed weighted fusion with the same strong backbone. It is the most direct, low-risk exploitation of the current best configuration, testing a single variable change. Expected cost is similar to config_001 (~4.5–5.5 GPU hours) since the architecture is identical apart from the fusion head, making it a cheap, high-information experiment that either finds a new best or confirms weighted fusion is optimal before we spend remaining budget on broader exploration.

Evidence: The strongest results (0.7062–0.7150) all use scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool, with concat fusion outperforming weighted by ~0.9%. The RNA encoder is the largest untested dimension—scgpt has never been evaluated. This experiment tests whether scgpt, paired with the proven-best image encoder (ViT-L), aggregation (avgpool), and fusion (concat), can surpass the current best (config_042, 0.7150). It is the best next step because it isolates the single most impactful unexplored variable while holding all other components at their empirically validated settings, reducing confounds. If scgpt matches or beats scvi_n200, the remaining 3 experiments can exploit that finding (e.g., testing transformer aggregation or singleprofile variants around scgpt). Expected relative cost: comparable to config_042 (~4.5 GPU hours), since it shares the same image encoder, aggregation, and fusion strategy; scgpt training cost should be in the same range as scvi_n200.

The current best (config_042, 0.7150) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat in multiprofile mode. All 7 completed experiments are multiprofile, so the profile-setting axis is completely unexplored for this best encoder/fusion pair. config_021 tests the singleprofile variant (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat, no aggregation), which removes the multiprofile averaging step. This is the most important remaining design uncertainty: if singleprofile matches or exceeds 0.7150, it simplifies the pipeline; if it underperforms, it confirms multiprofile is essential and we can lock in config_042 as the final answer with remaining budget. Expected cost is moderate (~3–4 GPU hours), slightly below config_042's 4.49 h since no multiprofile aggregation is needed, making it a low-risk, high-information experiment with 2 runs still remaining to exploit or pivot.

The current best is config_042 (scvi_n200, vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy. Evidence strongly supports scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + concat as the optimal recipe. The one untested dimension within this recipe is aggregation: transformer vs. avgpool. The only prior transformer test (config_013, 0.573) used weaker encoders (pca_n2000, resnet50), so it doesn't rule out transformer aggregation with the stronger scvi_n200/vit_l pair. Config_029 (scvi_n200, vit_l, transformer, concat) directly tests whether a transformer aggregator can exploit the richer per-profile representations from these encoders to exceed 0.715. This is the highest-value experiment: if it succeeds, it sets a new best; if it fails, it confirms avgpool is optimal and we can confidently lock in config_042 for the final experiment. Expected cost is moderate (~7–8 GPU hours, slightly above config_042's 4.49 due to transformer self-attention over profiles), keeping total budget well within reason.

Evidence: The top-3 results (config_029: 0.7207, config_042: 0.7150, config_001: 0.7062) all share scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile, and consistently show concat > weighted fusion and transformer ≥ avgpool aggregation. config_012 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is the only untested variant in this best-performing 2×2 aggregation×fusion grid. Question: Does transformer aggregation provide a benefit even with weighted fusion, or is the concat+transformer synergy specific to concat? While the evidence strongly favors concat (0.715 vs 0.706 at avgpool), testing this final cell completes the design-space picture and is the only remaining configuration that could theoretically exceed our current best of 0.7207. As the final experiment, this is the highest-expected-value exploitation choice. Expected cost: ~4.5–5 GPU hours (comparable to config_029 at 4.65 h and config_042 at 4.49 h, since it uses the same imagenet_vit_l encoder and transformer aggregation). Total budget would be ~56.5–57 GPU hours.

With no prior evidence, the first experiment should establish a strong upper-bound baseline to anchor all subsequent comparisons. config_001 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) combines the most powerful and well-motivated choices across every design axis: multimodal captures complementary RNA+image signal, multiprofile with transformer aggregation is the most expressive way to pool multiple cell profiles, scvi_n200 is the standard learned single-cell RNA representation, ViT-L is the strongest image encoder available, and weighted fusion lets the model learn modality importance. Testing this 'full-power' configuration first tells us the achievable ceiling; if it performs well, later experiments can ablate components (e.g., swap ViT-L→ResNet50, transformer→avgpool, multiprofile→singleprofile) to find cheaper near-equivalent configurations. If it underperforms, we learn early that the architecture needs rethinking. Expected relative cost: HIGH (ViT-L + transformer aggregation + multiprofile + scvi encoder makes this among the most expensive configurations in the search space), but justifiable as the first experiment since establishing the accuracy ceiling is the highest-value information to gain before spending the remaining 9 experiments on targeted ablations.

Evidence: config_001 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted fusion) achieved 72.5% accuracy at 3.60 GPU hours, giving us a single data point in a high-capacity region of the search space. The most important immediate question is whether the weighted fusion mechanism is actually contributing over a simpler concatenation, since all other components (encoders, aggregation, profile setting) are identical. This experiment (config_003) is a controlled A/B test changing only fusion from weighted to concat, directly testing whether the current best can be improved or confirmed. If concat matches or exceeds weighted, it opens a cheaper/simpler design axis; if weighted clearly wins, we can lock in that choice and explore other dimensions (RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation) in subsequent experiments. This is the best use of experiment 2 because it exploits the one strong signal we have with a minimal, interpretable change rather than jumping to a very different architecture, and it reduces uncertainty about a core design choice before we spend remaining budget on broader exploration. Expected relative cost: approximately equal to config_001 (~3.5–3.7 GPU hours), since the architecture and encoders are identical and only the fusion head differs.

Evidence: Both completed experiments (config_001, config_003) use the same architecture (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer) with only fusion differing (weighted > concat by ~0.4% acc). The current best is 72.5% acc at 3.60 GPU hrs. The largest untested variable is the image encoder: imagenet_vit_l is the most expensive component in the pipeline, and we have no evidence yet that a large ViT is necessary versus a lighter ResNet50. Question: Does replacing imagenet_vit_l with resnet50 (keeping scvi_n200, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, multiprofile all identical to config_001) significantly degrade accuracy, or is the performance comparable? This is a clean single-variable ablation. Rationale: With 7 experiments remaining, establishing whether the expensive ViT-L is truly needed is critical for both accuracy ceiling estimation and cost management. If ResNet50 matches within ~0.5%, we can redirect GPU budget toward exploring RNA encoders (scgpt, PCA) and aggregation strategies; if it degrades notably, we confirm ViT-L's importance and focus on other variables. Expected relative cost: moderate-to-low, roughly 2.0–2.5 GPU hours (ResNet50 is substantially smaller than ViT-Large), saving ~1+ GPU hour versus config_001 while providing high-information content about the image modality's contribution.

The current best (config_001, acc=0.725) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted in multiprofile mode. The single largest unexplored variable is the RNA encoder: we have only tested scvi_n200 across all three completed experiments. config_043 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) is a clean single-variable swap of the RNA encoder while holding all other components at their best-performing settings. This directly tests whether scgpt can match or exceed scvi_n200 in the top architecture, reducing uncertainty about a core design choice before we invest remaining budget in fine-tuning other axes (aggregation, profile setting, image encoder). If scgpt performs comparably, it opens a broader search space; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 as critical and we can focus remaining experiments on aggregation and profile-setting variants. Expected cost: moderate, roughly 4–5 GPU hours (scgpt is slightly heavier than scvi_n200, but the imagenet_vit_l + transformer pipeline matches config_001's 3.60 h baseline, so the total should be in a similar or slightly higher range).

Evidence: config_001 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) is our best at 0.725 acc, but all tested multimodal multiprofile configs use transformer aggregation. We have no data on whether avgpool aggregation would perform comparably with these same encoders. Question: Does transformer aggregation provide a meaningful accuracy gain over the simpler avgpool, or is it just adding compute cost? This experiment (config_027) is a clean single-variable ablation—identical to config_001 except aggregation changes from transformer to avgpool. Why now: With 5 experiments remaining, resolving whether transformer is necessary frees up budget (avgpool should be ~20-30% cheaper than transformer, estimated ~2.5-3.0 GPU hrs vs 3.60) and clarifies whether we should invest remaining experiments in other axes (RNA encoder, profile setting). If avgpool matches transformer, we save cost; if it falls short, we confirm transformer is essential and can focus exploitation on the remaining untested levers (pca_n2000, singleprofile) without ambiguity.

Evidence: The top-3 configs (config_001: 0.725, config_003: 0.721, config_015: 0.713) all use multimodal + multiprofile + transformer aggregation, and scvi_n200 clearly outperforms scgpt (0.725 vs 0.520). The one major untested variable in this best-performing family is the RNA encoder: we have not yet tested pca_n2000 paired with imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted. This experiment (config_011) directly tests whether a simpler PCA projection can match or exceed the learned scvi representation in the full multimodal pipeline. If pca_n2000 performs comparably, it would be a cheaper alternative; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 is essential and we can focus remaining budget on fine-tuning around config_001. Expected relative cost: low (~2–3 GPU hours), since PCA encoding is substantially lighter than scvi, making this a cost-efficient probe of a critical design axis with 4 experiments still remaining.

Evidence: All 6 completed experiments use multiprofile; the profile_setting dimension is completely unexplored. The best config (config_001: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.725 acc. Within multiprofile, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion are clearly superior to avgpool/concat, and scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l dominates other encoder pairs. Uncertainty: We do not know whether singleprofile (which eliminates the aggregation step entirely) could be competitive or even superior with the best encoders, or whether multiprofile's transformer aggregation is essential. This experiment (config_050: singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted) directly tests the profile_setting axis using the best-known components. It is also cheaper (no transformer aggregation, estimated ~2.0–2.5 GPU hours vs 3.60 for config_001). If it matches config_001, we gain a cost-effective alternative; if it underperforms, we confirm multiprofile is critical and can spend remaining budget confirming config_001 as the final answer. With 3 experiments left after this, resolving this key architectural question is the highest-value use of the next slot.

Evidence: The top-3 configs all share scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile, with transformer+weighted (0.725) > transformer+concat (0.721) > avgpool+weighted (0.706). The only untested combination for these two best encoders is avgpool+concat (config_036). Question: Does the avgpool+concat interaction produce a different (possibly better) result than the sum of its individual penalties? While both avgpool and concat were individually slightly inferior, completing the 2×2 grid eliminates residual uncertainty about whether a favorable interaction exists. Why this is the best use of experiment 8: It uses the two proven-best encoders, is likely the cheapest remaining option (~4.5–5 GPU hours, comparable to config_027 at 4.82), and if it does not beat 0.725 it definitively confirms config_001 as the optimal architecture, allowing the final 2 experiments to either validate or be spent on a cheap confirmation rather than further exploration. Expected relative cost: moderate (~4.5–5 GPU hours), lower than the resnet50+transformer alternatives (~6+ GPU hours).

Evidence: config_001 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) leads at 0.725 acc, with all four components individually validated as the best choices (scvi_n200 >> pca/scgpt; imagenet_vit_l > resnet50; transformer > avgpool; weighted ≥ concat). No remaining untested config combines all four best components, so beating 0.725 is unlikely. This experiment tests the closest untested variant—swapping imagenet_vit_l→resnet50 and weighted→concat while keeping the top RNA encoder and transformer aggregation—clarifying whether a cheaper image backbone with concat fusion can approach the best accuracy. It is the most informative remaining test because it isolates the combined effect of the two 'second-best' choices, directly informing the cost-accuracy tradeoff. Expected relative cost: moderate, roughly 4–6 GPU hours (resnet50+transformer previously cost 6.22 in config_015; concat fusion adds little overhead), which is comparable to or slightly below the imagenet_vit_l transformer runs.

Evidence: config_001 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + transformer + weighted) at 0.725 accuracy is the clear best, and all four aggregation×fusion combinations for this exact encoder pair have been tested. No untested configuration uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile, and every alternative (resnet50, pca_n2000, scgpt, singleprofile) has been shown to underperform by 1–20+ points. It is highly unlikely any untested config will exceed 0.725. Question: This final experiment provides a cheap RNA-only baseline (scvi_n200, singleprofile, no aggregation) to confirm the magnitude of the multimodal/multiprofile advantage and close the search. Why this is the best use: Since no untested config is expected to beat config_001, the priority shifts to minimizing total GPU hours. config_047 requires only the scvi_n200 RNA encoder on a single profile with no image processing or aggregation, making it the cheapest untested option (estimated ~0.5 GPU hours, well below the 3.6–6.2 hours of multimodal configs). This keeps the total budget near 37.4 GPU hours while still yielding a useful ablation data point.

With no prior evidence, the first experiment should establish a baseline for the multimodal approach (the study's primary hypothesis) using standard, well-understood components to reduce uncertainty about overall feasibility. config_001 uses multimodal + multiprofile with pca_n2000 (cheap, standard RNA representation), resnet50 (standard image encoder), avgpool (simple aggregation), and weighted fusion (common fusion strategy). This tests whether a straightforward multimodal pipeline achieves competitive validation accuracy and provides a reference point for all subsequent ablations (e.g., swapping encoders, aggregation, or fusion). It is a moderate-cost experiment—cheaper than configurations using imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, or scgpt—so it preserves GPU budget for more expensive explorations in later experiments. Starting here lets me quickly determine whether multimodal fusion is beneficial and which component (RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, fusion) is most likely to be the bottleneck, guiding the remaining 9 experiments efficiently.

Evidence: config_001 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieved 63.9% accuracy at 10.60 GPU hours, establishing a baseline. With only one data point, the most impactful uncertainty is whether the image encoder is a bottleneck in the multimodal pipeline. Question: config_006 is a single-variable change from config_001—only the image encoder is upgraded from ResNet50 to ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L—keeping PCA RNA encoder, average-pool aggregation, weighted fusion, and multiprofile setting identical. This cleanly isolates the contribution of a stronger visual feature extractor, which is likely a major performance driver in cellular imaging where spatial/morphological patterns matter. Rationale: Upgrading the image encoder is the highest-leverage single modification available; if ViT-L meaningfully improves accuracy, it anchors a promising direction for the remaining 8 experiments (e.g., pairing it with better RNA encoders or transformer aggregation). If it does not, we confirm ResNet50 suffices and redirect budget toward RNA-encoder or aggregation upgrades. Expected relative cost: moderate increase over config_001 (ViT-L is ~2× the parameter count of ResNet50), estimated at roughly 14–18 GPU hours, which is acceptable given the high information value of this comparison.

Evidence: Both completed experiments (config_001: 0.639, config_006: 0.635) use pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder with avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion, differing only in image encoder (resnet50 vs vit_l) with a negligible ~0.4% gap. This gives a baseline of ~0.635-0.639 but tells us nothing about whether the RNA representation is a bottleneck. Question: config_025 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 (linear, 2000-dim) to scvi_n200 (learned, 200-dim) while keeping resnet50, avgpool, weighted fusion, and multiprofile identical to the best config (config_001). This is a clean single-variable test of whether a learned, biologically-informed RNA representation outperforms a simple linear projection. Rationale: The RNA encoder is the most fundamental untested design axis; if scvi_n200 improves accuracy, it opens a rich exploitation path (scvi + transformer aggregation, scvi + vit_l, etc.). If it doesn't, we can rule out RNA representation as the bottleneck and focus on aggregation/fusion. With 7 experiments remaining, resolving this high-uncertainty dimension early is the best use of the next slot. Expected cost: scvi_n200 produces a 200-dim representation (vs 2000 for PCA), so the downstream multimodal model is smaller; I estimate ~8-10 GPU hours, roughly comparable to or slightly below config_001's 10.60.

Evidence: config_025 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted) is the clear best at 0.678 acc / 0.646 F1 and also the cheapest (5.90 GPU-h). The RNA encoder switch from pca_n2000→scvi_n200 gave a large +0.039 boost, while the image encoder swap (resnet50→imagenet_vit_l) with pca_n2000 was roughly neutral (0.639 vs 0.635). Question: does a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) interact beneficially with the scvi_n200 RNA encoder, where the representation is richer and may complement a more powerful visual backbone? This experiment (config_018) is a single-variable change from config_025 (resnet50→imagenet_vit_l), keeping everything else fixed, so any accuracy shift is cleanly attributable to the image encoder. It is the best use of experiment 4 because it directly extends the most promising direction, costs a moderate ~6–7 GPU hours (comparable to config_006's 7.02), and if it improves accuracy it identifies a new best baseline to further exploit in the remaining 6 experiments; if it does not, it confirms resnet50 suffices and we can pivot to aggregation/fusion changes next.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_018 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.706, cost=4.82 GPU hrs), which clearly outperforms all other tested setups. Both scvi_n200 and imagenet_vit_l are consistently superior to their alternatives. The remaining untested variation within this top encoder pair is the aggregation method: all completed experiments use avgpool, so we haven't tested whether transformer aggregation can capture richer inter-profile interactions. This experiment (config_024: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) isolates the aggregation change while keeping the proven weighted fusion, directly testing whether attention-based profile aggregation can push accuracy beyond 0.706. It is the highest-value exploitation step: it extends the single best result along the most promising unexplored axis. Expected relative cost: moderate increase over config_018 (est. ~6-9 GPU hrs) due to transformer attention over profiles, but the vit_l encoder dominates training cost so the increment is manageable. With 5 experiments remaining, this balances the risk of a large cost spike against the high probability of meaningful accuracy gain.

The current best is config_024 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc=0.7250, 3.60 GPU hrs). All completed experiments use weighted fusion; concat fusion is completely untested. config_002 is identical to config_024 except for fusion=concat, making it the most direct exploitation of the strongest configuration to test whether concatenating modality features (letting the classifier learn cross-modal interactions) outperforms weighted averaging. This reduces uncertainty on the last untested dimension of the best-known architecture. If concat improves accuracy, we gain a new best; if not, we confirm weighted fusion is optimal and can pivot to exploring scgpt RNA encoder in remaining experiments. Expected cost is ~3.5–4.0 GPU hours, essentially the same as config_024 since only the fusion head changes, keeping total budget well within limits.

The evidence strongly points to scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted as the best configuration (config_024, 0.725 acc). The only major untested design axis is the RNA encoder: scgpt has not been evaluated in any completed experiment. Config_041 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) directly tests whether the more expressive scgpt encoder can push accuracy beyond 0.725 in the already-validated best architecture. This is the highest-information experiment: if scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, we gain a new best and can exploit it in the remaining 3 slots; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 as optimal and can spend remaining budget on minor fusion/aggregation refinements. Expected relative cost: scgpt is a larger generative encoder than scvi_n200, so I estimate ~5–7 GPU hours (moderately above config_024's 3.60 h but well within budget), making it a reasonable investment given the potential accuracy gain.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_024 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) at 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. All experiments to date use multiprofile, so the profile-setting dimension is unexplored with the strongest component combination. scgpt is clearly inferior (0.520) and pca_n2000 is clearly worse than scvi_n200, so the RNA encoder space is well-characterized. Question: Does singleprofile (which removes the aggregation step entirely) with scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + weighted fusion match or exceed the multiprofile result? This tests whether the multiprofile aggregation adds genuine signal or whether a simpler single-profile pipeline avoids overfitting. Why this is the best use of experiment 8: It is the only remaining high-value architectural axis untested with the top-performing components, and it is likely cheaper (no aggregation step) at an estimated ~2.5–3.5 GPU hours, well below the multiprofile transformer configs. If it matches or beats 0.725, we have a cheaper best; if not, we confirm multiprofile is essential and can spend the final 2 experiments on fine-tuning around config_024 (e.g., testing config_022 or a small perturbation) with high confidence.

The current best is config_024 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc=0.7250). All top-performing components have been identified: scvi_n200 >> pca_n2000 >> scgpt for RNA, imagenet_vit_l > resnet50 for image, transformer > avgpool for aggregation, and weighted ≥ concat for fusion. No untested configuration combines all best components in a new way, so beating 0.7250 is unlikely. However, config_045 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) is the most informative remaining experiment: it tests whether the ~2% transformer-over-avgpool gain observed with scvi_n200 (0.7250 vs 0.7062) generalizes to pca_n2000, clarifying whether aggregation method interacts with RNA encoder quality. This completes a key cell in the encoder × aggregation grid and provides evidence for the final experiment's selection. Expected cost is moderate (~5–6 GPU hours), comparable to config_006 (7.02) but likely lower since transformer aggregation was cheaper than avgpool in prior runs (3.60 vs 4.82 for the scvi_n200/vit_l pair).

Evidence: The best result (config_024, 0.7250) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted + multiprofile. All major design choices (RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, fusion, profile) have been explored, and no untested configuration combines all four 'best' settings simultaneously. The only untested variant in the top-performing neighborhood that retains three of the four strongest choices (scvi_n200, transformer, weighted) while varying the image encoder is config_014 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted). This tests whether the transformer aggregation provides a similar boost with resnet50 as it did with imagenet_vit_l (config_018→config_024 gave +0.019), or whether the image encoder quality is the dominant factor. Since this is the final experiment and our best (0.7250) is unlikely to be surpassed by any remaining option, this is the most informative exploitation test in the high-accuracy region. Expected cost: moderate (~4–5 GPU hours, comparable to other transformer+resnet50 multiprofile runs), keeping total budget around ~49 GPU hours.

With no prior evidence, the most important uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion (RNA + image) meaningfully improves accuracy over single-modality baselines, and which encoder combination is strongest. config_005 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion) directly tests this core hypothesis using a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200) and a strong pretrained image encoder (ViT-L) with a simple concat fusion. It avoids the added cost of multiprofile aggregation, keeping training time moderate (estimated medium cost: ViT-L is the main expense, but single-profile and no aggregation module keep it well below the multiprofile+transformer configs). A strong result here establishes a high-accuracy reference and justifies investing later experiments in multiprofile aggregation and transformer fusion; a weak result would redirect exploration toward single-modality or alternative encoders. This is the best use of experiment 1 because it maximally reduces uncertainty about the central design axis (multimodal vs. unimodal, and encoder quality) while remaining cost-efficient enough to leave budget for follow-up exploitation.

Evidence: config_005 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieved only 0.532 accuracy at 0.62 GPU hours, leaving substantial room for improvement. The single most impactful untested lever is whether multiprofile aggregation unlocks additional information beyond a single profile. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile (with the same scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l encoders and concat fusion) meaningfully improve validation accuracy? config_031 changes exactly one architectural dimension (single→multiprofile with avgpool aggregation), giving a clean controlled comparison against the baseline. I choose avgpool over transformer aggregation because it is cheaper and sufficient to establish whether multiprofile helps at all; if it does, a transformer-aggregation variant can be tested as a logical follow-up. Expected cost: roughly 1.5–2.5× the 0.62 GPU-hour baseline (≈1–1.5 GPU hours) due to processing multiple profiles per cell, still well within budget. This is the best use of experiment 2 because it resolves the largest source of uncertainty (profile-level information) while keeping the comparison clean and the cost moderate, preserving budget for subsequent encoder and aggregation refinements.

Evidence: The jump from singleprofile (config_005, acc=0.532) to multiprofile with avgpool (config_031, acc=0.715) shows that profile aggregation is the dominant design lever, yielding ~18 points. The aggregation mechanism itself (avgpool) is a simple mean; a transformer aggregator can model inter-profile dependencies and may capture complementary information across profiles that avgpool discards. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool when all other components (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion, multiprofile) are held constant at the current best? This is a clean single-variable test of the highest-impact design choice. Rationale: With 7 experiments remaining, exploiting the strongest evidence (multiprofile + aggregation) by upgrading the aggregation to a more expressive mechanism is the best expected-value move. If transformer helps, it sets a new ceiling; if it doesn't, we've confirmed avgpool is sufficient and can pivot to fusion or encoder choices. Expected cost: transformer aggregation adds self-attention over profiles, so I estimate ~5.5–6.5 GPU hours (moderately higher than config_031's 4.49), which is affordable within the remaining budget and justified by the potential accuracy gain.

Evidence: Multiprofile is clearly superior to singleprofile (0.715–0.721 vs 0.532), and among multiprofile multimodal configs with scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation (config_032, acc=0.721) edges out avgpool (config_031, acc=0.715), though the gap is small and F1 slightly favors avgpool. The fusion method (concat vs weighted) is the primary untested dimension within this best-performing backbone. This experiment tests whether weighted fusion can improve over concat with the transformer-aggregated, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l setup—a direct logical extension of the current best. If weighted fusion helps, it could push accuracy above 0.721; if not, it confirms concat is sufficient and redirects effort toward encoder choices. Expected cost is comparable to config_032 (~4.7 GPU hrs), since weighted fusion adds only a small parameter overhead over concat with the same transformer aggregation.

Evidence: The top-3 configs (0.715–0.725) all share multiprofile + imagenet_vit_l + transformer aggregation, with weighted fusion giving the best result (config_001, 0.725). The remaining uncertainty is whether the RNA encoder (scvi_n200) is the bottleneck. Question: config_034 swaps scvi_n200 for scgpt while keeping the best-performing aggregation (transformer) and fusion (weighted) with imagenet_vit_l, directly testing whether a more expressive learned RNA encoder can push accuracy beyond 0.725. Why this is the best next experiment: it is the most targeted extension of the current best configuration, isolating the RNA encoder as the single variable. With 5 experiments remaining, committing to the most promising encoder swap maximizes the chance of finding a new best before budget runs out. Expected cost: ~4–5 GPU hours (scgpt encoder is comparable to or slightly heavier than scvi_n200; transformer aggregation with multiprofile and weighted fusion matches the ~3.6–4.7 h range seen in similar configs), which is acceptable given the potential accuracy gain.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_001 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc / 3.60 GPU hrs. RNA encoder choice shows enormous variance (scgpt drops accuracy to 0.520 vs scvi_n200 at 0.725), yet pca_n2000 — a fundamentally different linear encoder — has never been tested in the multiprofile multimodal setting. This experiment tests whether pca_n2000 can match or approach scvi_n200 while keeping all other hyperparameters at their best-known values (transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, imagenet_vit_l). Resolving the RNA encoder question is the highest-priority uncertainty: if pca_n2000 is competitive, it may offer a cheaper path; if it underperforms significantly, we confirm scvi_n200 is essential and can focus remaining budget on image-encoder variations (resnet50). Expected relative cost: pca_n2000 is a linear projection rather than a learned VAE, so training should be slightly cheaper than config_001, estimated around 2.5–3.5 GPU hours.

The evidence strongly supports scvi_n200 as the best RNA encoder (0.725 vs 0.52 for scgpt, 0.59 for pca_n2000), transformer aggregation (0.721 vs 0.715 for avgpool), and weighted fusion (0.725 vs 0.721 for concat). The current best (config_001, 0.725) uses imagenet_vit_l, but we have not yet tested resnet50 with this optimal combination of scvi_n200 + transformer + weighted in multiprofile. Config_040 directly tests whether the lighter ResNet50 image encoder can match or approach ViT-L performance under the best other settings. If it performs comparably, it offers a cheaper path to the same accuracy; if it underperforms, it confirms ViT-L is necessary. This is the highest-information experiment remaining: it resolves the last major unexplored axis (image encoder) for the proven-best configuration. Expected relative cost: ResNet50 is substantially smaller than ViT-L, so I estimate ~2.5–3.0 GPU hours, cheaper than config_001's 3.60 hours.

The evidence strongly identifies scvi_n200 + multiprofile + imagenet_vit_l as the best encoder combination, with config_001 (transformer+weighted) at 0.725 as the current best. The 2×2 aggregation×fusion matrix for this combination is nearly complete: transformer+concat (0.721), transformer+weighted (0.725), avgpool+concat (0.715). Config_033 (avgpool+weighted) is the missing cell. Testing it clarifies whether the transformer aggregation is genuinely contributing or whether avgpool+weighted captures most of the benefit at lower cost. If config_033 lands near 0.725, it confirms a cheaper path and frees GPU budget for the remaining 2 experiments; if it drops to ~0.715, it confirms the transformer is necessary. Expected cost is moderate (~3.5–4.5 GPU hours, comparable to config_031's 4.49 for avgpool+concat and config_001's 3.60 for transformer+weighted), making it a cost-efficient experiment that reduces uncertainty about the aggregation choice without risking a large compute spend on a configuration unlikely to beat the current best.

The current best (config_001, acc=0.725) uses scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer + weighted + imagenet_vit_l. The strongest pattern is that transformer aggregation and scvi_n200 are consistently the best choices. The only untested scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer combination is config_050 (resnet50, transformer, concat). This tests whether the concat fusion (which outperformed weighted under avgpool in config_031 vs 033) might synergize differently with resnet50 under transformer aggregation, potentially closing the small gap to 0.725. It also clarifies whether resnet50's higher F1 (0.695 in config_040) reflects a genuinely competitive classifier that could be further improved. Expected cost is moderate-to-high (~5.5–6.5 GPU hours, comparable to config_040's 6.22) due to resnet50 + transformer processing. With only one experiment remaining after this, the result will directly inform whether the final experiment should exploit a near-best configuration or accept config_001 as the winner.

Evidence: The top-performing configurations all use scvi_n200 (RNA) + multiprofile, with transformer+weighted (config_001, 0.725) and transformer+concat (config_032, 0.721) as the best. Weighted fusion consistently outperforms concat with transformer aggregation, and scvi_n200 is the clear best RNA encoder. The only untested multimodal+multiprofile+scvi_n200 configs are config_016 (resnet50, avgpool, weighted) and config_049 (resnet50, avgpool, concat). Question: Whether the weighted-fusion advantage holds under avgpool aggregation with resnet50, providing a data point on the aggregation×fusion interaction for the resnet50 backbone. Why this is the best last experiment: It is the closest untested variant to the proven best-performing family (scvi_n200 + multiprofile + weighted fusion), giving the highest expected accuracy among remaining options (~0.70-0.71). It is unlikely to beat config_001's 0.725, but it is the most rational exploitation of existing evidence. Expected cost: moderate, roughly 4-5 GPU hours (avgpool is cheaper than transformer; resnet50 is comparable to vit_l), keeping total budget around 41-42 GPU hours.

With no prior evidence, the most important uncertainty is whether the full multimodal pipeline (best RNA encoder + best image encoder + expressive aggregation + multiprofile data) can achieve high validation accuracy, establishing a performance ceiling. config_001 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + transformer aggregation + concat fusion, multiprofile) is the strongest 'full-featured' multimodal configuration available. Testing it first gives the highest information gain: if it performs well, subsequent experiments can ablate individual components (e.g., swap ViT-L→ResNet50, transformer→avgpool, multiprofile→singleprofile) to identify which design choices drive accuracy; if it underperforms, I immediately know the ceiling is lower and should explore simpler or unimodal alternatives. This is the most expensive configuration (scgpt is a large generative pretrained encoder, ViT-L is a large vision transformer, transformer aggregation adds parameters, and multiprofile increases sequence length), so I expect it to be roughly 2–3× the GPU-hours of a singleprofile/ResNet50/avgpool baseline. However, as experiment 1 of 10, establishing the upper bound is the single most valuable piece of information for directing the remaining 9 experiments efficiently.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat → acc 0.507, F1 0.455, 3.95 GPU-hrs), the primary uncertainty is whether the transformer aggregation layer—the most computationally expensive component—is actually contributing to performance or simply adding overfitting risk and cost. Config_009 is a clean single-variable ablation of config_001 (transformer → avgpool, everything else identical), so any accuracy difference can be attributed to the aggregation strategy. If avgpool matches or exceeds 0.507, we can confidently drop transformer-based configs from the remaining 8 experiments, saving ~1–1.5 GPU-hrs each. If it is clearly worse, we confirm the transformer is necessary and can focus subsequent experiments on tuning around it. This is the highest-information-per-GPU-hour next step: it reduces uncertainty about the single most costly architectural choice while staying within the same multimodal + multiprofile direction. Expected relative cost: moderate (~2.5–3.0 GPU-hrs), roughly 20–30% cheaper than config_001 since avgpool is far lighter than a transformer while still processing the same heavy scgpt and ViT-L encoders.

Evidence: config_009 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is the best so far at 0.518 acc / 0.484 F1, outperforming config_001 (same but transformer aggregation) by ~1.1% acc and ~2.9% F1. The fusion strategy is the only untested variable within this otherwise-identical architecture. Question: Does weighted fusion (config_016) improve over simple concat while keeping the winning avgpool aggregation? This is a minimal, single-variable change from the current best, making it a clean exploitation step that will clarify whether fusion strategy is a meaningful lever. If weighted fusion helps, it opens a clear path to combine with other improvements; if not, we confirm concat is sufficient and can pivot to testing alternative encoders. Cost: expected ~7 GPU hours (same architecture as config_009, only fusion module changes), keeping total spend moderate with 7 experiments remaining.

Evidence: All three completed experiments share scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile, varying only aggregation and fusion. The clear winner is config_016 (avgpool + weighted, acc=0.542, cost=2.94). The major untested dimension is the RNA encoder: we have only tried scgpt. This experiment tests scvi_n200 (a VAE-based learned representation) in place of scgpt while holding the best-performing aggregation (avgpool), fusion (weighted), image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), and profile setting (multiprofile) constant. This isolates the effect of the RNA encoder and tells us whether the current best can be improved by switching to a different learned representation. It is the best use of experiment 4 because it reduces uncertainty on the single largest unexplored architectural axis while preserving the settings that already produced the best result, and it keeps 6 experiments to exploit whichever direction wins. Expected cost: scvi_n200 is a compact VAE (200-dim latent) and should train faster than scgpt, so I estimate ~2–3 GPU hours, comparable to or slightly below config_016's 2.94.

The strongest evidence so far is that switching the RNA encoder from scgpt to scvi_n200 produced a massive accuracy jump (0.542 → 0.706), making scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted (config_011) the clear best. The key uncertainty now is whether the aggregation method that was suboptimal for scgpt (transformer, 0.507 vs avgpool 0.518) could actually outperform avgpool when paired with scvi_n200's richer, more structured latent representations. Transformer aggregation can model inter-profile dependencies that avgpool discards, and this interaction with the encoder is the most plausible path to pushing accuracy beyond 0.706. Config_013 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) tests exactly this single variable change from the current best, keeping the proven weighted fusion. Expected cost is moderate (~5-6 GPU hours), slightly above config_011's 4.82 due to transformer aggregation overhead, but well within budget. With 5 experiments remaining, this is the highest-information experiment: if transformer helps, it opens a new optimization axis; if not, we confirm avgpool is the right aggregation and can focus remaining budget on image-encoder or other refinements.

The evidence strongly points to scvi_n200 + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion as the best-performing combination (config_013: 0.725 acc, 3.60 GPU hrs). The only major untested design axis within this top-performing family is the image encoder: all five completed experiments used imagenet_vit_l. Config_017 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted, multiprofile, multimodal) directly tests whether resnet50 can match or approach the ViT-L performance while keeping the same aggregation and fusion. This is the highest-value uncertainty to resolve: if resnet50 is competitive, we gain a cheaper configuration; if it lags significantly, we confirm ViT-L is essential and can focus remaining budget on fine-tuning around the current best. Expected cost is moderate (~3–3.5 GPU hrs), slightly below config_013 since ResNet50 (~25M params) is much lighter than ViT-L (~307M params), making this a cost-efficient exploration of the image-encoder dimension with 4 experiments still remaining.

Evidence: config_013 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) is the current best at 0.725 accuracy / 0.685 F1. All scvi_n200 multiprofile experiments confirm that transformer aggregation and weighted fusion are the top-performing choices, but concat fusion has never been tested with scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer. Question: Does concat fusion perform comparably to weighted fusion in the scvi_n200 regime, or is weighted clearly superior? This is a single-variable change from the best config, so it cleanly isolates the fusion effect. Rationale: This is the cheapest informative next step (~3.5–4 GPU hours, similar to config_013's 3.60), confirming whether our best config's fusion choice is robust. If concat is close, it gives flexibility; if it lags, we lock in weighted fusion with high confidence and can spend remaining budget on less certain directions (e.g., pca_n2000 or singleprofile variants). With 3 experiments left, a low-cost confirmation here preserves budget for higher-variance exploration.

The current best (config_013, 0.7250) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted. The largest remaining uncertainty is the RNA encoder: pca_n2000 has never been tested in any completed experiment. config_019 isolates this variable by pairing pca_n2000 with the known-best architecture (imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted), directly testing whether a high-dimensional linear encoder can match or exceed the nonlinear scVI encoder. If pca_n2000 performs comparably, it would be a cheaper encoder to build on; if it underperforms significantly, it confirms scvi_n200 is essential and the remaining 2 experiments should focus on fine-tuning around the scvi_n200 + transformer + weighted + imagenet_vit_l core. This is the highest-information experiment available: it reduces uncertainty on the single most impactful untested design axis while keeping the rest of the architecture at proven-optimal settings. Expected cost is moderate (~3–3.5 GPU hours), slightly below config_013's 3.60 since PCA projection is cheaper than scVI encoding, with the transformer aggregation and ViT-L image backbone dominating runtime.

Evidence: The current best is config_013 (scvi_n200, vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. All scvi_n200 multiprofile configs outperform scgpt and pca_n2000 by wide margins. Transformer aggregation consistently beats avgpool, and weighted fusion slightly edges concat (0.725 vs 0.721). However, config_017 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) achieved a notably higher F1 (0.695) than config_013 (0.685) despite lower accuracy, suggesting resnet50 features may complement transformer aggregation differently. Question: Does combining resnet50 with transformer aggregation and concat fusion (config_012) yield a configuration that matches or exceeds 0.725? This is the only untested scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer variant remaining, making it the highest-potential exploitation of the strong scvi_n200 + transformer evidence. Why best use of experiment 9: With only 2 experiments left, testing the closest untested neighbor of the current best maximizes the chance of finding a marginal improvement while the remaining experiment can serve as a fallback. Expected cost is moderate (~5–6 GPU hours, comparable to config_017's 6.22), keeping total budget manageable for the final experiment.

Evidence: scvi_n200 is the dominant RNA encoder (0.69–0.725 vs 0.51–0.59 for alternatives), imagenet_vit_l is the best image encoder, and multiprofile+multimodal is the proven best architecture. The current best is config_013 (scvi_n200 + vit_l + transformer + weighted = 0.725). All transformer-aggregation scvi_n200 multimodal multiprofile configs are already tested, so the remaining untested scvi_n200 multiprofile multimodal options all use avgpool. config_029 (scvi_n200 + vit_l + avgpool + concat) is the closest untested variant to the top performer, retaining both best encoders. It tests whether the small concat-vs-weighted gap seen with transformer (0.721 vs 0.725) persists with avgpool, and whether the ~0.019 transformer-over-avgpool penalty (config_013 vs config_011) is uniform across fusion types. Expected accuracy is ~0.70–0.71, unlikely to beat 0.725 but the highest among remaining options. Cost: avgpool aggregation is cheaper than transformer; config_011 (same encoders, avgpool, weighted) cost 4.82 GPU hrs, so config_029 is expected at roughly 3.5–4.5 GPU hrs—moderate cost. As the final experiment, this is the best use of the last slot: it confirms the robustness of the scvi_n200 + vit_l combination and provides the tightest bracket around the best-known configuration, while remaining cost-efficient.

With no prior evidence, the priority is to establish a clean multimodal baseline that is cheap and interpretable. config_001 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the simplest full multimodal configuration: PCA is nearly free, ResNet50 is a moderate-cost CNN, singleprofile avoids aggregation overhead, and concat is trivial. This experiment tests whether a straightforward multimodal fusion of standard features achieves a competitive accuracy, giving us a floor to compare against more expensive encoders (scgpt, ViT-L), multiprofile aggregation, and alternative fusion strategies in subsequent runs. It is the best use of experiment 1 because it is low-cost (expected relative cost: low, roughly 1× a baseline run), preserves GPU budget for the 9 remaining experiments, and immediately tells us whether the multimodal signal is strong enough to justify investing in heavier encoders and aggregation in later trials.

Evidence: config_001 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved only 52.7% validation accuracy at 0.85 GPU hours. With just one data point, the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality is actually contributing signal or adding noise. Question tested: config_045 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is a clean A/B comparison that removes only the image branch while keeping the RNA encoder, profile setting, and architecture identical to config_001. If RNA-alone matches or exceeds 52.7%, the image modality is not helping and I should redirect remaining budget toward RNA encoder upgrades (scgpt, scvi_n200) and multiprofile aggregation. If RNA-alone is substantially lower, multimodal fusion is confirmed valuable and I should prioritize image encoder (ViT-L) and fusion strategy improvements. Why this is the best next experiment: it is extremely cheap (~0.3–0.5 GPU hours, RNA-only with PCA and no image processing), so it costs a small fraction of the budget while resolving the single most consequential design question—whether to invest remaining experiments in multimodal or unimodal architectures. This information will shape the strategy for all 8 remaining experiments far more effectively than a small incremental change (e.g., switching concat→weighted fusion) or a costly multimodal variant that conflates multiple variables.

Evidence: config_001 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc, clearly outperforming the RNA-only baseline (0.485 acc), confirming that image information adds value. However, all tested configs use singleprofile; the multiprofile dimension is completely untested and represents a major architectural change that could significantly improve performance by aggregating information across multiple profiles. Question: Does multiprofile with avgpool aggregation improve over singleprofile when keeping the same encoders (pca_n2000, resnet50) and fusion (concat)? This isolates the multiprofile+aggregation effect cleanly. Rationale: With 7 experiments remaining, resolving whether multiprofile helps is the highest-value uncertainty to reduce—if it does, it opens a large family of multiprofile variants (scgpt, ViT-L, transformer aggregation) to exploit; if it doesn't, we avoid wasting budget on expensive multiprofile configs. config_038 uses avgpool (cheaper than transformer) and keeps the same encoders/fusion as config_001, making it a controlled comparison. Expected cost: ~1.3–1.6 GPU hours (moderately higher than config_001's 0.85 due to multiprofile processing and avgpool aggregation, but well below transformer-based variants).

Evidence: config_038 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved the best accuracy so far (0.6186), a large jump over the singleprofile baseline (0.5266). The multiprofile + avgpool + concat + resnet50 pipeline is validated as strong. The weakest component in that pipeline is the RNA encoder: pca_n2000 is a linear dimensionality reduction that may discard nonlinear biological signal. Question: Does upgrading the RNA encoder to scgpt (a pretrained transformer capturing gene-expression semantics) while holding all other components fixed improve validation accuracy beyond 0.6186? This is the single most impactful untested change on the current best configuration. Why this is the best use of experiment 4: it directly exploits the strongest evidence (config_038) with a one-variable extension, reducing uncertainty about whether a richer RNA representation can push accuracy higher. Expected relative cost: scgpt is a transformer-based encoder applied per-cell across multiple profiles, so this will be moderately more expensive than config_038's 36.42 GPU-hr run—estimated ~45–55 GPU hours—making it the most expensive option among the single-change extensions, but justified because it targets the component most likely to yield a meaningful accuracy gain.

Evidence: config_038 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the clear best at 0.619 acc, showing that multiprofile+avgpool aggregation and PCA-2000 are the key winning factors. The image modality contributes meaningfully (config_001 multimodal 0.527 vs config_045 RNA-only 0.485), but ResNet50 may be a bottleneck for image representation quality. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L (a substantially stronger pretrained visual backbone) improve on the 0.619 baseline while keeping all other settings identical? This is a single-variable change from the best config, isolating the image encoder's contribution. Why this is the best next experiment: With 5 experiments remaining, the highest-leverage untested axis is the image encoder strength. A stronger visual representation is the most plausible path to a meaningful accuracy gain over 0.619. Expected relative cost: ViT-L is larger than ResNet50, so this will be more expensive than config_038's 36.42 GPU hours—estimated ~45-55 GPU hours. This is a significant cost, but justified because it directly targets the most likely improvement over the current best, and a failure here would still leave 4 experiments to explore weighted fusion or transformer aggregation variants.

The evidence strongly points to multiprofile + pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l as the optimal backbone: config_049 (avgpool, concat) achieved 0.629 acc at only 4.54 GPU hrs, beating config_038 (resnet50, 36.42 GPU hrs) and config_021 (scgpt, 0.512 acc). The remaining uncertainty is whether weighted fusion can improve over simple concat at the same aggregation level. config_009 isolates exactly this one variable (concat → weighted) while keeping all other hyperparameters at their proven-best values. It is expected to cost roughly the same as config_049 (~4.5 GPU hrs), making it a cheap, high-information experiment. If weighted fusion yields a meaningful gain, subsequent experiments can layer on transformer aggregation; if not, we can pivot to testing transformer aggregation (config_022/037) with the remaining budget. This is the best use of experiment 6 because it reduces uncertainty on the last untested dimension of the current best configuration at minimal cost.

The current best (config_009, acc=0.6352) uses pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted. The only untested dimension for this top-performing combination is aggregation type: all top configs use avgpool, but transformer aggregation has never been paired with this exact set of encoders and weighted fusion. config_037 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) isolates that single change. Evidence strongly favors pca_n2000 over scgpt (0.61–0.64 vs 0.51) and imagenet_vit_l over resnet50 (0.63 vs 0.62), so exploring a different aggregation on this proven backbone is the highest-information next step. If transformer aggregation captures cross-profile interactions better than simple averaging, it could push accuracy above 0.635; if not, it confirms avgpool is optimal and the remaining 3 experiments can target other levers. Expected cost: moderate—transformer aggregation adds self-attention over profiles on top of the ViT-L backbone, so I estimate roughly 10–15 GPU hours (about 1.5–2× config_009's 7.02 hrs), which is well within the remaining budget of ~47 GPU hours.

The current best is config_009 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) at 0.635 accuracy. The architecture components—multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool aggregation, and weighted fusion—are well-supported by the evidence (avgpool > transformer by ~5 pts; weighted ≥ concat; multiprofile >> singleprofile; imagenet_vit_l > resnet50 at similar cost). The main untested variable that could push accuracy higher is the RNA encoder: scgpt was clearly worse (0.512), but scvi_n200 (a learned variational encoder) has not been paired with the best image/fusion stack. config_032 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) directly tests whether a learned RNA representation can outperform PCA while keeping all other parameters at their proven-optimal settings. This is a focused exploitation of the strongest configuration with one targeted change. Expected cost is moderate (~5–8 GPU hours), comparable to config_009 (7.02 h) since scvi_n200 is a learned encoder similar in complexity to scgpt (4.33 h in config_021), keeping total budget well within limits for the remaining 2 experiments.

The current best is config_032 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + avgpool + weighted) at 0.706 accuracy. The strongest evidence shows scvi_n200 is the dominant RNA encoder, imagenet_vit_l the best image encoder, and multiprofile > singleprofile. The one remaining uncertainty is aggregation: transformer underperformed avgpool with pca_n2000 (config_037: 0.586 vs config_009: 0.635), but scvi_n200 produces a richer learned representation that may benefit more from attention-based aggregation than a static PCA projection. config_019 (scvi_n200 + vit_l + transformer + weighted) directly tests this hypothesis while keeping the proven weighted fusion. This is the only untested configuration with a realistic chance of exceeding 0.706, since all other untested scvi_n200+vit_l variants either use concat (weaker evidence) or singleprofile (weaker evidence). Expected cost is moderate (~5–7 GPU hours), comparable to config_037 (4.55) and config_032 (4.82), since scvi_n200 is a compact encoder and the transformer aggregation adds only modest overhead over avgpool.

The current best is config_019 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc=0.725). The evidence strongly supports scvi_n200 as the best RNA encoder (~8% gain over pca_n2000), imagenet_vit_l as the best image encoder, transformer aggregation over avgpool (~2% gain), and weighted fusion over concat (~1-2% gain). The only untested variant within this top-performing design space is config_046 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat). While weighted fusion has consistently outperformed concat in prior comparisons, this is the last experiment and config_046 is the closest untested neighbor to the best configuration, offering a small chance of competitive performance while confirming the fusion-choice conclusion. All other untested configs involve a known inferior component (scgpt, resnet50, singleprofile, rna_only) and are very unlikely to beat 0.725. Expected relative cost: moderate (~3.5–4.5 GPU hours), comparable to config_019 and config_037, making it a low-risk final experiment that does not add disproportionate cost to the 66.18 GPU hours already spent.

With no prior evidence, the first experiment must establish a strong multimodal baseline to anchor all subsequent comparisons. config_009 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, resnet50, weighted fusion) is chosen because: (1) multimodal is the most promising model setting for cellular profiling, combining complementary RNA and image signals; (2) scgpt is a learned biological encoder expected to outperform PCA at capturing cell-state structure; (3) resnet50 is a well-validated image encoder that is substantially cheaper than imagenet_vit_l, keeping the first experiment affordable; (4) singleprofile avoids aggregation overhead, isolating the core multimodal fusion signal; (5) weighted fusion is a standard, interpretable fusion strategy. This configuration sits in the moderate-cost tier—more expensive than unimodal or PCA-based configs but well below ViT-L + transformer-aggregation setups—leaving ample GPU budget for the remaining 9 experiments to explore multiprofile aggregation, ViT-L, and alternative fusion strategies. If it performs well, I can exploit by adding multiprofile/transformer/ViT-L; if it underperforms, I learn that the basic multimodal pairing needs rethinking before investing in more complex variants.

Evidence: Only one experiment (config_009) is complete, yielding 42.1% accuracy with multimodal singleprofile (scgpt + resnet50, weighted fusion). This is a single data point, so uncertainty is high about which design dimensions matter most. Question: config_019 is a minimal, controlled extension of config_009—identical encoders (scgpt, resnet50) and fusion (weighted)—but switches from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. This isolates the effect of multi-profile aggregation, which is a core design choice in cellular profiling and likely a major source of signal. Why this is the best next step: (1) It directly exploits the one data point we have by testing the most impactful architectural change while holding all else constant, giving a clean read on whether multiprofile helps. (2) If accuracy improves substantially, the remaining 7 experiments can exploit multiprofile with better encoders/aggregation; if it does not, we pivot to modality or encoder choices. (3) Cost: multiprofile with avgpool adds moderate overhead over singleprofile (no transformer), so expected training cost is roughly 1.4–1.7 GPU hours—only ~30-50% more than config_009's 1.08 h—keeping total spend low while resolving a key uncertainty early in the budget.

Evidence: config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieved 0.525 accuracy, a large jump over config_009's 0.421, confirming that multiprofile+avgpool aggregation is the key driver. The remaining uncertainty is whether the fusion strategy (weighted vs. concat) can further improve performance on top of this strong base. This experiment tests exactly that: config_003 is identical to config_019 except fusion changes from weighted to concat, making it a clean single-variable ablation. It is the best use of experiment 3 because (a) it exploits the clearly promising multiprofile+scgpt+resnet50+avgpool direction, (b) it reduces uncertainty about a core design choice (fusion) before committing to more expensive architectural changes (e.g., ViT-L image encoder or transformer aggregation), and (c) its expected training cost is comparable to config_019 (~4.4 GPU hours) since the architecture is the same, keeping total budget manageable with 7 experiments remaining.

The best result so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.5251 acc. The single most important finding is that multiprofile with weighted fusion and scGPT+ResNet50 is a strong baseline. The key untested axis within this proven recipe is the aggregation method: avgpool vs. transformer. Config_013 is identical to config_019 except it replaces avgpool with transformer aggregation, making it a clean ablation. If transformer aggregation captures richer inter-profile interactions, we expect a meaningful accuracy gain; if not, we confirm avgpool is sufficient and can redirect remaining budget toward upgrading the image encoder (ViT-L) or RNA encoder. Expected cost is moderate—roughly 5–6 GPU hours (transformer adds ~1–2 hrs over the 4.42 hrs of config_019 due to attention over profiles), which is well within budget. This is the best use of experiment 4 because it isolates one variable from the current best, reduces uncertainty about a high-impact design choice, and sets up a clear exploitation path for experiments 5–10.

Evidence: config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the best at 0.5251 acc, clearly showing that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted is the strongest architecture pattern. Transformer aggregation (config_013) underperformed and was expensive (12.31 GPU hrs), so the remaining lever for improvement is the image encoder. Question: Does upgrading from ResNet50 to ImageNet-pretrained ViT-Large (imagenet_vit_l) improve accuracy while keeping the proven avgpool+weighted fusion? This directly isolates the image-encoder effect on the best-known configuration. Why this experiment: It is the most logical exploitation of the current best result with a single high-impact change. The expected cost is moderate (~6-9 GPU hours, higher than the 4.42 for ResNet50 due to ViT-L's larger parameters, but well below the 12+ GPU hours of transformer aggregation). With 5 experiments remaining, spending one moderate-cost experiment to test whether a stronger image encoder breaks past the 0.525 ceiling is the best risk/reward tradeoff. If it succeeds, subsequent experiments can refine around it; if it fails, we learn the image encoder is not the bottleneck and can pivot to RNA encoder alternatives (e.g., config_020 or config_031) in the remaining budget.

Evidence: The current best (config_037, acc=0.5420) uses scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted. Multiprofile with avgpool and weighted fusion is clearly superior (config_019 vs 009: +0.10; weighted vs concat: +0.013; avgpool vs transformer: +0.03 at 1/4 the cost). The image encoder upgrade (resnet50→ViT) gave +0.017. The remaining major untested variable in this best architecture is the RNA encoder: scvi_n200 has not been paired with ViT+avgpool+weighted. This experiment tests whether scvi_n200 (a variational encoder) can match or exceed scgpt in the strongest multimodal setup, potentially capturing complementary cell-state information. It is the best use of experiment 6 because it directly probes the highest-leverage untested axis (RNA encoder) within the confirmed best architecture, with expected cost comparable to config_037 (~3 GPU hours, since the heavy components—ViT and multiprofile avgpool—remain the same). A positive result would open a new exploitation direction for the remaining 3 experiments; a negative result confirms scgpt as the optimal RNA encoder and narrows the search space.

The current best (config_046: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc 0.706) strongly suggests that scvi_n200 and imagenet_vit_l are the key components. The one untested dimension within this exact combination is the fusion mechanism. For scgpt, weighted slightly outperformed concat (0.525 vs 0.512), but scvi_n200 produces a fundamentally different latent representation, so the optimal fusion may differ. Config_042 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat) is a minimal, low-risk exploitation of the best-known region. Expected cost is ~4–5 GPU hours (similar to config_046's 4.82), making it a cheap experiment that either confirms weighted as the correct fusion or reveals a small gain from concat. With 3 experiments remaining after this, keeping cost low preserves budget for further exploration if needed.

The current best (config_042: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat, acc=0.715) uses the strongest encoder pair found so far. The only untested design dimension with this encoder combination is aggregation method. With scgpt, transformer aggregation was slightly worse than avgpool (0.494 vs 0.525), but scvi_n200 produces more structured, denoised latent representations that may benefit from attention-based aggregation in a way the weaker scgpt features did not. Config_018 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) directly tests this hypothesis while keeping the concat fusion that already outperformed weighted (0.715 vs 0.706). This is the highest-information experiment remaining: if transformer aggregation helps, it could push accuracy above 0.715; if not, it confirms avgpool is optimal and frees the final experiment for a cheaper refinement. Expected cost is high (~12–15 GPU hours) due to the transformer aggregation layer over ViT-L features, but the potential accuracy gain and the fact that we still have one experiment of budget remaining make this the best use of experiment 8.

Evidence: The top-3 configs (config_018: 0.7207, config_042: 0.7150, config_046: 0.7062) all use scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile, confirming this is the dominant design. Within this space, we have tested 3 of 4 aggregation×fusion combinations: transformer+concat (0.7207), avgpool+concat (0.7150), avgpool+weighted (0.7062). The missing cell is transformer+weighted (config_017). Question: Does transformer aggregation maintain its ~1.5% advantage over avgpool when paired with weighted fusion, or is the benefit specific to concat? This clarifies the interaction between aggregation and fusion. Why this is the best use: It is the only untested configuration in the proven best-encoder pair, it completes the 2×2 design grid to reduce residual uncertainty before the final experiment, and its expected cost (~4.5–5 GPU hours, comparable to config_018's 4.65) is modest. Even if it does not surpass 0.7207, the result will inform whether the final experiment should explore a tangential direction or confirm the current best. Expected relative cost: medium, roughly equal to config_018 (transformer aggregation with the same encoders; fusion method has negligible cost impact).

Evidence: The strongest results (0.706–0.725) all come from the scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile recipe, with transformer aggregation + weighted fusion (config_017, 0.725) as the best. All four aggregation×fusion combinations for that recipe are now tested. Question: config_045 (scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) isolates the image-encoder contribution by swapping imagenet_vit_l for resnet50 while keeping the best RNA encoder, aggregation, and fusion. This clarifies how much of the 0.725 accuracy is attributable to the ViT-L image encoder versus the other components. Why this is the best last experiment: No remaining untested configuration uses the full winning recipe (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile), so beating 0.725 is very unlikely. Among remaining options, config_045 has the highest expected accuracy because it retains 3 of the 4 winning components. It also provides a useful ablation for the study. Expected cost is moderate (~3–4 GPU hours, slightly cheaper than config_017's 3.60 h since resnet50 is smaller than ViT-L), keeping total budget reasonable.

With no prior evidence, the most critical uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion (RNA + image) meaningfully outperforms single-modality baselines, and which moderate-complexity multimodal setup provides a strong reference point. config_008 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat fusion) tests this core hypothesis with a balanced architecture: pca_n2000 gives a solid 2000-dim RNA representation, resnet50 is a proven but not the most expensive image encoder, and concat fusion is a straightforward combination strategy. It avoids the added cost of multiprofile aggregation and ViT-L, keeping training time moderate (estimated ~middle of the cost range, roughly 1.5–2x a single-modality run). If it performs well, I can exploit by adding multiprofile, upgrading to ViT-L, or testing transformer aggregation in subsequent experiments. If it underperforms, I learn early that the multimodal pipeline needs different encoders or fusion, saving budget. This is the best use of experiment 1: it directly addresses the highest-impact design question (does multimodal help?) at moderate cost, establishing a strong anchor for the remaining 9 experiments.

With only one completed experiment (config_008: multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat → 52.7% acc, 0.85 GPU hrs), the evidence is very sparse and the most critical uncertainty is whether moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with aggregation meaningfully improves performance. Config_003 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the cleanest single-axis comparison to config_008: it changes only the profile setting (single→multi) and adds avgpool aggregation, keeping the RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion method identical. This isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation, which is likely one of the highest-impact architectural decisions in this search space. If multiprofile helps, it unlocks a large family of promising configs (002, 004, 012, 014, etc.); if it does not, we can focus budget on encoder/fusion choices within singleprofile.
