Expected relative cost: moderate, roughly 1.5–2.0 GPU hours (multiprofile adds per-profile forward passes but avgpool is a cheap aggregation step, and ResNet50 is the lighter image encoder), making it a cost-effective information-gathering experiment early in the budget.

Evidence: config_003 (multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.619 accuracy, a ~9% jump over the singleprofile baseline (config_008, 0.527), confirming that multiprofile aggregation with avgpool is a critical design choice. The remaining untested variable most likely to yield a comparable gain is the image encoder: ResNet50 is a mid-tier backbone, while ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L is substantially more expressive. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L improve validation accuracy when all other settings (multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool, concat) are held constant at their best-known values? This is a clean single-variable ablation of the image encoder. Why this is the best next experiment: With 7 experiments remaining, isolating the image-encoder effect on the current best architecture gives the highest information gain per experiment. If ViT-L helps, it establishes a new ceiling and guides subsequent experiments (e.g., pairing ViT-L with weighted fusion or transformer aggregation). If it does not help, it rules out the image encoder as a bottleneck and redirects effort toward RNA encoders or fusion strategies. Expected relative cost: moderately higher than config_003 (~36 GPU hrs) due to the larger ViT-L encoder, estimated around 50–70 GPU hrs, but justified because this configuration is the most likely candidate to become the best-performing model in the search.

Evidence: config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is the best so far at 0.6287 acc / 0.5993 F1, and config_003 (same but resnet50) is close at 0.6186. Both top configs use concat fusion; weighted fusion has not been tested with this architecture. Question: Does weighted fusion improve over simple concatenation for the best-performing multimodal multiprofile setup? This is a single-variable change from config_004, making the result cleanly interpretable. Why this is the best next step: It is the cheapest logical extension of the current best result (expected cost ~4–5 GPU hours, comparable to config_004's 4.54 hrs, since weighted fusion adds negligible compute over concat). With 6 experiments remaining and 41.82 GPU hours already spent, a low-cost experiment that tests a high-impact design axis (fusion strategy) before moving to more expensive changes (transformer aggregation, new RNA encoders) is the most budget-efficient use of experiment 4. If weighted fusion helps, it informs all subsequent multimodal runs; if not, we rule it out cheaply and pivot to aggregation or encoder exploration.

The current best (config_012: pca_n2000 + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.6352) establishes that multiprofile + ViT-L + weighted fusion is the strongest combination. The two main untested levers are (a) aggregation method (avgpool vs. transformer) and (b) RNA encoder (PCA vs. learned scvi/scgpt). I choose config_015, which is a clean single-variable change from the current best—swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation while keeping pca_n2000, ViT-L, and weighted fusion fixed. This directly tests whether a learned, attention-based aggregation of multiprofile representations can outperform the simple mean-pooling that has been the default. If transformer aggregation captures non-uniform profile importance, it could push accuracy above 0.635; if not, we rule out that direction cheaply and pivot to RNA-encoder exploration (scgpt/scvi) in the remaining budget. Expected cost: transformer aggregation adds self-attention compute over the profile set, so I estimate roughly 10–14 GPU hours—moderate, well within the remaining budget of ~51 GPU hours, and justified by the high information value of resolving the aggregation question before committing later experiments to a fixed aggregation strategy.

The best result so far is config_012 (acc=0.635, F1=0.618) using multiprofile + pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted. The only major untested dimension within this winning recipe is the RNA encoder: all top configs use PCA (a linear projection), and it is unclear whether a learned nonlinear encoder (scvi_n200) could capture richer cell-state structure and push accuracy higher. config_027 isolates exactly that change—swapping pca_n2000 for scvi_n200 while keeping the proven multiprofile/avgpool/weighted/ViT-L backbone—so any accuracy gain or loss can be attributed to the RNA representation. This is a high-value exploitation step: if scvi helps, we get a new best config; if it doesn't, we confirm PCA is sufficient and can focus remaining budget on other axes (e.g., scgpt or image-only baselines). Expected cost is moderate, roughly 6–8 GPU hours, comparable to config_012's 7.02 h since the architecture and image encoder are identical and scvi_n200 is a compact VAE.

The current best (config_027, acc=0.706) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted. The largest single gain in this search came from switching the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 (+0.071 accuracy). config_040 tests whether scgpt—a more powerful, generative RNA encoder—can push accuracy further while keeping all other settings at their proven-optimal values (imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile). This is the highest-information experiment: if scgpt beats scvi_n200, it opens a new promising direction for the remaining 3 experiments; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 is the best RNA encoder and focuses remaining budget on aggregation/fusion refinements. Expected cost is moderate (~5–7 GPU hours), comparable to config_027 (4.82) since scgpt is a similar-scale encoder to scvi_n200 and the image/aggregation pipeline is identical.

The current best (config_027, acc=0.706) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted. The only untested variation within this strong sub-space is the aggregation method. Transformer aggregation was tested only with pca_n2000 (config_015, acc=0.586 vs 0.629 for avgpool), where it underperformed. However, scvi_n200 produces a learned, structured latent representation rather than a linear PCA projection, so attention-based aggregation across profiles may extract richer cross-profile interactions that avgpool would average away. This experiment directly tests whether the aggregation choice that was suboptimal for PCA becomes beneficial for the superior scvi_n200 encoder, while keeping all other hyperparameters at their best-known values. Expected cost is moderate (~4.5–5 GPU hours, comparable to config_015 at 4.55 and config_027 at 4.82), making it a low-risk, high-information experiment. If transformer aggregation improves on 0.706, it would set a new best; if not, it confirms avgpool is optimal for scvi_n200 and the remaining budget can focus on other directions.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_022 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) at 0.7250 accuracy, with config_027 (same encoders, avgpool + weighted) at 0.7062. Across all experiments, scvi_n200 and imagenet_vit_l are clearly superior encoders, multiprofile outperforms singleprofile, and transformer aggregation beats avgpool. The only untested variant within this top-performing encoder/aggregation family is concat fusion (config_050: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat). Question: Does concat fusion interact differently with transformer aggregation than it did with avgpool (where weighted consistently beat concat, e.g., config_012 vs config_004)? This is the best use of experiment 9 because it completes the 2×2 fusion×aggregation grid for the best encoder pair, confirming or refuting whether weighted fusion is strictly dominant. If config_050 matches or exceeds 0.725, it becomes the new best; if not, it solidifies config_022 as the final answer for the last experiment. Expected cost: ~3.5–4 GPU hours (same architecture as config_022, only fusion layer differs), well within budget.

Evidence: The top-3 performers (config_022: 0.7250, config_050: 0.7207, config_027: 0.7062) all use scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile, establishing this as the dominant encoder combination. Within this space, the 2×2 grid of aggregation (avgpool/transformer) × fusion (weighted/concat) is nearly complete: transformer+weighted (0.7250), transformer+concat (0.7207), avgpool+weighted (0.7062) are done. The only missing cell is avgpool+concat (config_020). Question: This experiment completes the grid and confirms whether the observed monotonic ordering (transformer > avgpool, weighted > concat) holds consistently, solidifying config_022 as the best configuration. Why this is the best use of the final slot: No remaining untested configuration (scgpt, pca_n2000, resnet50, or singleprofile variants) has a realistic chance of exceeding 0.7250 given the large performance gaps observed (scgpt ~0.54, pca ~0.62, singleprofile ~0.53). Config_020 is the only untested config in the proven best-encoder space, provides a clean confirmation of the optimal architecture at moderate cost (~4 GPU hours, comparable to config_027's 4.82 and config_050's 4.65), and minimizes total budget while closing the experimental loop.

With no prior experiments, the key uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion (RNA + image) with multiprofile aggregation provides a meaningful accuracy boost over unimodal baselines, and which component choices matter most. Config_002 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) serves as a strong, moderate-cost baseline: it tests the core multimodal hypothesis with a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200), a standard image encoder (resnet50), a simple aggregation (avgpool), and the simplest fusion (concat). This is not the most expensive configuration (no transformer aggregation, no ViT-L), so it preserves GPU budget for follow-up experiments that can isolate which axis (RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, fusion) drives performance. The result will anchor the search: if accuracy is strong, we exploit by upgrading individual components (e.g., transformer aggregation or ViT-L); if weak, we pivot to unimodal baselines or simpler encoders. Expected relative cost: moderate—multiprofile processing and a learned RNA encoder add cost, but avgpool and resnet50 keep it well below the most expensive configs (ViT-L + transformer).

With only one completed experiment (config_002, acc=0.6315, 7.27 GPU-hrs), evidence is sparse and the most important uncertainty is whether the simple avgpool aggregation in the multiprofile setting is suboptimal. Config_018 is a clean single-variable change from config_002: it replaces avgpool with transformer aggregation while keeping all other settings identical (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat fusion). Transformer aggregation allows the model to learn profile-level attention weights, which is a well-motivated improvement when multiple profiles carry heterogeneous signal. This experiment directly tests whether a more expressive aggregation mechanism can lift accuracy beyond 0.63. Expected relative cost: moderately higher than config_002 (~8–10 GPU-hrs, roughly 10–40% more) due to the added self-attention layers in the transformer, but still well within budget given 8 experiments remain. This is the best use of experiment 2 because it isolates one high-impact architectural choice without confounding variables, giving clear signal for subsequent decisions.

Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly outperforms avgpool (+5.6% accuracy: 0.6878 vs 0.6315) with the same scvi_n200/resnet50/concat setup, making transformer the proven aggregation choice. The largest unexplored architectural variable is the image encoder: resnet50 is a relatively modest CNN, while imagenet_vit_l (ViT-Large) offers substantially richer visual representations. This experiment (config_028) isolates the image-encoder upgrade by keeping all other settings identical to the current best (config_018: scvi_n200, transformer, concat, multiprofile), so any accuracy change can be attributed to the image encoder. Rationale: With 7 experiments remaining, testing the highest-impact unexplored dimension (image representation quality) is more informative than a small fusion-method tweak (concat→weighted). If ViT-L delivers a meaningful gain, subsequent experiments can layer in weighted fusion or scgpt on top. Expected cost: ViT-L is considerably larger than ResNet50, so I estimate ~9–12 GPU hours (roughly 2× the 5.16 h of config_018), but the potential accuracy uplift justifies the higher compute spend relative to a marginal fusion change.

Evidence: The three completed experiments show a clear progression: transformer aggregation beats avgpool (+5.6 pp), and imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 (+3.3 pp), with config_028 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat, multiprofile) achieving the best accuracy at 0.7207. The only untested variable in this top configuration is the fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted). Question: Does weighted fusion improve over concat when the strong transformer+ViT-L backbone is already in place? This is a single-variable exploitation of the best-performing setup, directly testing whether the fusion mechanism can squeeze additional accuracy from the same representations. Why this is the best next experiment: With 6 experiments remaining, exploiting the strongest direction first locks in a high-accuracy baseline early. Config_039 differs from config_028 only in fusion (weighted vs. concat), so any accuracy change is cleanly attributable to fusion. Expected cost is similar to config_028 (~4.6–5.0 GPU hours) since the architecture is nearly identical—only the final fusion layer changes—making it a cheap, high-information experiment.

The current best (config_039, acc=0.7250) uses scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder with imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, and weighted fusion. The only major unexplored dimension in this proven architecture is the RNA encoder. Config_036 swaps scvi_n200 for scgpt while keeping all other settings at their best-known values (imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile). This directly tests whether a different learned RNA encoder can push accuracy beyond 0.7250 or confirm that scvi_n200 is near-optimal. If scgpt performs comparably, we gain confidence the RNA encoder is not the bottleneck; if it improves, we identify a new best. Expected cost is moderate (~4–5 GPU hours), similar to config_039's 3.60 h since the dominant cost drivers (ViT-L image encoder + transformer aggregation) are unchanged, with scgpt adding a modest overhead over scvi_n200. With 5 experiments remaining, this is the highest-information experiment that exploits the strongest evidence while exploring the largest untested design axis.

The current best is config_039 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.7250 acc. The evidence strongly favors imagenet_vit_l over resnet50, transformer over avgpool, and weighted over concat, while scvi_n200 dominates scgpt (0.725 vs 0.52). The one major untested variable within this best-performing family is the RNA encoder pca_n2000. Config_041 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) directly tests whether the simpler, cheaper PCA encoder can match scvi_n200 in the top configuration. If it performs comparably, we confirm a cheaper alternative; if it underperforms, we lock in scvi_n200 as the definitive RNA encoder and can spend remaining budget on finer refinements. This is the highest-information experiment available: it resolves the last major design-axis uncertainty in the promising region without venturing into low-probability areas (e.g., scgpt, which already showed a 20-point accuracy drop). Expected cost: pca_n2000 is a linear projection (no learned encoder), so training should be slightly cheaper than config_039's 3.60 GPU hours—estimated ~3.0–3.5 GPU hours, keeping total budget well within limits.

Evidence: config_039 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is the current best at 0.7250 accuracy. All four design dimensions point to this combination: scvi_n200 >> pca/scgpt for RNA, imagenet_vit_l > resnet50 for image, transformer > avgpool for aggregation, and weighted ≥ concat for fusion. The remaining uncertainty is whether the transformer aggregation advantage (seen with resnet50: 0.688 vs 0.632) is robust when paired with the stronger imagenet_vit_l encoder, or whether avgpool + weighted fusion could be nearly as good at lower cost. This experiment (config_021: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is the single closest untested variant to our best config, changing only the aggregation. If it lands within ~0.01 of 0.7250, it offers a cheaper alternative; if it drops substantially, it confirms transformer is essential and we can confidently lock in config_039 as the final answer with the remaining 2 experiments. Expected cost: slightly lower than config_039's 3.60 GPU hours since avgpool is computationally simpler than a transformer aggregator, likely ~3.0–3.5 GPU hours.

The current best (config_039, 0.725) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted in the multiprofile setting. All 7 completed experiments are multiprofile, so the singleprofile dimension is completely unexplored. config_007 tests whether a single profile (no aggregation step) with the best-known encoders (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l) and weighted fusion can match or exceed the multiprofile result. This is critical because: (1) it reduces model complexity and training cost (no transformer aggregation), (2) it clarifies whether the multiprofile aggregation is genuinely adding signal or just adding parameters, and (3) if it matches the current best at lower cost, it frees GPU budget for the final 2 experiments to explore other directions. Expected cost: ~2.5–3.0 GPU hours (cheaper than config_039's 3.60 since there is no multiprofile transformer aggregation). This is the highest-information experiment remaining: it either confirms multiprofile is necessary or reveals a simpler, cheaper path to comparable accuracy.

The current best (config_039, acc=0.725) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted + multiprofile. All individual factor comparisons strongly support this combination: scvi_n200 >> scgpt/pca, imagenet_vit_l > resnet50, transformer > avgpool, weighted > concat, multiprofile >> singleprofile. Config_004 is the only remaining untested multiprofile configuration with the best RNA and image encoders (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l), using avgpool + concat. Testing it confirms that the transformer+weighted pairing is indeed superior and rules out any unexpected interaction that could push accuracy above 0.725. Based on config_021 (avgpool+weighted, 0.706) and config_028 (transformer+concat, 0.721), config_004 is expected to land around 0.68–0.70, well below the current best. Its expected cost is moderate (~4–5 GPU hours, comparable to config_021's 4.82 h since it uses avgpool rather than transformer). This is the best use of experiment 9 because it closes the last meaningful gap in the multiprofile scvi_n200+ViT-L design space, leaving experiment 10 free for a minimal-cost run to keep total GPU hours low.

Evidence: All four aggregation×fusion combinations for the clearly superior base (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile) have been tested, with config_039 (transformer+weighted) at 0.725 being the best. RNA encoder (scvi_n200 >> scgpt/pca), image encoder (vit_l >> resnet50), and profile setting (multiprofile >> singleprofile) are all well-established. No remaining untested configuration falls in the promising region; all alternatives involve a materially weaker component. Question: Since no untested config can plausibly exceed 0.725, this final experiment should minimize additional GPU cost. config_032 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible architecture—no image processing, no aggregation, no fusion—so its expected training cost is very low (~0.2–0.5 GPU hours), the cheapest option in the untested pool. Rationale: The best validation accuracy (0.725) is already secured; running the cheapest remaining config minimizes total GPU hours (currently 37.93) while satisfying the budget constraint, making this the most cost-efficient use of the final experiment slot.

With no prior evidence, the first experiment must establish a strong baseline while reducing uncertainty across the key design axes (multimodal vs. unimodal, multiprofile vs. singleprofile, aggregation strategy, fusion strategy). config_009 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) tests the full multimodal + multiprofile architecture with the strongest image encoder (ViT-L) and the most expressive aggregation (transformer), paired with a fast, low-cost RNA encoder (PCA-2000) and weighted fusion. This will clarify: (1) whether the multimodal + multiprofile + transformer pipeline is viable and high-performing, (2) whether PCA is sufficient for the RNA branch or whether scgpt/scvi_n200 would be needed, and (3) how weighted fusion behaves in this setting. Choosing PCA over scgpt keeps training cost moderate (ViT-L and transformer are the main cost drivers; PCA is negligible), estimated at roughly 60-70% of the most expensive configurations (scgpt + ViT-L + transformer). This saves GPU budget for follow-up experiments that can swap in scgpt or test concat fusion if PCA proves to be the bottleneck. It is the best use of experiment 1 because it maximally informs the architecture while leaving room to exploit or pivot in the remaining 9 experiments.

The only completed experiment (config_009: pca_n2000, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) achieved 58.6% accuracy at 4.55 GPU hours. The biggest uncertainty is whether the simple linear PCA encoder is a bottleneck for the RNA modality. Config_017 changes only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200 (a learned VAE) while keeping all other settings identical (multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted), giving a clean single-variable ablation. If scvi improves accuracy, it confirms that non-linear RNA representations matter and motivates trying scgpt next; if it does not, PCA is sufficient and we can redirect effort toward fusion or aggregation. This is the highest-information experiment for resolving the RNA-encoding question. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 5–6 GPU hours (slightly above config_009's 4.55) due to the VAE training overhead, which is acceptable given 8 experiments remain.

Evidence: config_017 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) achieved 0.725 acc, dramatically outperforming config_009 (pca_n2000, same other settings) at 0.586 acc, confirming scvi_n200 as the superior RNA encoder. The current best configuration uses weighted fusion. Question: config_007 is an exact single-variable ablation of config_017, changing only fusion from weighted to concat while keeping scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, and multiprofile multimodal identical. This tests whether concatenating modality representations before the head outperforms weighted averaging, a fundamental architectural choice that could unlock further gains. Why this is the best next step: with 7 experiments remaining, establishing the optimal fusion strategy for the proven scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer backbone is the highest-information experiment—it directly extends the strongest evidence we have and will guide all subsequent multiprofile multimodal experiments. Expected cost is similar to config_017 (~3.5-3.7 GPU hours) since the architecture is identical except for the fusion operation.

Evidence: The three completed experiments establish that scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted achieves 0.725 accuracy, far outperforming pca_n2000 (0.586), and that weighted fusion is marginally better than concat (0.725 vs 0.721). The most important unexplored dimension is the RNA encoder: scgpt has not been tested yet and is a more expressive generative encoder than scvi_n200. Question: Can scgpt, paired with the known-best image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (transformer), and fusion (weighted), surpass the current best of 0.725? Why this is the best next step: It isolates the single highest-impact untested variable (RNA encoder) while holding all other settings at their empirically validated best values, maximizing information gain per experiment. With 6 experiments remaining, confirming or ruling out scgpt early guides all subsequent choices. Expected relative cost: scgpt is a generative model and will likely add ~0.5–1.0 GPU hours over config_017's 3.60 hrs, so I estimate ~4.5–5.0 GPU hours total—moderately more expensive than config_017 but well within budget and justified by the potential accuracy gain.

Evidence: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + weighted fusion is the clear best combination (config_017: 0.725 acc, 3.60 GPU hrs), with transformer aggregation. The only untested variation within this top-performing family is the aggregation method (avgpool vs transformer). Question: Does the transformer aggregation provide meaningful benefit over simple average pooling for multiprofile aggregation, or is the cross-attention overkill? This is important because avgpool is substantially cheaper (no self-attention over profiles), so if it matches transformer within ~1%, we get a cost-efficient configuration. Why this is the best next step: It keeps all three proven-best components (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted) and isolates the single remaining architectural uncertainty in the top-performing family. With 5 experiments left, confirming or ruling out the transformer's contribution lets us either exploit a cheaper equivalent or confidently invest remaining budget in other dimensions (e.g., resnet50 image encoder, single-profile). Expected relative cost: ~2.5–3.0 GPU hours, roughly 20-30% cheaper than config_017's 3.60 hrs since avgpool replaces the transformer attention layer.

Evidence: All top-3 experiments (config_017: 0.725, config_007: 0.721, config_020: 0.706) share scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder and use imagenet_vit_l as the image encoder. The RNA encoder is the dominant factor (scvi_n200 >> pca_n2000 >> scgpt), and transformer aggregation with weighted fusion is the best combination tested. However, the image encoder dimension is completely unexplored—every completed experiment uses imagenet_vit_l. This experiment (config_027: scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted) tests whether a smaller, cheaper image encoder can match or exceed imagenet_vit_l in the best-performing multimodal setup. If resnet50 performs comparably (~0.72), it confirms a cheaper path forward; if it underperforms significantly, it validates imagenet_vit_l and narrows the search. This is the best use of the next slot because it resolves a major architectural uncertainty in the top-performing region while keeping expected cost moderate (~2.5–3.5 GPU hours, lower than config_017's 3.60 since resnet50 has fewer parameters than ViT-L). With 4 experiments remaining after this, confirming the image encoder choice early preserves budget for fine-tuning other dimensions.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_017 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, multiprofile) at 0.7250. All completed experiments are multiprofile, leaving the singleprofile multimodal dimension entirely unexplored. The RNA encoder (scvi_n200), image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), and fusion (weighted) choices are well-supported by the data. Question: config_023 tests whether singleprofile multimodal (no aggregation step) with the best-known components can match or exceed the multiprofile ceiling. This is critical because singleprofile removes the aggregation bottleneck and could either (a) match multiprofile at lower cost, or (b) reveal that multiprofile aggregation is essential. Why this is the best use of experiment 7: With only 3 experiments remaining, exploring this untested architectural axis is the highest-information experiment. If singleprofile performs comparably, it opens a cheaper path; if it underperforms significantly, it confirms multiprofile + transformer is the right direction and we can focus remaining budget on fine-tuning. Expected relative cost: moderate-to-low (~2.5–3.5 GPU hours), since it eliminates the transformer aggregation step present in the multiprofile configs (3.6–4.85 hrs) while retaining the imagenet_vit_l image encoding.

Evidence: config_017 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is the current best at 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1 (3.60 GPU hrs). config_027 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) scored 0.713 acc but notably higher F1 (0.695) at 6.22 GPU hrs, suggesting resnet50 features complement the classifier well. Fusion choice (weighted vs concat) showed only a 0.004 gap with imagenet_vit_l (0.725 vs 0.721), so the interaction between resnet50 and concat fusion is untested and could shift the balance. Question: Does scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + concat (config_041) beat the current best 0.725? This is the most logical single extension of the top-2 configurations, combining the strongest RNA encoder and aggregation with the only untested image-encoder/fusion pairing in that neighborhood. With 2 experiments remaining after this, confirming or slightly improving on 0.725 is the highest-value use of the next slot. Expected cost: ~6 GPU hours (similar to config_027, same resnet50 + transformer + multiprofile architecture), which is higher than the imagenet_vit_l variants (~3.6–4.8 hrs) but justified since resnet50 has already shown competitive accuracy and the best-F1 signal.

The current best (config_017, acc=0.725) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted. All component-level comparisons show scvi_n200 and imagenet_vit_l are the strongest encoders, transformer > avgpool (~0.019 gap), and weighted > concat (~0.004 gap). No untested config replicates the exact best combination, so the goal is to find the closest viable variant. config_049 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) retains both top encoders while testing whether the avgpool+concat interaction might produce a different (possibly complementary) signal compared to the individually tested avgpool (config_020, 0.706) and concat (config_007, 0.721) results. It is the highest-expected-accuracy untested option among scvi_n200 multimodal multiprofile configs. Expected cost is moderate (~4.5–5 GPU hours), similar to config_020 (4.82) but potentially slightly cheaper due to concat fusion. This is the best use of experiment 9: it gives a small chance of a surprise interaction effect beating 0.725 while keeping cost reasonable, and the single remaining experiment can then be used to confirm or explore further if needed.

Evidence: The best configuration found is config_017 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc=0.7250). All top-6 results use scvi_n200 with multiprofile, and the structural choices (imagenet_vit_l > resnet50, transformer > avgpool, weighted ≥ concat) are well-established. config_040 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted) is the last untested combination within the scvi_n200 + multiprofile subspace, completing systematic coverage. Question: It tests whether the weighted-fusion benefit observed with transformer aggregation (config_017 vs 007) also holds with avgpool + resnet50, and whether any residual synergy between these components could close the gap to the current best. Why this is the best last experiment: No untested configuration combines all the individually-best components (that would be config_017 itself), so beating 0.7250 is unlikely. config_040 is the most informative remaining test at moderate cost (~4–5 GPU hours, estimated from comparable resnet50+avgpool configs like config_020 at 4.82h and config_041 at 5.16h). It avoids wasting the final budget on a clearly inferior singleprofile or unimodal setup while still providing a useful data point to confirm the design-space ranking. Total GPU hours will remain under ~42.

With no prior evidence, the first experiment should establish a strong multimodal baseline to anchor the search. config_010 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) pairs the most expressive RNA encoder (scgpt, a pretrained transformer capturing gene-gene context) with a solid but cost-effective image encoder (resnet50) and a cheap aggregation (avgpool) plus weighted fusion. This tests whether the combination of a learned RNA encoder with moderate image features and simple aggregation yields competitive accuracy, giving a high-quality reference point. It avoids the highest-cost stack (ViT-L + transformer aggregation) while still using the strongest RNA encoder, so the expected relative cost is medium-high (~60-70% of the most expensive multimodal config). If this performs well, subsequent experiments can probe whether upgrading the image encoder to ViT-L or the aggregation to transformer yields meaningful gains; if it underperforms, I learn that the bottleneck lies elsewhere (e.g., fusion strategy or profile setting) and can redirect exploration efficiently within the remaining 9 experiments.

With only one completed experiment (config_010: scgpt+resnet50+avgpool+weighted, acc=0.525), the evidence is sparse and the most critical uncertainty is whether the image encoder is a bottleneck. Config_020 makes a single clean change—upgrading resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l—while holding all other factors (scgpt, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile, multimodal) constant. This isolates the contribution of a stronger pretrained image encoder, which is likely a major driver of multimodal performance. If ViT-L improves accuracy, it justifies investing remaining budget in ViT-L-based configs; if not, we save substantial GPU hours by sticking with ResNet50. Expected relative cost: moderate-to-high, roughly 6–7 GPU hours (ViT-L has ~300M params vs ResNet50's ~25M, increasing per-step compute), but this is a pivotal architectural decision worth the investment given 8 experiments remain.

Evidence: The two completed experiments (config_010, config_020) both use scgpt + multiprofile + avgpool + weighted, differing only in image encoder. config_020 (imagenet_vit_l) achieves the best accuracy (0.542) at a lower cost (2.94 GPU hrs) than config_010 (resnet50, 0.525, 4.42 GPU hrs). The remaining uncertainty is whether the simple avgpool aggregation is bottlenecking performance—averaging multiple profiles discards inter-profile structure that a transformer could capture. This experiment (config_019: scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) isolates the aggregation change while keeping the best-performing base (scgpt + vit_l + weighted fusion), making the result interpretable. It is the best use of experiment 3 because it tests the single most impactful architectural lever (aggregation) on the current best configuration, and a positive result would justify further exploitation of the transformer+vit_l direction in remaining budget. Expected relative cost: transformer aggregation adds attention computation over multiple profiles, so I estimate ~3.5–4.5 GPU hrs—moderately more expensive than config_020's 2.94 hrs but still within a reasonable range, and justified by the potential accuracy gain.

Evidence: config_020 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) is the current best at 0.542 acc, outperforming both the resnet50 variant (config_010, 0.525) and the transformer-aggregation variant (config_019, 0.520). This establishes scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool as the strongest backbone. The only untested dimension within this best-performing setup is the fusion method (all three completed experiments used weighted fusion). Question: Does concat fusion outperform or match weighted fusion when paired with the best backbone? This is a minimal, focused change (only fusion: weighted→concat) that directly tests whether we can push accuracy above 0.542 or confirm weighted as optimal. Rationale: With 6 experiments left, exploiting the clearly best configuration by testing its last unexplored hyperparameter is the highest-information-per-cost move. Expected cost is similar to config_020 (~2.9–3.0 GPU hours) since the architecture is identical and concat fusion is marginally cheaper than weighted fusion. If concat matches or beats weighted, we lock in the best multimodal multiprofile setup; if not, we confirm weighted and can pivot to exploring alternative RNA encoders (pca_n2000, scvi_n200) in subsequent experiments.

Evidence: All four completed experiments used scgpt as the RNA encoder, with config_020 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) achieving the best accuracy at 0.542. We have no evidence about how other RNA encoders perform with this best image/fusion/aggregation setup. Question: config_008 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) isolates the RNA encoder choice while holding the three best-performing hyperparameters fixed. This tests whether a lighter, learned nonlinear encoder (scvi_n200) can match or exceed scgpt, or whether scgpt's pretrained biological knowledge is essential. Why this is the best next step: With 5 experiments remaining, confirming or refuting the RNA encoder's contribution is the highest-uncertainty question. If scvi_n200 matches scgpt, we unlock cheaper future experiments; if it falls short, we confirm scgpt is the right choice and can focus remaining budget on other axes. Expected cost: scvi_n200 is a compact 200-dim VAE, significantly lighter than scgpt, so this should train in roughly 2–2.5 GPU hours—cheaper than config_020's 2.94 hours while using the same imagenet_vit_l backbone.

The dominant finding across all 5 completed experiments is that the scvi_n200 RNA encoder (config_008, 70.6% acc) dramatically outperforms scgpt (~52-54%), making it the clear backbone to build on. Among scgpt experiments, avgpool+weighted and ViT-L were the best-performing aggregation/fusion/image-encoder choices, which is exactly the recipe in config_008. The remaining untested variation within this 'best-of-each' family is the aggregation method: transformer vs. avgpool. With scvi_n200's richer learned latent space, transformer-based cross-profile aggregation may capture interactions that simple averaging misses (the scgpt evidence for avgpool>transformer was only ~2 pts and may not transfer to a different feature space). config_039 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L + transformer + weighted) keeps the two strongest factors and the best fusion while testing this one architectural question. Expected cost is moderate (~4-5 GPU hours, comparable to config_008's 4.82 h, with a small increase from transformer attention). This is the highest-value single experiment: if it beats 70.6%, we have a new best; if it matches or falls slightly short, we confirm avgpool is optimal and can spend remaining budget on other directions (e.g., singleprofile or PCA variants) with confidence.

The evidence strongly identifies scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l as the dominant architecture (0.706–0.725 vs. 0.518–0.542 for scgpt), and transformer aggregation outperforms avgpool by ~2 points (config_039: 0.725 vs. config_008: 0.706). The only untested dimension within this clearly best subspace is the fusion method: all scvi_n200 results so far use 'weighted' fusion. Config_031 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat) directly tests whether concat fusion can push accuracy beyond the current best of 0.725. With scgpt, concat was slightly worse than weighted (0.518 vs. 0.542), but the interaction with the much stronger scvi_n200 representation may differ. This is the highest-value exploitation step: it refines the single most promising configuration. Expected cost is moderate-to-high (~5–7 GPU hours) because concat fusion increases parameter count (as seen in config_021 at 7.18 h vs. config_020 at 2.94 h), but the transformer aggregation component keeps it comparable to config_039's 3.60 h baseline; I estimate roughly 5–6 GPU hours. With 3 experiments remaining after this one, confirming or improving the top configuration is the best use of the next slot.

Evidence: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted (config_039, acc=0.725) is the clear best, with transformer aggregation and weighted fusion both outperforming alternatives. The image encoder choice (vit_l vs resnet50) is the one major axis not yet tested with the top RNA encoder + transformer + weighted combo. Question: Does resnet50 with transformer aggregation and weighted fusion remain competitive with imagenet_vit_l, or is vit_l essential? This clarifies whether a potentially cheaper image backbone could match the current best, or whether vit_l is irreplaceable. Why this experiment: With only 2 runs left, confirming or ruling out resnet50 in the top-performing architecture family is the highest-information test. If resnet50 is competitive, it offers a cost-saving alternative; if not, it locks in the config_039 family and frees the final experiment for a targeted refinement. Expected relative cost: moderate (~3.5–4.5 GPU hours), comparable to config_039's 3.60, since resnet50 is a lighter backbone than vit_l but transformer aggregation adds some overhead.

The current best (config_039: scvi_n200 + vit_l + transformer + weighted, 0.725 acc) has been well-characterized, and all remaining untested scvi_n200 multimodal variants use either a weaker image encoder (resnet50) or weaker aggregation/fusion (avgpool/concat), making it unlikely any will surpass 0.725. The largest remaining uncertainty is the PCA RNA encoder, which has never been tested in the multimodal setting. Config_002 pairs PCA (pca_n2000) with the otherwise best-known pipeline (imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted), isolating the RNA-encoder variable. If PCA is competitive, it opens a new optimization axis for the final experiment; if not, it confirms scvi_n200 is essential and we can bank the 0.725 result. Expected cost is moderate (~2.5–3.5 GPU hours), as PCA encoding is far cheaper than the scvi_n200 VAE while the vit_l + transformer backbone dominates runtime, making it roughly on par with or slightly below config_039's 3.60 GPU hours.

Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.706–0.725 vs 0.52–0.59 for others), imagenet_vit_l and weighted fusion are the top image/fusion choices, and transformer aggregation beats avgpool by ~2%. The current best is config_039 (scvi_n200 + vit_l + transformer + weighted, 0.725). The only major unexplored architectural dimension with scvi_n200 is singleprofile (no aggregation step). Question: Does removing the multiprofile aggregation step (which may introduce noise or information loss) while keeping the best encoders and weighted fusion yield a competitive or superior result? Rationale: This is the final experiment, so I want maximum information value. config_042 pairs the two best-performing encoders (scvi_n200, vit_l) with the best fusion (weighted) and tests the singleprofile hypothesis. If it matches or exceeds 0.725, it reveals a simpler, cheaper architecture; if it falls short, it definitively confirms that multiprofile + transformer aggregation is essential. Expected cost: moderate-to-low (~2.5–3.5 GPU hours) since singleprofile eliminates the aggregation network, making it cheaper than the multiprofile transformer configs (~3.6–6.2 hrs). This keeps total GPU hours reasonable while resolving the last key architectural uncertainty.

No prior evidence exists, so the first experiment must establish a strong baseline and reduce uncertainty about the most impactful design axes: (1) whether multimodal (RNA+image) outperforms single-modality, (2) whether the strongest available encoders (scgpt for RNA, ViT-L for image) provide a meaningful advantage, and (3) whether multiprofile aggregation helps. config_003 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) tests all three of these hypotheses simultaneously while using avgpool aggregation instead of the more expensive transformer, keeping training cost in the upper-moderate range (roughly 70-80% of the most expensive configs) without sacrificing the ability to aggregate multiple profiles. If it performs well, subsequent experiments can test whether upgrading to transformer aggregation (config_007) or swapping RNA encoders yields further gains. If it underperforms, the result localizes the problem to modality combination, encoder choice, or aggregation strategy, guiding the remaining 9 experiments efficiently. Weighted fusion is preferred over concat as it allows the model to learn modality-specific importance, which is particularly useful when RNA and image signals may have unequal informativeness.

Evidence: config_003 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) achieved 0.542 accuracy at 2.94 GPU hours, but we have only one data point so sensitivity to individual design choices is unknown. Question: Does the fusion method (weighted vs. concat) meaningfully affect performance when all other components are held fixed? config_009 is identical to config_003 except fusion=concat, making it a clean single-variable ablation. This is the best next experiment because it is the most minimal perturbation of our current best, directly tests whether weighted fusion provides a real advantage over simple concatenation, and costs essentially the same (~2.94 GPU hours) since only the lightweight fusion operation changes. If concat matches weighted, we gain flexibility in later experiments; if it is clearly worse, we confirm weighted fusion is a key contributor and can focus subsequent experiments on other dimensions (aggregation, profile setting, encoders).

Evidence: config_003 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) achieved the best accuracy (0.542) at low cost (2.94 GPU hrs), clearly outperforming config_009 (same architecture but concat fusion, acc=0.518, cost=7.18). This establishes weighted fusion as superior and identifies scgpt/imagenet_vit_l as a strong backbone. Uncertainty: we have only tested avgpool aggregation; transformer aggregation could capture richer inter-profile interactions that avgpool discards. This experiment (config_041) tests transformer aggregation while holding all other proven components constant (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, multiprofile), making it a clean single-variable extension of our best result. It is the best use of experiment 3 because: (1) it directly exploits the strongest evidence while probing the most impactful untested design axis (aggregation), (2) a positive result would give a clear exploitation path for remaining budget, and (3) a negative result would confirm avgpool sufficiency and redirect exploration toward RNA/image encoder choices. Expected relative cost: moderate (~4-6 GPU hrs), higher than avgpool due to attention computation but well below the concat-fusion overhead seen in config_009.

Evidence: All three completed experiments share the same encoders (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l) and multiprofile setting, with config_003 (avgpool + weighted) leading at 0.542 acc. We have zero information about whether the RNA encoder choice matters. Question: config_036 swaps scgpt for scvi_n200 while keeping the best-performing image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (avgpool), and fusion (weighted) fixed, isolating the effect of the RNA representation. scvi_n200 is a learned VAE-based encoder that captures nonlinear cell-state structure differently from the generative scgpt model, so it provides a strong, informative contrast. Why this is the best next experiment: With 6 experiments remaining, we must resolve the large uncertainty around RNA encoder choice before committing further budget to the scgpt family. If scvi_n200 matches or beats scgpt, it unlocks a broader, potentially cheaper search space; if it underperforms, it confirms scgpt's value and we can exploit that. Expected cost is similar to config_003 (~2.5–3 GPU hours) since the architecture (avgpool + weighted, ViT-L image) is unchanged and scvi_n200 inference is comparable or slightly cheaper than scgpt.

Evidence: config_036 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) achieved 0.706 accuracy, dramatically outperforming all scgpt-based configs (~0.52-0.54), establishing scvi_n200 as the dominant RNA encoder. The remaining uncertainty is whether transformer aggregation can further improve upon avgpool with this stronger encoder. Question tested: config_038 isolates the aggregation axis (avgpool→transformer) while holding the proven scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + weighted fusion stack constant. With scgpt, transformer was slightly worse (0.520 vs 0.542), but scvi_n200 produces a richer latent representation where learned attention over profiles may capture interactions that simple averaging misses. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a single-variable, high-information test around the current best configuration, directly informing whether to exploit transformer aggregation in subsequent runs or confirm avgpool as optimal. Expected cost: ~4.7–5.0 GPU hours (comparable to config_036's 4.82, since transformer vs avgpool showed negligible cost difference in the scgpt comparisons), keeping total budget well within limits with 5 experiments remaining.

Evidence: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted (config_038, acc=0.725) is the clear best so far, substantially outperforming scgpt-based configs (~0.52-0.54). Transformer aggregation edges out avgpool (+2% over config_036). The only untested variant within this top-performing sub-space is the fusion type: we have tested weighted fusion but not concat fusion with scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer. Question: Does concat fusion match or exceed weighted fusion in this architecture? With scgpt, weighted was slightly better than concat, but the dynamics may differ with the stronger scvi_n200 encoder. This is a cheap, targeted exploitation experiment (expected cost ~3.5-4 GPU hours, comparable to config_038's 3.60) that either finds a new best or confirms weighted as optimal, reducing uncertainty before spending remaining budget on broader architectural changes. With 4 experiments left after this, confirming the best fusion for the top architecture is the highest-value next step.

The best configuration so far (config_038: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc 0.725) establishes that scvi_n200 is the dominant factor over scgpt (0.54), and transformer+weighted is the best aggregation/fusion combo. The key remaining uncertainty is whether the image encoder (imagenet_vit_l vs resnet50) meaningfully contributes to performance with the best RNA encoder. Config_045 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted) isolates this variable while keeping all other settings at their known-best values. If resnet50 performs within ~1-2% of 0.725, it offers a cheaper alternative; if it drops significantly, it confirms imagenet_vit_l is essential and we should lock in the current best. This is the highest-information experiment among remaining options: it tests an unexplored axis (image encoder) with the strongest RNA encoder, rather than testing a likely-inferior RNA encoder (pca_n2000) or a combination of individually-worse choices (avgpool+concat in config_040). Expected relative cost: moderate-to-low, roughly 2.5–3.5 GPU hours, since resnet50 is substantially smaller than ViT-L, making this cheaper than config_038 (3.60 hrs) while retaining the transformer aggregation overhead.

The current best (config_038, 0.725 acc) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + transformer + weighted. All multiprofile scvi_n200 variants have been tested and cluster tightly between 0.706–0.725, suggesting the architecture is near a plateau. The key unexplored dimension is profile_setting: no singleprofile configuration has been tested with the best RNA encoder (scvi_n200) and best image encoder (imagenet_vit_l). config_051 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + singleprofile + weighted) tests whether the multiprofile + transformer aggregation is providing meaningful benefit or whether a simpler singleprofile architecture achieves comparable accuracy at substantially lower cost. If it lands within ~1–2% of 0.725, it would be a much cheaper solution (estimated ~2–2.5 GPU hrs vs 3.6 for config_038, since it skips multiprofile processing and aggregation). If it drops significantly, it confirms that multiprofile + transformer is essential, and the final experiment can focus on confirming the current best or a minor variant. This is the highest-information experiment for the remaining 2-slot budget: it reduces uncertainty about a major architectural axis at low cost, and the result directly guides the final experiment choice.

The evidence strongly identifies scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile as the dominant architecture (0.706–0.725 accuracy vs. ~0.52–0.54 for scgpt and 0.537 for singleprofile). Within this family, transformer aggregation + weighted fusion (config_038, 0.725) is the best, with transformer+concat (0.721) and avgpool+weighted (0.706) close behind. The only untested cell in this 2×2 aggregation×fusion matrix is avgpool+concat (config_040). Testing it completes the design-space map for the best architecture, confirming that the performance ranking (transformer+weighted > transformer+concat > avgpool+weighted > avgpool+concat) holds and that no hidden interaction could push accuracy above 0.725. This is the best use of experiment 9 because it is low-cost (avgpool avoids the transformer's extra compute; expected ~3.5–4.5 GPU hours, similar to or slightly below config_036's 4.82 h), it removes residual uncertainty about the best configuration before the final experiment, and it leaves experiment 10 free for a targeted exploration (e.g., a pca_n2000 or resnet50 variant) if the result confirms config_038 as the clear winner.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_038 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.7250 accuracy. All four aggregation×fusion combinations with scvi_n200+imagenet_vit_l+multiprofile have been tested, and scgpt and singleprofile are clearly inferior. The only untested RNA encoder in the optimal architecture is pca_n2000. This experiment tests whether pca_n2000 with the best-performing architecture (transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, imagenet_vit_l) can match or exceed scvi_n200, or confirm that scvi_n200 is the dominant RNA encoder. While scgpt underperformed, pca is a different (simpler, linear) method and its performance is genuinely uncertain. As the final experiment, this provides the most informative remaining data point about the RNA encoder axis while using the already-validated optimal architecture. Expected cost: moderate (~3–4 GPU hours), comparable to config_038 (3.60 hrs) since the architecture is identical and PCA encoding is slightly cheaper than scVI, keeping total budget reasonable.

With no prior evidence, I need to establish a strong baseline while reducing uncertainty about the core design hypothesis: that combining multimodal inputs (RNA + image) with multiprofile aggregation and well-pretrained encoders yields the best accuracy. config_009 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) tests this 'expected-best' combination: it uses both modalities, leverages multiple profiles for richer representation, pairs a well-established RNA encoder (scvi_n200) with a strong pretrained image encoder (ViT-L), and uses a simple but effective aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (weighted) strategy. This gives a high-probability competitive result to anchor the search, while also establishing whether the multimodal+multiprofile paradigm outperforms simpler alternatives. Expected relative cost: medium-high — ViT-L and multiprofile processing add compute over ResNet50/singleprofile configs, but avgpool aggregation and scvi_n200 keep it well below the most expensive options (transformer aggregation, scgpt). This is the best use of experiment 1 because it sets a strong reference point from which the remaining 9 experiments can efficiently explore encoder swaps, aggregation strategies, and fusion choices.

With only one completed experiment (config_009: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted → 0.706 acc), the most impactful uncertainty to resolve is whether the multiprofile aggregation step is actually contributing to performance or just adding cost. Config_004 is a minimal, controlled change: identical to config_009 except profile_setting switches from multiprofile to singleprofile (removing the avgpool aggregation step). This directly tests whether the multiprofile architecture is worth its ~1.5 GPU-hour overhead. If singleprofile matches or approaches 0.706, all future experiments can be substantially cheaper, freeing budget for exploring other axes (RNA encoder, fusion method, transformer aggregation). If multiprofile is clearly superior, we confirm the direction and can focus remaining budget on optimizing within the multiprofile space. Expected cost is ~3.0–3.5 GPU hours (no multiprofile aggregation, but still multimodal with ViT-L), making it a cost-effective information-gathering step relative to the 4.82 hours of config_009.

Evidence: config_009 (multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) achieved 0.706 accuracy, far outperforming the singleprofile baseline (0.537), confirming that multiprofile aggregation is critical. The current best uses avgpool, a simple uniform-weight aggregation that treats all profiles equally. Question: config_041 isolates the aggregation method, replacing avgpool with a transformer that can learn attention weights across profiles, while keeping all other settings (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, multiprofile) identical to the best result. This is a single-variable change, making the result easy to interpret. Rationale: Transformer aggregation is the most natural and impactful architectural upgrade from avgpool for multiprofile settings, as it can learn which profiles carry more signal. With 7 experiments remaining, this high-information experiment either confirms avgpool is sufficient (freeing us to explore encoders/fusion) or unlocks a new best result to build on. Expected cost: transformer aggregation adds self-attention over profiles, so I estimate ~6–7 GPU hours (moderately higher than config_009's 4.82), bringing the running total to roughly 11–12 GPU hours — acceptable given the strong expected accuracy upside.

Evidence: config_041 (multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is the current best at 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1, beating config_009 (same but avgpool) by ~2%. The transformer aggregation clearly helps. Uncertainty: we haven't tested whether concat fusion outperforms weighted fusion under transformer aggregation—fusion type is a key architectural choice that determines how modality representations combine. This experiment (config_025: transformer + concat, all else identical to config_041) is a clean single-variable A/B test against the current best. If concat is superior, it raises the ceiling for all subsequent multiprofile+transformer experiments; if weighted remains better, we confirm the current best and can pivot to RNA encoder exploration (scgpt/pca) in later runs. Expected cost is similar to config_041 (~3.5–4.0 GPU hours) since the architecture is identical except for the fusion operation, making this a high-information, low-marginal-cost experiment with 6 runs still remaining.

Evidence: All four completed experiments confirm that multiprofile + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion is the strongest architecture (best: config_041, acc=0.725, F1=0.685). The only major design axis not yet explored within this optimal architecture is the RNA encoder—scvi_n200 has been used in every experiment, while scgpt (a more expressive generative single-cell model) remains untested in this setting. Question: Does replacing scvi_n200 with scgpt, while keeping imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted + multiprofile fixed, yield a further accuracy gain? Why this is the best next experiment: It directly exploits the strongest known architecture and tests the single most impactful untested variable (RNA encoder quality). scgpt's richer learned representation plausibly captures cell-state information that scvi_n200 misses, making it the highest-expected-value exploration. If it improves, we have a new best; if not, we confirm scvi_n200 is optimal and can pivot to image-encoder variations. Expected relative cost: scgpt is a larger generative model than scvi_n200, so I estimate ~4.5–5.5 GPU hours—moderately higher than config_041 (3.60) but comparable to config_025 (4.65). This is justified given the potential accuracy upside and the 5 remaining experiments.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_041 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc / 3.60 GPU-hrs, with config_025 (concat fusion) a close second at 0.721. Multiprofile + transformer aggregation + scvi_n200 + weighted fusion is strongly supported. However, the image encoder has only been tested as imagenet_vit_l in this top-performing architecture. Question: Does swapping to resnet50 (config_015) preserve the 0.725-level accuracy, or is ViT-L's larger representational capacity critical? This is the single most unexplored axis in the best-performing setup. Rationale: With 4 experiments remaining, confirming or ruling out the image encoder's contribution is high-value—if resnet50 matches, we save ~1+ GPU-hr per run and can redirect budget; if it underperforms, we lock in ViT-L and focus remaining experiments on fine-tuning. Expected relative cost: moderate, roughly 2.5–3.5 GPU-hrs (resnet50 is substantially lighter than ViT-L, reducing the dominant image-encoding cost while retaining transformer aggregation over multiprofile). This is the best use of experiment 6 because it reduces uncertainty on a major architectural choice without repeating any prior configuration.

The current best is config_041 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc=0.7250). All major design axes have been explored and point to this configuration: multiprofile >> singleprofile, transformer > avgpool, scvi_n200 >> scgpt, ViT-L > resnet50, weighted ≥ concat. The one major untested dimension with all other settings at their known-best values is the RNA encoder: pca_n2000 has never been paired with (imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile). Testing config_039 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) directly clarifies whether a linear PCA representation can match or exceed the learned scvi embedding in this strong multimodal pipeline. If it performs comparably, it confirms scvi_n200's advantage is modest and we can focus remaining budget on fine-tuning around config_041; if it is clearly worse, it locks in scvi_n200 and lets us exploit the remaining 3 experiments on micro-variants. Expected cost is moderate (~3.0–3.5 GPU hours), slightly below config_041's 3.60 h since PCA is a cheap linear projection compared to the scvi encoder, making this a high-information, relatively cheap experiment.

Evidence: The top-3 configs all use scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer aggregation. Within this family, vit_l+weighted (config_041, acc=0.7250) is best on accuracy, but resnet50+weighted (config_015, acc=0.7131) achieves the best F1 (0.6945), suggesting resnet50 captures complementary discriminative information. The vit_l+concat variant (config_025, acc=0.7207) is only marginally below weighted. Question: Does resnet50+concat (config_049) synergize—combining resnet50's stronger F1 signal with concat's feature-preserving fusion—to match or exceed 0.7250? This completes the 2×2 grid {vit_l, resnet50}×{weighted, concat} for the best architecture, resolving the last uncertainty in the top-performing family. Why this experiment: With 2 runs remaining, this is the highest-information test within the proven best architecture; if it underperforms, we confirm config_041 as the winner and can spend remaining budget on a cheap confirmation or a long-shot alternative. Expected cost: ~5.5 GPU hours (transformer aggregation + resnet50, comparable to config_015's 6.22 but concat fusion is slightly cheaper than weighted), making it a moderate-cost experiment relative to the budget already spent (27.22 GPU hrs).

Evidence: The top-4 configurations all use scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer/avgpool, with config_041 (transformer+weighted, 0.7250) as the clear best. We have tested transformer+weighted (0.7250), transformer+concat (0.7207), and avgpool+weighted (0.7062) for the scvi_n200+imagenet_vit_l pair, but the avgpool+concat cell (config_012) remains untested. This experiment completes the 2×2 aggregation×fusion matrix for the best encoder combination, confirming whether the transformer aggregation advantage is robust to fusion choice. It is unlikely to beat config_041 (both avgpool and concat are individually inferior), but it solidifies confidence that no untested variant in this top region can surpass 0.7250, freeing the final experiment for a low-cost confirmation or a different direction. Expected relative cost: moderate (~4–5 GPU hrs), comparable to config_009 (4.82 hrs) since it uses avgpool (cheaper than transformer) with imagenet_vit_l and concat fusion.

Evidence: The best configuration found is config_041 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, 0.7250 acc). All scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer variants with both fusion types have been tested. The remaining untested scvi_n200 + multiprofile configs (config_001, config_036) both use avgpool + resnet50, which are individually weaker choices (avgpool < transformer, resnet50 < vit_l). However, config_001 (avgpool + weighted) is the more promising of the two since weighted fusion has consistently outperformed concat (0.725 vs 0.721 for transformer; 0.706 vs 0.715 for avgpool is close). This experiment tests whether the scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted combination can close the gap to the current best, though it is unlikely to exceed 0.725. It is the best use of the final experiment because it is the highest-expected-accuracy untested configuration, confirming the design space is exhausted. Expected cost: ~3.5–4.5 GPU hours (avgpool is cheaper than transformer, resnet50 is comparable to vit_l), making it a moderate-cost final experiment.

With no prior evidence, the primary uncertainty is whether a strong multimodal, multiprofile configuration will set a high performance ceiling. config_001 (scgpt + resnet50 + transformer aggregation + concat fusion, multiprofile) tests the full multimodal pipeline with a learned RNA encoder (scgpt), a well-established image encoder (resnet50), and the most expressive aggregation (transformer) for combining multiple profiles. This is the best first experiment because: (1) it is likely near the top of the accuracy range, giving a strong baseline to beat; (2) it simultaneously validates the multimodal hypothesis, the multiprofile+transformer aggregation choice, and the scgpt encoder in one shot, reducing uncertainty across multiple design axes; (3) it avoids the highest-cost image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) while still using a solid one, keeping GPU cost moderate-high rather than maximum. If it performs well, subsequent experiments can ablate individual components (e.g., swap to vit_l, try weighted fusion, or test alternative RNA encoders). If it underperforms, the result will guide which axis to simplify. Expected relative cost: moderate-high (~60-70% of the most expensive configs like those using imagenet_vit_l + transformer + scgpt), making it a reasonable investment for the first data point.

Evidence: config_001 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, transformer, concat) achieved 47.1% accuracy at a high cost of 9.06 GPU hours, with the transformer aggregation likely being the dominant cost driver. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether the transformer aggregation is meaningfully contributing to performance or whether a simpler avgpool aggregation would yield comparable accuracy at a fraction of the cost. This experiment (config_002) is a clean single-variable ablation—changing only aggregation from transformer to avgpool while keeping all other settings identical—so any accuracy difference can be attributed to the aggregation method. If avgpool performs similarly (~47%), we can eliminate transformer-based configs from the search, saving substantial GPU hours across the remaining 8 experiments and redirecting budget toward exploring other dimensions (RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting). If transformer is clearly superior, we retain it for future experiments. Expected relative cost: significantly lower than config_001 (estimated ~4–5 GPU hours vs 9.06), since avgpool replaces the compute-heavy transformer layer. This is the best use of experiment 2 because it directly reduces uncertainty about the most expensive architectural component with a minimal, interpretable change, and the cost savings (or confirmation) will shape the strategy for all remaining experiments.

Evidence: config_002 (scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.512 acc outperforms config_001 (same but transformer aggregation) at 0.471 acc, establishing avgpool as the preferred aggregation for multiprofile and confirming the scgpt+resnet50+avgpool+concat baseline. The biggest untested lever is the image encoder: ResNet50 (~25M params) vs ImageNet ViT-L (~300M+ params), which is a substantially stronger pretrained visual feature extractor. Question: does upgrading the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l while holding aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat) constant yield a meaningful accuracy gain? This is a clean single-variable extension of our current best config. It is the best use of experiment 3 because (a) the image encoder is likely the highest-impact remaining design choice, (b) it isolates one variable so we can attribute any change to the encoder, and (c) the result directly informs which image encoder to pair with other improvements (RNA encoder, fusion) in subsequent experiments. Expected relative cost: moderate-to-high (~6-8 GPU hours) due to the larger ViT-L backbone, but still well below the transformer-aggregation cost seen in config_001 (9.06 hrs) since we retain the cheaper avgpool aggregation.

Evidence: All three completed experiments (config_001, 002, 035) are multimodal/multiprofile/scgpt. The data clearly shows avgpool > transformer for aggregation (0.512 vs 0.471) and imagenet_vit_l ≥ resnet50 for image encoder (0.518 vs 0.512). The best config (035: scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat) achieves 0.518. The only untested dimension within this best-performing architecture is fusion type — all three experiments used concat. This experiment (config_019) tests weighted fusion with the identical architecture (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool), isolating the effect of fusion. It is the cleanest single-variable extension of the current best result. Expected cost: similar to config_035 (~7.2 GPU hours) since weighted fusion adds negligible compute over concat. Evidence: The best result so far (config_019, acc=0.542) uses scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted. Question: Can scvi_n200 (a learned 200-dim VAE embedding) match or exceed scgpt when paired with the best-known image/aggregation/fusion settings? config_026 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable swap from config_019, isolating the RNA encoder effect. The dominant finding is that scvi_n200 as RNA encoder produces a massive accuracy jump (0.706 in config_026 vs 0.542 best scgpt), and the best configuration combines scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted. The one remaining untested axis with this winning combination is transformer aggregation (config_027: scvi_n200, vit_l, transformer, weighted). This is a direct exploitation of the strongest evidence (keeping all three winning components) while testing the one variable that could plausibly push accuracy beyond 0.706. If transformer does not help, it confirms avgpool as optimal and we can pivot to other axes (e.g., singleprofile or concat fusion) in the remaining 4 experiments. Expected cost: ~7–8 GPU hours (transformer aggregation adds roughly 3–4 hours over the 4.82-hour avgpool baseline, based on the transformer/avgpool gap observed with scgpt), which is moderate and justified by the potential for a meaningful accuracy gain.

The current best is config_027 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.7250 acc. The evidence strongly supports scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder, imagenet_vit_l as the image encoder, transformer aggregation, and weighted fusion. If concat performs comparably, the architecture is robust and we can focus remaining budget on confirming the best; if weighted is clearly better, we lock in config_027 as the final answer with high confidence. Expected cost is ~3.5–4 GPU hours (same architecture as config_027 at 3.60, only fusion layer changes), making it a low-cost, high-information experiment. With 3 experiments remaining after this, this targeted test maximizes the chance of either finding a marginal improvement or confidently confirming the optimum within budget.

The current best (config_027, acc=0.725) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted. The evidence strongly supports scvi_n200 over scgpt (~20pp gain) and imagenet_vit_l over resnet50 (~2-3pp gain). The remaining uncertainty within the best encoder pair is the aggregation×fusion interaction: we've tested transformer+weighted (0.725), transformer+concat (0.721), and avgpool+weighted (0.706), but not avgpool+concat. Expected cost is moderate (~4-5 GPU hours), comparable to config_026's 4.82h since avgpool is cheaper than transformer and concat is simpler than weighted fusion.

Evidence: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted (config_027) is the clear best at 0.725 acc, and all four aggregation/fusion combos for that pair have been tested. The only untested RNA encoder in this top architecture is pca_n2000. Cost: pca_n2000 is a simple linear projection (no VAE training), so expected training cost is modest—roughly 3–4 GPU hours, comparable to or slightly below config_027's 3.60 h, making it a low-cost, high-information experiment given only one run remains after this one.

Evidence: The top-4 experiments all use multiprofile + scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, with transformer+weighted (config_027, 0.7250) as the current best. All four aggregation/fusion combinations within that space have been tested, so further multiprofile variants with the same encoders offer no new information. The key remaining uncertainty is whether the singleprofile architecture (no aggregation step) with the same strong encoders could match or exceed the multiprofile results, perhaps by avoiding aggregation-induced noise. With no prior evidence, the first experiment should test the core multimodal hypothesis with a strong, well-balanced configuration to establish a high baseline and reduce uncertainty about whether multimodal fusion (RNA + image) with multiprofile transformer aggregation is the right direction. config_022 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) pairs a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200) with a solid, well-established image encoder (resnet50), uses transformer aggregation to handle multiprofile structure, and applies a simple concat fusion. This tests whether the combination of both modalities and multiprofile aggregation yields a strong signal. It is a moderate-cost choice: multimodal + multiprofile + transformer adds overhead, but resnet50 is substantially cheaper than ViT-L, keeping this in the mid-range of expected GPU hours. If it performs well, subsequent experiments can exploit the direction by swapping in ViT-L, weighted fusion, or scgpt; if it underperforms, we learn that the multimodal or aggregation strategy needs rethinking. This is the best use of experiment 1 because it maximally reduces uncertainty about the most important design axis (multimodal vs. single-modality) while setting a competitive accuracy bar within the 10-experiment budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_022: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion → 0.688 acc, 5.16 GPU hrs), evidence is very sparse. The most important uncertainty is whether the transformer aggregation layer is actually contributing meaningfully over a simpler average-pooling strategy, since it adds significant compute. Config_011 is a controlled single-variable change (transformer → avgpool) from the best result, keeping all other settings identical. If avgpool performs comparably, we save ~1-2 GPU hours per subsequent experiment and can redirect budget toward other dimensions (e.g., image encoder or RNA encoder). If transformer is clearly superior, we confirm the direction and can optimize within that space. Expected relative cost: moderately lower than config_022 (~3.5-4.5 GPU hrs vs 5.16), since avgpool replaces the transformer's attention layers in the aggregation step while retaining the same multimodal encoders.

Evidence: config_022 (transformer aggregation, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.688 acc, clearly outperforming config_011 (avgpool, same other settings) at 0.632 acc, establishing transformer aggregation as the strong baseline. The largest untested lever is the image encoder: resnet50 may be a bottleneck relative to the much larger imagenet_vit_l. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder to ViT-L (pretrained on ImageNet) while keeping the proven transformer+concat+scvi_n200+multiprofile pipeline yield a meaningful accuracy gain? This is a clean single-variable change from our best result.
