Evidence: config_014 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) is our best at 0.7250, and all top-5 configs use scvi_n200. The only remaining untested combination of these two best encoders is config_013 (avgpool + concat). While both changes (avgpool over transformer: 0.7062 vs 0.7250; concat over weighted: 0.7207 vs 0.7250) are individually negative, their joint effect is untested and there is a small chance of interaction effects. This experiment completes the full 2×2 grid of aggregation×fusion for the scvi_n200+imagenet_vit_l pair, eliminating residual uncertainty about whether any untested cell in that grid could exceed 0.7250. As the final experiment, it maximizes the (small) probability of finding a new best while confirming the current champion. Expected cost: ~4–5 GPU hours (similar to config_033 at 4.82 h, with concat fusion likely slightly cheaper than weighted), bringing total to roughly 45–46 GPU hours.

With no prior evidence, the goal is to establish a strong multimodal baseline that is informative about the overall design space. config_001 combines the strongest RNA encoder (scgpt, a pretrained single-cell foundation model) with the strongest image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) in a multimodal setting, uses multiprofile to capture richer cellular state, and applies avgpool aggregation with weighted fusion. This tests whether the full multimodal pipeline with top-tier encoders yields high validation accuracy, giving a high reference point for subsequent experiments. It also partially clarifies whether multiprofile + avgpool is competitive versus transformer aggregation (tested later in config_003). Expected relative cost: moderate-to-high, since it processes multiple profiles through both scgpt and ViT-L, but avgpool avoids the additional transformer-layer overhead, keeping it cheaper than the transformer-aggregation variants while still being a strong candidate for the best configuration.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted → acc 0.542), evidence is sparse. The most critical design choice to resolve in a multiprofile setting is the aggregation method: avgpool (simple mean) vs. transformer (attention-based). Config_003 is a clean single-variable change from config_001 (avgpool → transformer), directly testing whether more expressive profile aggregation improves validation accuracy. If transformer significantly outperforms avgpool, it signals a high-value direction for the remaining 7 experiments; if similar, we confirm avgpool suffices and save GPU hours on future runs. This reduces uncertainty about a core architectural choice before committing to further exploitation. Expected relative cost: moderately higher than config_001 (~3.5–4.0 GPU hours vs. 2.94) due to the transformer attention layers over profiles, but the information gain justifies the modest increase.

Evidence: config_001 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) achieved the best accuracy (0.542) and config_003 showed avgpool > transformer for the same encoder pair, establishing avgpool+weighted as the preferred aggregation/fusion. The biggest remaining uncertainty is whether the large imagenet_vit_l image encoder is actually contributing meaningfully or whether a lighter resnet50 backbone could perform comparably (or even better due to less overfitting). This experiment (config_039) is a clean single-variable test: it swaps only the image encoder from imagenet_vit_l to resnet50 while holding scgpt, avgpool, weighted, and multiprofile fixed. If resnet50 matches or exceeds 0.542, we gain a cheaper backbone for all subsequent experiments, freeing GPU budget. If it drops significantly, we confirm ViT-L is essential and can focus remaining budget on RNA-encoder and fusion variations. Expected cost: ~2.3–2.6 GPU hours, modestly cheaper than config_001 (2.94) since ResNet-50 has fewer parameters than ViT-Large.

Evidence: config_001 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) is the current best at 0.542 acc, and avgpool > transformer and imagenet_vit_l > resnet50 are established from the 3 completed runs. The one untested variable in this top-performing recipe is the RNA encoder—only scgpt has been tried. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether scgpt's pretrained representations are essential or whether the lighter scvi_n200 VAE encoder can match them. This experiment (config_030) changes only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200 while holding the proven-best image encoder, aggregation, and fusion constant, directly isolating the RNA-encoder contribution. If scvi_n200 matches scgpt, we gain a cheaper encoder for future runs; if it falls well short, we confirm scgpt is critical and can focus remaining budget on fusion or profile-setting variations. Expected cost: scvi_n200 is a smaller model than scgpt, so training should be roughly 20-30% cheaper than config_001's 2.94 GPU hours (~2.0–2.3 GPU hours), making this a high-information, low-cost experiment with 6 runs still remaining.

The dominant finding from experiments 1-4 is that switching the RNA encoder from scgpt to scvi_n200 yields a massive accuracy jump (0.542 → 0.706, config_030), making scvi_n200 the clear best encoder. With scgpt, avgpool aggregation was slightly better than transformer (0.542 vs 0.520), but scvi_n200 produces learned latent representations that are fundamentally different from scgpt's token-level outputs, so the aggregation method may interact differently. Config_007 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) isolates this one variable while keeping all other settings at their best-known values. This is the highest-value exploitation step: if transformer aggregation helps, we gain a meaningful accuracy boost on top of the already-strong 0.706; if it doesn't, we confirm avgpool is optimal and can focus remaining budget on fusion or image-encoder variations. Expected cost is moderate (~5.0–5.5 GPU hours), slightly above config_030's 4.82 due to the transformer attention layers over multiprofile tokens, but well within budget given 5 experiments remain.

Evidence: scvi_n200 RNA encoder dominates (0.706-0.725 vs 0.52-0.54 for scgpt), and among scvi_n200+imagenet_vit_l configs, transformer aggregation with weighted fusion (config_007, 0.725) is the current best. The only untested variation on this top-performing axis is the fusion strategy. This experiment tests whether concat fusion (config_036) can outperform weighted fusion when paired with transformer aggregation and the best image encoder. It is a minimal, targeted exploitation of the strongest evidence: only one parameter changes from the best result, so any accuracy difference is cleanly attributable to fusion. Expected cost is comparable to config_007 (~3.5-4 GPU hours) since architecture (transformer aggregation, multiprofile, multimodal) is identical. With 4 experiments remaining, confirming or improving the fusion choice on the top configuration is the highest-value next step before exploring image-encoder swaps.

Evidence: scvi_n200 is the dominant factor (0.706–0.725 vs ~0.52–0.54 for scgpt), and within scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation + weighted fusion (config_007, 0.725) is the best. However, we have not yet tested whether the image encoder choice matters when paired with the strong scvi_n200 encoder—resnet50 was only tested with the weaker scgpt. This experiment (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted) directly tests whether resnet50 can match or approach imagenet_vit_l in the best-performing regime. If it performs comparably, it may offer a cheaper path; if it lags, we confirm imagenet_vit_l is essential and can focus remaining budget on fine-tuning around config_007. This is the highest-information single experiment: it resolves the image-encoder question under the proven best RNA/aggregation/fusion settings. Expected cost: ~3.5–4.5 GPU hours (resnet50 is smaller than ViT-L, so likely at or slightly below config_007's 3.60 h, though transformer aggregation adds overhead).

The current best (config_007, acc=0.725) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + transformer + weighted. The multiprofile scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l 2×2 grid (aggregation × fusion) is nearly saturated (avgpool+weighted=0.706, transformer+weighted=0.725, transformer+concat=0.721), leaving only avgpool+concat (config_008) which is very unlikely to beat 0.725. The most uncertain remaining direction is the single-profile architecture with the best encoders: it removes the aggregation step entirely and fuses a single RNA profile with the image. config_025 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + singleprofile + weighted) tests whether bypassing multiprofile aggregation could yield comparable or better accuracy, since weighted fusion has been the slightly stronger choice. This is the best use of experiment 8 because: (1) it reduces uncertainty about a major architectural axis (single vs. multiprofile) that is completely unexplored with the top encoders, (2) if it performs competitively it opens a cheaper path to high accuracy, and (3) with only 2 experiments remaining, resolving this binary question informs the final experiment choice. Expected relative cost: lower than multiprofile transformer configs (~2–3 GPU hours vs. 3.6–4.8) since there is no aggregation step, making it a cost-efficient exploration.

Evidence: The top-4 configurations all share scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer aggregation, with config_007 (vit_l, weighted) at 0.725 as the current best. The only untested configuration in this high-performing neighborhood is config_050 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat). While resnet50 has been slightly lower in accuracy than vit_l (0.713 vs 0.725), config_031 showed resnet50 can achieve a higher F1 (0.695 vs 0.685), suggesting it captures complementary signal. This experiment tests whether the transformer+concat fusion with resnet50 might produce a small accuracy gain or at least confirm the ceiling of the scvi_n200+transformer family. It is the best use of experiment 9 because it is the highest-expected-accuracy untested option remaining; all other untested configs either drop to avgpool or use weaker encoders (scgpt, pca). Expected relative cost: high (~6 GPU hours), comparable to config_031 (6.22 hrs), due to multiprofile transformer aggregation with resnet50. Since accuracy is the primary objective and we have one experiment remaining, investing in the most competitive architecture is justified.

Evidence: The top-4 performers all use scvi_n200 + multiprofile + multimodal, with config_007 (vit_l + transformer + weighted, 0.7250) as the clear best. Transformer aggregation outperforms avgpool by ~0.019 (config_007 vs config_030), and weighted fusion edges out concat by ~0.004 (config_007 vs config_036). Question: config_008 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat) is the closest untested variant to the best performer, sharing the two most impactful choices (RNA encoder and image encoder). While I expect it to land around 0.70 (below config_007), it is the highest-expected-accuracy untested configuration in the proven design region and rules out any residual interaction benefit between avgpool and concat that the marginal evidence doesn't fully exclude. Why this is the best use of the final experiment: All other untested scvi_n200 multiprofile multimodal configs (config_037, config_049) swap in resnet50 and/or avgpool, making them strictly less promising. Single-profile and non-scvi_n200 configs are far below the 0.70 threshold. Since this is the last experiment, I select the configuration with the highest expected accuracy to give the best (albeit small) chance of exceeding 0.7250. Expected cost: ~4.5–5.0 GPU hours (similar to config_030's 4.82, since it shares the same encoders and uses the cheaper avgpool aggregation rather than transformer).

With no prior evidence, the most informative first experiment is to test the full-capability multimodal pipeline: multimodal (RNA+image), multiprofile with transformer aggregation, scgpt RNA encoder, and ViT-L image encoder with weighted fusion. This establishes the performance ceiling and simultaneously tests whether the combination of strong encoders, multiprofile aggregation, and multimodal fusion is viable. If it performs well, subsequent experiments can ablate individual components (e.g., replace scgpt with PCA, ViT-L with ResNet50, transformer with avgpool) to find cheaper configurations that match its accuracy. If it underperforms, it reveals which architectural choice is limiting. Expected relative cost: HIGH — this is the most expensive configuration in the set (scgpt foundation model + ViT-L + transformer aggregation + multiprofile processing), but as the single most informative experiment to anchor the search, the cost is justified given 9 remaining experiments to explore cheaper alternatives.

With only one completed experiment (config_018: multimodal/multiprofile/scgpt/ViT-L/transformer/weighted → acc 0.52, 2.86 GPU hrs), evidence is very sparse. The most important uncertainty is whether the expensive multiprofile + transformer aggregation pipeline is actually contributing to accuracy, or whether a simpler singleprofile setup with the same strong encoders (scgpt, ViT-L) and weighted fusion achieves comparable performance. Config_001 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, None, weighted) isolates this question by removing aggregation and multiprofile while keeping the core multimodal fusion. Expected cost is roughly 1.2–1.6 GPU hours (no transformer aggregation, single profile), significantly cheaper than config_018. If it matches or approaches 0.52, we save substantial compute for the remaining 8 experiments and can focus on tuning the cheaper singleprofile space. If it drops substantially, we confirm multiprofile + transformer aggregation is essential and should exploit that direction. This is the highest-information, cost-efficient next step under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) achieved 0.520 acc, significantly outperforming config_001 (singleprofile, no aggregation) at 0.422 acc, confirming that multiprofile + transformer aggregation is a strong design choice. The remaining key uncertainty within this promising backbone is the fusion method: weighted vs. concat. This experiment (config_042) is a direct one-variable change from config_018, swapping weighted fusion for concat fusion while keeping all other components identical. This is the best use of experiment 3 because it exploits the strongest evidence so far by testing the most impactful remaining design choice (fusion) within the already-validated architecture, reducing uncertainty about whether a simpler concat fusion could match or exceed the weighted approach. Expected cost is similar to config_018 (~2.8–3.0 GPU hours) since the architecture and encoders are identical, only the final fusion layer changes.

Evidence: The best config so far (config_018, acc=0.520) uses scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted in a multiprofile setting. The multiprofile+transformer architecture is clearly validated (0.52 vs 0.42 for singleprofile), and weighted fusion slightly edges concat (0.520 vs 0.507). However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (scgpt) in this winning architecture. Question: config_040 swaps scgpt for scvi_n200 while keeping all other settings identical (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted), directly isolating the RNA encoder's contribution. scvi_n200 is a well-established VAE that captures different biological variance than the GPT-based scgpt, and may complement the image modality differently. This is the highest-value unexplored dimension given our current best. Cost: scvi_n200 is a smaller encoder than scgpt, so RNA encoding should be marginally cheaper, but the dominant costs (ViT-L image encoder + transformer aggregation) remain, so expected cost is ~2.5–3.0 GPU hours, comparable to config_018. With 6 experiments remaining, this targeted comparison will either confirm scgpt's superiority or unlock a new best, guiding subsequent exploitation.

Evidence: config_040 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) achieved 0.725 acc, far exceeding all scgpt-based configs (~0.52). The RNA encoder is clearly the dominant factor. However, the fusion strategy (weighted vs concat) has only been tested with the weaker scgpt encoder, where weighted narrowly beat concat (0.520 vs 0.507). With the much stronger scvi_n200 representations, the fusion dynamics may differ. This experiment (config_008) is a clean single-variable A/B against config_040, changing only fusion from weighted to concat. It clarifies whether the current best config's fusion choice is truly optimal or whether concat could match/exceed it. If concat performs comparably, it confirms robustness; if weighted is clearly better, it locks in the best configuration. Expected cost: ~4.0 GPU hours (slightly higher than config_040's 3.6 based on the concat vs weighted cost difference seen in scgpt configs: 3.95 vs 2.86). This is the best use of experiment 5 because it directly exploits the strongest finding while resolving the one remaining untested design dimension in the top-performing architecture family, with 5 experiments still remaining for further exploration.

Evidence: scvi_n200 RNA encoder with multiprofile + transformer aggregation is clearly the dominant architecture (0.725 acc for config_040, 0.721 for config_008), far outperforming scgpt (~0.52) and singleprofile (~0.42). Fusion method (weighted vs concat) shows negligible difference (~0.4%). The key untested variable for this top-performing RNA encoder is the image encoder: all top configs use imagenet_vit_l, but resnet50 has never been paired with scvi_n200. This experiment (config_048: scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted) isolates the image-encoder choice while holding all other parameters at their best-known values. It clarifies whether the image modality's contribution is architecture-dependent and whether a different visual backbone could complement the RNA features to push accuracy above 0.725. Under the 4-remaining-experiment budget, this is the highest-information test: if resnet50 matches or beats ViT-L, we gain a cheaper image pathway; if it underperforms, we confirm ViT-L is optimal and can focus remaining budget on finer tuning. Expected relative cost: moderate-to-low (~2.5–3.0 GPU hours), since ResNet-50 is substantially smaller than ViT-Large, making this cheaper than config_040 (3.60 hrs) while maintaining the same transformer aggregation and fusion pipeline.

Evidence: The top-3 results (config_040: 0.725, config_008: 0.721, config_048: 0.713) all use scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer aggregation, confirming scvi_n200 as the dominant RNA encoder and multiprofile as essential. Within this region, weighted fusion slightly beats concat and imagenet_vit_l slightly beats resnet50 in accuracy. The one untested dimension in this promising region is the aggregation method (avgpool vs. transformer). Question: Does avgpool aggregation with the best encoders and weighted fusion (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + avgpool + weighted) approach or match the transformer-aggregation result of 0.725, or is the transformer's expressive capacity genuinely necessary? Why this is the best use: It tests the last unexplored design axis in the highest-performing configuration family, reduces uncertainty about whether the more expensive transformer aggregation is truly contributing or merely adding complexity, and if avgpool performs comparably it offers a cheaper path to the same accuracy. Expected relative cost: avgpool is a simple pooling operation with no self-attention, so this should train faster than config_040 (3.60 GPU hrs); I estimate ~2.5–3.0 GPU hours, making it a moderate-cost experiment that preserves budget for the remaining 3 trials.

Evidence: config_040 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is the current best at 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. Within the scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer region, we have tested vit_l+weighted (0.725), vit_l+concat (0.721), and resnet50+weighted (0.713). The only untested cell in this 2×2 grid is resnet50+concat (config_010). Question: does the resnet50+concat combination produce any synergistic effect that could match or exceed 0.725, or does it confirm that vit_l+weighted is the optimal pairing? This is the best use of experiment 8 because (a) it completes the critical design-space grid for the top-performing architecture family, (b) it directly tests the last plausible alternative to the current best, and (c) if it fails to beat config_040, the remaining experiment 9 can be used to test a lower-priority variation (e.g., avgpool aggregation) or simply confirm the winner. Expected cost: ~5–6 GPU hours (resnet50 + transformer aggregation, comparable to config_048's 6.22 h), bringing total to ~32–33 GPU hours, well within a reasonable budget for 10 experiments.

The current best (config_040, 0.725) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted. All tested scvi_n200 multiprofile variants are at or below this level, so further exploitation of that encoder family has diminishing returns. The largest untested variable is the RNA encoder: pca_n2000 has never been evaluated in the multiprofile multimodal setting. Config_004 pairs pca_n2000 with the proven-best downstream architecture (imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted), directly testing whether a simpler linear encoder can approach scvi_n200's performance. This is the highest-information experiment: if pca_n2000 reaches ~0.70+, it offers a cheaper alternative (expected ~2.5–3.0 GPU hours vs. 3.60 for scvi_n200), and the remaining experiment could explore further pca_n2000 variants; if it falls well below, it confirms scvi_n200 is essential and locks in config_040 as the final answer. Expected relative cost: moderate-to-low (~2.5–3.0 GPU hours), cheaper than the current best due to the simpler PCA encoder.

Evidence: The best configuration found is config_040 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy. All top performers share multiprofile + scvi_n200 + transformer aggregation. The singleprofile experiment (config_001) used scgpt and scored only 0.422, but we have not tested singleprofile with the superior scvi_n200 encoder. This experiment tests whether the RNA encoder quality advantage of scvi_n200 carries over to singleprofile mode, clarifying the interaction between profile setting and encoder choice. It is very unlikely to beat 0.725 (no aggregation mechanism), but as the final experiment with the best already identified, it is the most cost-effective choice (~0.7 GPU hours, similar to config_001) that still yields informative data about component interactions. Expected relative cost: very low, roughly 1/5 of the multiprofile transformer experiments.

With no prior experiments, the most critical uncertainty is whether combining RNA and image modalities with strong learned encoders (scGPT for RNA, ViT-L for image) in a multimodal setting yields a meaningful accuracy gain over what single-modality or weaker-encoder approaches could achieve. Config_001 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, concat) tests this core hypothesis in the simplest structural form—no aggregation layer, single profile—so any performance signal is cleanly attributable to the encoder quality and modality combination rather than confounded by aggregation or multiprofile complexity. If it performs well, subsequent experiments can exploit by adding multiprofile + transformer/avgpool aggregation; if it underperforms, I can ablate to identify whether the RNA encoder, image encoder, or fusion strategy is the bottleneck. Cost: moderate-to-high (two large pretrained encoders: scGPT and ViT-L), but no aggregation overhead, making it roughly 60-70% of the cost of the most expensive multiprofile+transformer configs. This is the best use of experiment 1 because it establishes a strong anchor point and isolates the single most impactful design question (multimodal + strong encoders) before spending budget on finer-grained ablations.

Evidence: config_001 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieved only 43.5% accuracy, which is low and suggests the single-profile architecture may be a bottleneck. With just one data point, the most important uncertainty is whether multiprofile aggregation—a major architectural axis—can substantially improve performance. Question tested: config_006 keeps the exact same RNA encoder (scgpt), image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), and fusion (concat) as config_001 but switches to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, isolating the effect of multiprofile aggregation. Why this is the best next experiment: it is the minimal, most direct extension of the only completed experiment, so any accuracy change can be attributed to the multiprofile+aggregation shift. Avgpool is the cheapest aggregation (vs. transformer), keeping cost moderate while still testing the key hypothesis. If multiprofile helps, the remaining 7 experiments can exploit that direction (try transformer, weighted fusion, different encoders); if it does not, we learn the bottleneck lies in the encoders or fusion and can pivot. Expected relative cost: moderate increase over config_001 (~1.5–2×, roughly 1.4–1.9 GPU hours) due to processing multiple profiles and the avgpool aggregation step, but still well within budget with 8 experiments remaining.

Evidence: config_006 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieved the best accuracy (0.5176) with a large margin over config_001 (singleprofile, 0.4348), confirming that multiprofile + avgpool aggregation is the key architectural choice. The only untested variable within this exact architecture is the fusion method (concat vs. weighted). Question: Does weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation when combining scgpt RNA and ViT-L image features after avgpool aggregation? This is a clean single-variable ablation of the best configuration. Rationale: With 7 experiments remaining, testing the minimal change (fusion only) on the strongest known architecture is the highest-information, lowest-risk next step. If weighted fusion helps, we gain a free accuracy boost; if not, we can rule it out and focus subsequent experiments on aggregation (transformer) or encoder swaps. Expected cost: approximately 7.2 GPU hours, comparable to config_006 since the architecture (multiprofile, scgpt, ViT-L, avgpool) is identical—only the fusion layer changes.

Evidence: The best configuration so far (config_013, acc=0.542) uses multiprofile + scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted fusion. Moving from singleprofile→multiprofile gave +8.3% acc, and concat→weighted fusion gave +2.4% acc, confirming that richer profile aggregation and learned fusion weights help. The key remaining uncertainty is whether a more expressive aggregation mechanism (transformer attention) can outperform simple average pooling when combining multiple profiles. This experiment (config_035) tests exactly that: it swaps avgpool→transformer while keeping all other settings identical to the current best (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, weighted, multiprofile). If transformer aggregation captures inter-profile relationships better than mean pooling, we expect a meaningful accuracy gain; if not, it confirms avgpool is sufficient and we can pivot to other axes (e.g., RNA encoder or image encoder). Cost: transformer aggregation adds self-attention layers over profiles, so I estimate ~4–6 GPU hours (moderately more expensive than config_013's 2.94 h but well within budget). This is the highest-value exploitation step: it directly extends the best-known direction with a single, well-motivated change, and with 6 experiments remaining, confirming or ruling out transformer aggregation early will guide the rest of the search efficiently.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_013 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) at 0.5420 accuracy. The multiprofile + avgpool + weighted combination is strongly validated across experiments (config_006, 013, 035 all confirm multiprofile >> singleprofile, and avgpool+weighted > other combos). Uncertainty: Whether scgpt is specifically required or whether scvi_n200 (a learned 200-dim RNA representation) can match or exceed it within the same proven architecture. This experiment (config_021: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable test of the RNA encoder while holding all other settings at their proven-best values. It reduces uncertainty about encoder choice and, if scvi_n200 performs comparably, offers a cheaper alternative for future runs. Expected cost: scvi_n200 is a smaller encoder than scgpt, so I estimate ~2.0–2.5 GPU hours, slightly below config_013's 2.94. This is the best use of experiment 5 because it exploits the strongest architectural direction while probing the single most impactful remaining design variable (RNA encoder quality) before committing remaining budget to further exploitation or alternative image encoders.

The strongest evidence from 5 experiments is that scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder is the dominant factor: config_021 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) achieved 0.706 accuracy vs. ~0.54 for all scgpt configs. The remaining uncertainty is whether transformer aggregation can improve on avgpool for scvi_n200. With scgpt, avgpool (0.542) slightly beat transformer (0.520), but scvi_n200's learned latent representations may interact differently with attention-based aggregation. Config_024 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) is a single-variable extension of the current best config, directly testing whether transformer aggregation can push accuracy above 0.706. Expected cost is moderate (~3–5 GPU hours, comparable to config_035's 2.86 with scgpt+transformer and config_021's 4.82 with scvi_n200+avgpool), making it a focused, informative exploitation step that leaves 4 experiments to further refine the best configuration.

The evidence strongly shows scvi_n200 as the dominant RNA encoder (0.706–0.725 vs ≤0.542 for scgpt), with transformer aggregation and weighted fusion as the best settings (config_024: 0.725). However, all top-performing configs use imagenet_vit_l as the image encoder, leaving the image-encoder dimension untested for the scvi_n200 family. config_022 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) isolates the image-encoder variable while holding the best aggregation and fusion fixed. If resnet50 matches vit_l, we confirm the image encoder is not a bottleneck and save GPU hours for remaining experiments; if it underperforms, we confirm vit_l is essential and can focus the last 2 experiments on fine-tuning other aspects. Expected cost is moderate-to-low (~2.5–3.5 GPU hours), cheaper than config_024 (3.60 h) since resnet50 is a smaller backbone than ViT-L, making this an efficient uncertainty-reduction experiment with 3 experiments still in budget.

Evidence: config_024 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) is our best at 0.725 accuracy. We've confirmed that multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, and imagenet_vit_l are the optimal settings for their respective axes. The only untested variable in this 'best architecture' is the RNA encoder: we've tested scgpt (poor, ~0.54) and scvi_n200 (excellent, ~0.725), but pca_n2000 remains untested in the multiprofile+transformer+weighted setting. Question: Could the higher-dimensional linear representation (n2000 vs n200) of PCA capture complementary information that the learned scvi encoder misses, potentially matching or exceeding 0.725? Rationale: With only 2 experiments remaining, this is the highest-information experiment—if pca_n2000 is competitive, we gain a new candidate; if not, we confirm scvi_n200 is optimal and can spend remaining budget on a final confirmation or minor variant. Expected cost: ~3–4 GPU hours (PCA encoding is cheaper than scvi, but transformer aggregation and multimodal fusion dominate), comparable to config_024's 3.60 GPU hours.

The evidence strongly identifies scvi_n200 + multiprofile + weighted fusion as the dominant configuration family (0.706–0.725 vs ≤0.586 for all other RNA encoders). Within this family, the 2×2 design of image encoder (imagenet_vit_l vs resnet50) × aggregation (transformer vs avgpool) has three of four cells filled: transformer+ViT-L=0.725 (best), avgpool+ViT-L=0.706, transformer+ResNet50=0.713. Config_041 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the only remaining cell. It tests whether the ResNet50+avgpool combination could rival or exceed the current best (0.725), or confirm that the transformer+ViT-L pairing in config_024 is the optimal setting. Given only one experiment remains after this, completing the factorial design maximizes information: if config_041 lands near 0.71–0.72, it confirms config_024 as the winner; if it unexpectedly exceeds 0.725, we capture a new best. Expected relative cost: moderate (~4–5 GPU hours, comparable to config_021's 4.82 h for avgpool+ViT-L and below config_022's 6.22 h for transformer+ResNet50), keeping total budget around ~37–38 GPU hours.

Evidence: The best configuration found is config_024 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy. All top performers share scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer + weighted, with imagenet_vit_l slightly outperforming resnet50. The only untested variant of this near-optimal combination is config_044, which swaps weighted→concat fusion while keeping the best RNA encoder, image encoder, and aggregation. Question: Can concat fusion with transformer aggregation on scvi_n200+imagenet_vit_l match or exceed the weighted-fusion result? While weighted has been consistently superior in prior comparisons (e.g., 0.542 vs 0.518 for scgpt+imagenet_vit_l), a direct test under the strongest encoder/aggregation stack is the most informative remaining experiment. Why this is the best final choice: It is the closest untested neighbor to the current best, giving the highest (albeit modest) probability of a small improvement, while remaining relatively cheap (~3.5–4.0 GPU hours, comparable to config_024's 3.60). This keeps total GPU hours near ~43, well below the cost of resnet50-based alternatives (~6+ GPU hours). No other untested configuration has a realistic chance of exceeding 0.725 given the strong encoder and aggregation evidence.

With no prior results, the key uncertainty is whether a multimodal (RNA+image) single-profile model with a biologically-informed RNA encoder and a standard CNN image encoder provides a strong baseline. config_026 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, weighted fusion) tests this core premise: it uses scvi_n200 (a learned encoder capturing cell-type structure, likely superior to PCA for downstream classification) paired with resnet50 (a solid but not maximally expensive image backbone) and a simple weighted fusion. This gives a competitive reference point at moderate cost—scvi_n200 is more expensive than PCA but far cheaper than scgpt, resnet50 is cheaper than ViT-L, and singleprofile avoids the overhead of multiprofile aggregation. Establishing this baseline early lets subsequent experiments efficiently probe whether upgrading the image encoder (ViT-L), switching to multiprofile, or changing fusion/aggregation yields meaningful gains, rather than wasting budget on an overly expensive first trial. Expected relative cost: moderate (roughly 1.5–2× a PCA+resnet50 singleprofile run, well below multiprofile+ViT-L+transformer configurations).

The single completed experiment (config_026, multimodal singleprofile scvi_n200+resnet50 weighted) achieved ~54% accuracy, providing only a weak baseline. The most impactful untested design choice is whether multiprofile aggregation improves over singleprofile, as it fundamentally changes how cellular information is integrated. config_030 isolates this variable: it keeps the same RNA encoder (scvi_n200), image encoder (resnet50), and fusion strategy (weighted) as the baseline, changing only singleprofile→multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. This is a controlled, informative test: if multiprofile+avgpool improves accuracy, it justifies further investment in stronger aggregators (transformer); if not, it confirms singleprofile suffices and saves GPU hours. Expected relative cost is moderate—roughly 1.5–2× the 0.59 GPU hours of the baseline (≈0.9–1.2 GPU hours) due to processing multiple profiles and the avgpool step, but well below transformer-aggregation variants. This is the best use of experiment 2 because it reduces the largest architectural uncertainty at a controlled cost, preserving budget for follow-up exploitation in the remaining 7 experiments.

Evidence: config_030 (multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieved 0.678 accuracy, a large jump over config_026 (singleprofile, same encoders/fusion) at 0.540, confirming multiprofile aggregation is the dominant design lever. The remaining uncertainty is whether the simple avgpool aggregation is sufficient or whether a transformer-based aggregation over profiles can capture richer inter-profile interactions. Question tested: config_020 keeps the exact same encoders (scvi_n200, resnet50) and fusion (weighted) as config_030 but replaces avgpool with transformer aggregation, isolating the aggregation method as the single variable. Why this is the best next experiment: it is the most direct and informative extension of our best result, targeting the component most likely to yield further accuracy gains (profile-to-profile relationship modeling). The expected cost is moderate—roughly 7–8 GPU hours (slightly above config_030's 5.90 due to attention over profiles, but no heavier image encoder), keeping total spend around ~14 GPU hours and leaving ample budget for 6 follow-up experiments to explore image-encoder upgrades or fusion changes if transformer aggregation proves beneficial.

Evidence: The current best (config_020, acc=0.713) uses multimodal + multiprofile + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion with scvi_n200/resnet50. The progression from single→multiprofile (+0.138) and avgpool→transformer (+0.035) shows strong gains from richer architecture. The fusion strategy (weighted vs. concat) is the one untested variable within this exact architecture. Question: Does concat fusion outperform weighted fusion when combining RNA and image features after transformer-based multiprofile aggregation? This is a single-variable change from the current best, so any accuracy difference is cleanly attributable to the fusion method. Why this experiment: It is the cheapest and most direct way to reduce uncertainty about an important design choice while preserving the proven multiprofile+transformer backbone. Expected cost is very similar to config_020 (~6.2 GPU hours, same encoders and aggregation), keeping total spend around ~19 GPU hours and leaving ample budget for 5 further experiments. If concat wins, it opens a new axis of improvement; if weighted holds, we confirm the current best and can pivot to testing a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) or alternative RNA encoder in subsequent runs.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) at 0.713 acc. All four completed experiments use resnet50 as the image encoder, so the impact of a stronger image encoder is completely untested. The multiprofile + transformer + weighted combination is clearly the winning architecture (0.713 vs 0.540 singleprofile, 0.678 avgpool, 0.688 concat). Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l improve accuracy in this proven-best multimodal setup? config_010 is config_020 with only the image encoder changed, isolating this single variable. Rationale: The image encoder is the largest untested design axis, and ViT-L is substantially more expressive than ResNet50; if it helps, it could push accuracy well above 0.713. With 5 experiments left, identifying whether the larger encoder is worth its cost is the highest-value uncertainty to resolve. Expected relative cost: higher than config_020 (6.22 GPU hrs) due to the larger ViT-L backbone, likely ~9-12 GPU hrs, but justified because it tests the most promising accuracy lever.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_010 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc / 3.60 GPU hrs. Key findings: multiprofile >> single profile, transformer > avgpool aggregation, weighted > concat fusion, and imagenet_vit_l ≥ resnet50 (while being cheaper). The RNA encoder is the one major axis not yet varied within this best architecture. Question: Does scgpt (a generative-pretrained RNA encoder) produce better cell-level representations than scvi_n200 (a VAE) when paired with the strong ViT_L + transformer + weighted pipeline? This is a high-value exploration because if scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, it confirms the architecture is robust to encoder choice; if it underperforms, it validates scvi_n200 as the right encoder and narrows the search. Cost: Expected training cost is comparable to config_010 (~3.5–4.5 GPU hrs) since the dominant cost drivers (ViT_L image processing, transformer aggregation) are identical; scgpt's forward pass is modestly more expensive than scvi_n200 but not dramatically so. With 4 experiments remaining, this is the best balance of exploitation (staying in the proven top architecture) and exploration (testing the last major untested variable), maximizing the chance of finding a >0.725 configuration before the budget ends.

The current best is config_010 (0.725 acc) with multiprofile + scvi_n200 + vit_l + transformer + weighted. The main untested dimension in this top-performing architecture is the RNA encoder: we know scvi_n200 works well and scgpt is poor (0.520), but pca_n2000 has never been paired with vit_l + transformer + weighted. Config_017 (pca_n2000, vit_l, transformer, weighted) directly tests whether a simpler, cheaper linear RNA encoder can match or exceed scvi_n200 in the best-known architecture. If it performs comparably, it reduces compute cost for future runs; if it is clearly worse, it confirms scvi_n200 is essential and we can focus remaining budget on fine-tuning around config_010. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves the last major untested variable in the top-performing configuration space, and with only 3 experiments remaining after this one, we need to confirm the optimal RNA encoder before exploiting. Expected cost: ~2.5–3.5 GPU hours (pca_n2000 is a linear projection, much cheaper than the scvi VAE, so this should be notably cheaper than config_010's 3.60 hrs).

The current best is config_010 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc=0.7250). All major design axes have been explored: multiprofile >> singleprofile, transformer > avgpool, scvi_n200 >> scgpt/pca_n2000, and vit_l > resnet50. The only untested variant of this top architecture is the fusion method (concat vs. weighted). While config_007 vs config_020 suggests weighted > concat with resnet50, that evidence was gathered with a weaker image encoder; it is possible the interaction with vit_l's higher-dimensional features shifts the balance. Testing config_050 directly clarifies whether config_010's 0.7250 is the ceiling for this architecture family or whether a different fusion could nudge it higher. With only 2 experiments remaining, this is the highest-information, lowest-risk exploitation step: if it matches or beats config_010, we have a strong final answer; if it falls short, we confirm config_010 as the best and can use the last experiment for a final confirmation or a cheap sanity check. Expected cost is similar to config_010 (~3.5–4.0 GPU hours) since the architecture is identical except for the fusion operation, making it a moderate-cost experiment relative to the transformer-aggregation multiprofile runs (~6 GPU hours).

Evidence: The current best is config_010 (scvi_n200, vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc, with config_050 (same but concat) at 0.721 and config_020 (resnet50 instead of vit_l) at 0.713. All four scvi_n200+transformer combinations are tested, and the pattern is clear: scvi_n200 > pca_n2000 > scgpt, vit_l ≥ resnet50, transformer > avgpool, weighted ≥ concat. Question: config_041 (scvi_n200, vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is the closest untested variant to the best configuration, swapping only transformer→avgpool. It tests whether the ~3.5% transformer advantage seen with resnet50 (config_020 vs config_030) holds with vit_l, and whether avgpool could be a cheaper near-equivalent. Why this is the best use: With 1 experiment remaining after this, config_041 has the highest expected accuracy among all untested options (~0.69–0.71) while retaining all other optimal components. It is also expected to be relatively cheap (~3–4 GPU hours, comparable to config_010's 3.60 since vit_l configs train faster than resnet50 configs). If it underperforms as expected, it confirms transformer aggregation is necessary and solidifies config_010 as the final answer with high confidence, leaving the last experiment for a long-shot exploration if desired.

Evidence: The best configuration found is config_010 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc=0.7250). All other tested variants with the same encoders but different aggregation/fusion (config_050: transformer+concat=0.7207, config_041: avgpool+weighted=0.7062) show consistent degradation. The only untested configuration retaining both top encoders (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l) is config_016 (avgpool + concat). Question: This tests whether the avgpool+concat combination with the best encoders could unexpectedly match or exceed the transformer+weighted result, closing the last gap in the scvi_n200+ViT-L subgrid. Rationale: As the final experiment, this is the highest-ceiling untested option given that all other untested configs substitute a weaker RNA encoder (pca_n2000, scgpt) or image encoder (resnet50), both of which have shown substantial performance drops (0.52–0.59 range). While config_016 is unlikely to surpass 0.7250, it is the most informative remaining test and confirms the design-space boundary. Expected cost: ~4.5–5.0 GPU hours (similar to config_041 at 4.82 h, since avgpool+concat vs avgpool+weighted is a minor fusion change), bringing total to ~43 GPU hours.

With no prior evidence, the most critical uncertainty is whether a multimodal (RNA + image) model outperforms single-modality baselines, and what a reasonable multimodal baseline accuracy looks like. config_007 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, weighted fusion) tests this core hypothesis with a clean, interpretable setup: it combines both modalities using the cheapest RNA encoder (PCA) and the lighter image backbone (ResNet50), avoiding the added cost of multiprofile aggregation or transformer layers. This gives me a solid accuracy anchor to later compare against (a) single-modality configs to confirm multimodal benefit, (b) ViT-L vs ResNet50, (c) scGPT/scVI vs PCA, and (d) different fusion/aggregation strategies. Expected relative cost: low-to-moderate — ResNet50 is roughly half the parameter count of ViT-L, PCA encoding is negligible, singleprofile avoids multiprofile data overhead, and no aggregation module adds training time. This keeps GPU hours low, preserving budget for follow-up experiments that probe the most promising directions.

With only one completed experiment (config_007: multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, weighted fusion → 52.3% acc, 0.87 GPU-hr), the most critical uncertainty is whether moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with aggregation meaningfully improves performance. config_010 is the cleanest controlled extension of config_007: it keeps the same RNA encoder (pca_n2000), the same image encoder (resnet50), and the same fusion strategy (weighted), changing only the profile setting to multiprofile and adding avgpool aggregation. This isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation as the single variable. If accuracy improves, it validates the multiprofile direction and justifies investing remaining budget in stronger encoders (scgpt, ViT-L) or transformer aggregation on top of it. If it does not improve, it tells us singleprofile is sufficient and we should pivot to encoder upgrades. The expected cost is modestly higher than config_007 (~1.0–1.3 GPU-hr) due to multiprofile processing, but avgpool is a cheap aggregation, so the overhead is limited. Under an 8-experiment remaining budget, this controlled comparison is the highest-information-per-GPU-hour next step.

Evidence: config_010 (multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieved 0.639 accuracy, a large jump over config_007's 0.523 (singleprofile), confirming multiprofile+avgpool is the dominant design choice. Uncertainty: whether the weighted fusion is optimal or whether concatenation captures complementary modality information more effectively. This experiment tests exactly that—config_008 is identical to config_010 except fusion changes from weighted to concat. It is the minimal, most informative single-variable change from the current best, directly clarifying whether we can push accuracy higher with a different fusion strategy before investing in more expensive encoder or aggregation changes. Expected relative cost: similar to config_010 (~10–11 GPU hours) since the architecture (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool) is unchanged; only the fusion layer differs, so training time should be comparable.

Evidence: config_010 (multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is our best at 0.639 acc, and the multiprofile+weighted fusion combination is clearly superior to singleprofile (0.523) or concat fusion (0.619, at 3.4× the cost). The one untested axis within this exact architecture is the aggregation method: avgpool vs. transformer. Question: Does transformer-based aggregation (learning which profiles to emphasize) improve over simple average pooling while retaining the cheap weighted fusion? This is a single-variable extension of our best result, isolating the aggregation contribution. Rationale: With 6 experiments left, establishing whether transformer aggregation adds value is critical before investing in more expensive changes (larger image encoders, learned RNA encoders). If transformer helps, it becomes the new backbone for subsequent experiments; if not, we confirm avgpool suffices and redirect budget toward encoder upgrades. Expected cost: moderate, roughly 15–25 GPU hours (transformer attention over profiles adds cost over avgpool, but weighted fusion keeps it well below the 36+ hours seen with concat fusion).

Evidence: config_010 (multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the current best at 0.639 acc / 10.60 GPU hrs, clearly showing that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion is the strongest combination. The two untested levers that could push accuracy higher are the RNA encoder (PCA is linear and limited) and the image encoder (ResNet50 is mid-tier). This experiment tests upgrading the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l while holding all other settings at their proven best (multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool, weighted), giving a clean single-variable ablation. It clarifies whether the image representation is a bottleneck: if accuracy improves meaningfully over 0.639, the visual pathway is under-utilized and further gains may come from pairing ViT-L with a learned RNA encoder; if it does not, the RNA encoder is the priority. Expected cost: ViT-L is roughly 2× the parameters of ResNet50, so I estimate ~15–20 GPU hrs—moderately more expensive than config_010 but well within budget, and cheaper than the concat-fusion runs (~36 GPU hrs). With 5 experiments remaining, this focused test is the highest-information-per-cost choice before committing to a full dual-encoder upgrade.

Evidence: The current best (config_010, acc=0.639) uses multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion with pca_n2000 and resnet50. All five completed experiments use pca_n2000, so the RNA encoder is the largest untested design axis. The architecture (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) is well-supported: avgpool beat transformer (0.639 vs 0.573) and weighted beat concat (0.639 vs 0.619). Question: Does replacing the simple PCA projection with the pretrained scgpt encoder improve validation accuracy while keeping the proven aggregation/fusion pipeline? config_029 (scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable change from the current best, isolating the RNA encoder effect. Why this experiment: With 4 experiments remaining, testing the most impactful unexplored variable (RNA encoder) in the already-validated architecture gives the highest information gain. If scgpt helps, we can then explore scvi_n200 or combine with ViT in remaining trials. Expected cost: scgpt is a pretrained forward-pass encoder, so training cost should be comparable to the pca_n2000 baseline (~10–15 GPU hours), similar to config_010's 10.60 h, making it a moderate-cost experiment that doesn't risk exhausting the budget.

The current best is config_010 (pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) at 0.639 accuracy. Key evidence: (1) avgpool >> transformer (0.639 vs 0.573), (2) weighted >> concat (0.639 vs 0.619), (3) pca_n2000 >> scgpt (0.639 vs 0.525), and (4) resnet50 ≈ imagenet_vit_l (0.639 vs 0.635). The one major untested variable in the best-known architecture is the RNA encoder scvi_n200. config_035 isolates this single change (scvi_n200 replacing pca_n2000) while holding all other settings at their proven-best values. This is critical because scgpt was a different learned encoder that performed poorly, but scvi_n200 (a VAE-based 200-dim representation) is architecturally distinct and untested. If it improves, we have a new best; if not, we can confidently rule out learned RNA encoders and focus remaining budget on other axes. Expected relative cost: moderate, roughly 10–11 GPU hours (similar to config_010's 10.60 hrs since it uses the same resnet50 image encoder and multiprofile avgpool architecture, with a slightly smaller RNA representation).

The current best is config_035 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.678 accuracy. The key evidence is that scvi_n200 dramatically outperforms pca_n2000 (+4 pts) and scgpt (+15 pts), and avgpool+weighted is the best aggregation/fusion combo. The remaining uncertainty is whether a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) complements the richer scvi_n200 representation better than resnet50. With pca_n2000 the image encoder difference was negligible (0.639 vs 0.635), but scvi_n200 produces a more complex learned embedding that may interact differently with a higher-capacity vision backbone. config_047 is a single-variable upgrade of the best config (only image encoder changes), making the result cleanly interpretable. If it improves, it confirms the multimodal synergy hypothesis; if not, it confirms resnet50 is sufficient and we can focus remaining budget on other axes. Expected cost is ~7–8 GPU hours (comparable to config_042 at 7.02 with imagenet_vit_l, slightly above config_035's 5.90 due to the larger ViT-L), which is moderate and well within budget.

The current best is config_047 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.706). The evidence strongly supports scvi_n200 as the best RNA encoder, imagenet_vit_l as the best image encoder, and weighted fusion. The main uncertainty is whether transformer aggregation could outperform avgpool when paired with the richer scvi_n200 representations. Previous evidence against transformer (config_032: 0.573 vs config_010: 0.639) was obtained with the weaker pca_n2000 encoder; scvi_n200's more structured, high-dimensional latent space may benefit from the attention-based interactions that transformer aggregation captures, which a simple average would discard. This experiment tests that specific hypothesis while keeping all other components at their proven-best settings. Expected cost is moderate (~5-7 GPU hours), comparable to config_047's 4.82 hours plus a small transformer overhead, keeping total budget well within reasonable bounds. With only 1 experiment remaining after this, testing the single most uncertain design axis (aggregation) with the strongest encoder combination is the highest-value use of the slot.

The evidence strongly identifies scvi_n200 (RNA), imagenet_vit_l (image), and transformer aggregation as the best-performing components, with config_009 (all three + weighted fusion) achieving 0.7250 accuracy at only 3.60 GPU hours. The only untested variant of this top combination is config_021, which swaps weighted fusion for concat fusion. While prior evidence (config_010 vs config_008) suggests weighted outperforms concat by ~2%, this is the last experiment and the only remaining untested configuration that retains all three best components. It tests whether concat fusion might interact differently with transformer aggregation to potentially match or exceed config_009. Expected cost is similar to config_009 (~3–4 GPU hours), keeping total budget low. This is the best use of the final experiment: it either discovers a new best or confirms config_009 as the optimal configuration with minimal additional cost.

With no prior evidence, the first experiment should establish a strong multimodal baseline to anchor all subsequent comparisons. config_002 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) combines the most promising design choices: multiprofile for richer cell-level information, scgpt as a well-established pretrained RNA encoder, resnet50 as a solid yet relatively fast image backbone, avgpool for efficient multiprofile aggregation, and weighted fusion as a standard multimodal combination strategy. This tests the core hypothesis that combining RNA and image modalities with a strong encoder pair yields high validation accuracy. It is cost-moderate (resnet50 + avgpool is cheaper than imagenet_vit_l + transformer, but more expensive than single-modality baselines), making it an efficient first probe. The resulting accuracy will serve as the reference point for later ablations (e.g., swapping to imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, scvi_n200, or singleprofile) in the remaining 9 experiments.

With only one completed experiment (config_002, multimodal/multiprofile/scgpt/resnet50/avgpool/weighted at 52.5% acc, 4.42 GPU hrs), the most critical uncertainty is whether the multimodal combination is actually contributing over a single modality, or whether one modality dominates. config_005 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cheapest possible informative experiment—no RNA encoder, single profile (no aggregation), and resnet50 is a standard pretrained encoder—so expected cost is roughly 0.5–1.0 GPU hours, far below config_002. If image-only accuracy is close to 52.5%, RNA adds little value under this setup and future experiments should focus on image-encoder upgrades (e.g., ViT-L) or fusion refinements. If image-only is substantially lower (e.g., <40%), the RNA modality is clearly contributing and we should exploit that by testing RNA-encoder variants (scvi_n200, pca_n2000) and aggregation strategies. This single cheap experiment partitions the 8 remaining budget much more effectively than a second multimodal run, which would only give a small incremental signal on one sub-dimension while leaving the modality-contribution question unresolved.

Evidence: config_002 (scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.525 acc, while image-only (config_005) is only 0.208, confirming both modalities contribute. The single most impactful untested dimension is the image backbone: upgrading resnet50 (~25M params) to imagenet_vit_l (~300M params) is the largest representational capacity jump available. This experiment (config_018) changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l while holding all other settings identical to the current best (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted), isolating the effect of a stronger visual backbone. If it improves accuracy meaningfully, subsequent experiments can exploit ViT-L with transformer aggregation or different fusion; if it does not, we redirect to RNA-encoder or aggregation changes. Expected relative cost: roughly 2–3× config_002 (~8–12 GPU hours) due to ViT-L's larger parameter count and higher per-step compute, but this is justified as it is the most likely single change to yield the largest accuracy gain within our remaining 7-experiment budget.

Evidence: config_018 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) is the current best at 0.542 acc, clearly outperforming config_002 (resnet50) and confirming that multimodal + multiprofile + scgpt + imagenet_vit_l is the strongest backbone. The key untested dimension on this backbone is aggregation strategy. Question: Will transformer aggregation (config_015) outperform avgpool by capturing richer inter-profile relationships while retaining the proven scgpt/imagenet_vit_l/weighted-fusion components? Rationale: This is a minimal, high-information extension of the best config—only one variable (aggregation) changes, so any accuracy delta is cleanly attributable. Transformer aggregation is the most architecturally impactful remaining choice for multiprofile settings and could yield a meaningful jump over simple averaging. Expected cost: ~3.5–4.5 GPU hrs (moderately higher than config_018's 2.94 due to transformer attention over profiles, but well within budget with 6 experiments remaining and only 7.48 GPU hrs used so far).

Evidence: config_018 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is the current best at 0.542 acc / 0.483 F1 with 2.94 GPU hrs. All top-performing configs use weighted fusion; concat fusion has not yet been tested in any multiprofile multimodal setting. Question: Does concat fusion outperform weighted fusion when paired with the best-known backbone (scgpt + ViT-L + avgpool)? This is a clean single-variable change from config_018, isolating the fusion strategy. Why this experiment: With 5 experiments remaining, confirming or rejecting concat fusion early is critical because it interacts with every other design choice (RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation). If concat is superior, subsequent experiments can pair it with alternative RNA encoders (scvi_n200, pca_n2000) for further gains. Expected cost is similar to config_018 (~2.9–3.0 GPU hrs) since the architecture is identical except for the fusion operation, making this a low-risk, high-information experiment.

The best result so far is config_018 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.542). Across the tested configs, imagenet_vit_l > resnet50, avgpool > transformer, and weighted > concat, so the architecture is relatively well-optimized. The one major untested variable in this top-performing architecture is the RNA encoder: we've only tried scgpt. config_047 swaps scgpt for scvi_n200 while keeping the best image encoder, aggregation, and fusion. This directly tests whether a VAE-based RNA encoder captures complementary biological signal that could push accuracy above 0.542. Expected cost is similar to config_018 (~2.5–3.0 GPU hours) since the architecture is identical and scvi_n200 is a comparable or slightly smaller encoder than scgpt. With 4 experiments remaining, confirming or improving the RNA encoder choice in the best architecture is the highest-value next step before fine-tuning further.

The strongest result so far is config_047 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) at 0.706 accuracy, dramatically outperforming all scgpt-based configs (~0.52–0.54). The only untested design axis holding all other parameters at their best-known values is aggregation: transformer vs. avgpool. With scgpt, avgpool beat transformer by ~2 pts (0.542 vs 0.520), but scvi_n200 produces a fundamentally different variational 200-dim representation where attention-based aggregation could capture inter-profile interactions that simple averaging misses. This single-variable change from the best config is the most interpretable and highest-value test: if transformer helps, we push accuracy above 0.706; if not, we confirm avgpool is optimal and can spend remaining budget on other axes (e.g., concat fusion or singleprofile). Expected cost: ~4–5 GPU hours (comparable to config_047's 4.82, with a modest increase from transformer attention layers), keeping total well within a reasonable budget for the remaining 3 experiments.

Evidence: config_026 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is the clear best at 0.7250 accuracy, and config_047 (same but avgpool) at 0.7062 confirms transformer aggregation helps. The only untested variant in this top-performing architecture family is config_016, which swaps weighted fusion for concat while keeping transformer aggregation. Question: Does concat fusion complement transformer aggregation differently than weighted fusion does—perhaps because the transformer already models cross-modal interactions that weighted fusion would redundantly re-weight? With 2 experiments remaining after this, confirming or ruling out concat in the best architecture is critical: if it matches or beats 0.7250, it opens a new direction; if not, we lock in config_026 as the likely optimum and can use remaining budget for a final confirmation or minor perturbation. Expected cost: ~3.5–4.0 GPU hours (same encoders and transformer aggregation as config_026, only fusion differs), making it comparable to the current best and well within budget.

The current best is config_026 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy. The evidence strongly identifies scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile as the dominant architecture, with transformer > avgpool (~0.02 gap) and weighted ≈ concat (~0.004 gap). Config_045 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is the only untested cell in this top-performing 2×2 aggregation×fusion grid. While it is unlikely to surpass 0.725, testing it completes the design-space characterization at relatively low cost (avgpool is cheaper than transformer; expected ~4–5 GPU hours, similar to config_047's 4.82). With only one experiment remaining, this is the best use of the budget: it either confirms config_026 as the definitive best or reveals a small interaction effect, while keeping total GPU hours manageable (~35 total). No other untested configuration (pca_n2000 variants, resnet50 variants, singleprofile variants) has a plausible path to beating 0.725 given the large encoder gaps observed.

The current best is config_026 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, multiprofile) at 0.7250 accuracy. All four aggregation/fusion combinations with scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l have been tested, confirming transformer+weighted as optimal. The key remaining uncertainty is the image encoder's contribution when paired with the dominant scvi_n200 RNA encoder: in scgpt experiments, imagenet_vit_l beat resnet50 by ~1.7%, but with the much stronger scvi_n200 encoder the gap may narrow. Config_010 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted, multiprofile) tests this directly. If it approaches 0.725, it offers a significantly cheaper alternative (resnet50 is ~half the cost of imagenet_vit_l, estimated ~2.0–2.5 GPU hours vs ~3.6). If it underperforms, it confirms imagenet_vit_l is essential and locks in config_026 as the final answer. As the last experiment, this is the highest-information test among remaining options: it either finds a cheaper near-equivalent or definitively validates the current best. No other untested configuration (pca_n2000, singleprofile, rna_only) has a plausible path to exceeding 0.725 given the strong evidence for scvi_n200 + multimodal + multiprofile.

With no prior evidence, the first experiment must establish whether the core multimodal hypothesis holds and provide a reference point for the remaining 9 experiments. config_003 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) tests the central question—does combining RNA and image modalities with multiprofile aggregation improve classification accuracy—using moderate-cost components (ResNet-50, average pooling, PCA) that avoid committing to the most expensive encoders (ViT-L, transformer aggregation, scGPT) before we know the direction. If it performs well, subsequent experiments can escalate to ViT-L, transformer aggregation, or scGPT/scVI encoders to push accuracy higher. If it underperforms, the result localizes the problem (e.g., fusion strategy, encoder quality) and guides targeted follow-ups. Expected relative cost: moderate—roughly 1.5–2× a single-profile unimodal baseline due to multiprofile processing and dual-modality forward passes, but well below the ViT-L + transformer + multiprofile configurations (configs 001/007/020) which would be ~3–4× this cost. This makes it the most information-per-GPU-hour choice for experiment 1.

Evidence: Our single completed experiment (config_003) achieved 61.9% accuracy using PCA-2000 for RNA, ResNet50 for image, avgpool aggregation, and concat fusion in a multimodal multiprofile setting. The biggest uncertainty is whether the linear PCA representation is sufficient for the RNA modality or whether a learned nonlinear encoder (scvi_n200) would capture more biologically relevant structure and improve accuracy. Question tested: config_002 is a clean single-variable ablation of config_003—only the RNA encoder changes from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200, holding all other settings (multimodal, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat) constant. This isolates the contribution of the RNA representation. Why this is the best next experiment: With 8 experiments remaining, resolving whether the RNA encoder is a bottleneck is fundamental—if scvi_n200 helps, it unlocks a large family of scvi-based configurations for later exploitation; if it does not, PCA is confirmed as sufficient and we can focus budget on the image encoder, aggregation, and fusion dimensions. Expected relative cost: comparable to config_003 (~35–40 GPU hours), since scvi_n200 inference is a single forward pass through a pre-trained VAE encoder, only marginally more expensive than a PCA projection, while the rest of the pipeline (ResNet50, avgpool, concat, multiprofile) is unchanged.

Evidence: config_002 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved the best accuracy (0.6315) at low cost (7.27 GPU hrs), outperforming config_003 (pca_n2000, same other settings) by ~1.3% while being 5x cheaper. This establishes scvi_n200 as the preferred RNA encoder. Uncertainty: we have only tested concat fusion with avgpool aggregation; it is unclear whether weighted fusion can further improve on 0.6315. This experiment (config_016) makes the minimal single-variable change from the best config—switching fusion from concat to weighted while keeping scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, multiprofile, multimodal—directly testing whether weighted fusion yields a gain. It is the best use of experiment 3 because it exploits the strongest evidence (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool) at minimal additional cost (~7-8 GPU hrs, similar to config_002), reducing uncertainty about the fusion choice before committing budget to more expensive architectural changes (e.g., transformer aggregation or ViT image encoder). If weighted fusion helps, we can then layer in transformer aggregation; if not, we rule out that direction cheaply and pivot to exploring aggregation or image encoder upgrades in the remaining 6 experiments.

The current best (config_016: scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.6776 accuracy at only 5.90 GPU hours. The two most promising untested axes are upgrading the image encoder (resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l) and upgrading aggregation (avgpool → transformer). I choose config_010 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) as a clean single-variable extension of the current best: it replaces only the image encoder with a much stronger ViT-L pretrained on ImageNet while preserving the proven scvi_n200 RNA encoder and weighted fusion. This isolates the image-encoder contribution and tells us whether the bottleneck is image representation quality. If it helps, the next step is clearly to add transformer aggregation (config_020); if it doesn't, we pivot to aggregation. Expected cost is moderate (~15–25 GPU hours) due to ViT-L's larger parameter count, but well below config_003's 36.42 hours, leaving ample budget for follow-ups.

Evidence: The best-performing configuration so far is config_010 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.7062). Clear trends show weighted fusion > concat, imagenet_vit_l > resnet50, and scvi_n200 > pca_n2000. The one untested dimension within this strong setting is the aggregation method: all top configs use avgpool, but transformer aggregation could better model inter-profile relationships in the multiprofile setting. Question: Does upgrading aggregation from avgpool to transformer, while keeping the proven scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + weighted backbone, push accuracy above 0.706? Why this is the best next experiment: config_020 is a single-variable extension of the current best, directly testing whether the multiprofile aggregation bottleneck limits performance. It avoids the very high cost of PCA-based configs (config_003 cost 36.42 GPU hrs) while leveraging the cheap scvi_n200 encoder. Expected relative cost is moderate—slightly higher than config_010 (4.82 GPU hrs) due to the transformer aggregation layer, likely in the range of 8–15 GPU hours, making it a cost-effective high-information experiment with 5 experiments remaining in budget.

Evidence: The best configuration so far (config_020, acc=0.725) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted in a multiprofile multimodal setup. The progression config_002→config_016→config_010→config_020 shows consistent gains from upgrading each component (fusion→image encoder→aggregation). The RNA encoder has only been tested as scvi_n200 and pca_n2000 in this high-performing region, and scvi_n200 clearly outperformed pca_n2000. Question: config_045 tests scgpt (a generative-model-based RNA encoder) in the otherwise-identical best configuration (imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile). This is the single most informative untested variable in the top-performing region—scgpt could capture richer cell-type-specific gene expression patterns than scvi_n200's latent representation. Why this is the best next experiment: With 4 experiments remaining, exploiting the proven best architecture while exploring the one untested RNA encoder is the highest-expected-value move. If scgpt matches or beats scvi_n200, we gain a new best; if not, we confirm scvi_n200 is optimal and can focus remaining budget on fine-tuning. Expected cost: moderate—scgpt is likely slightly more expensive than scvi_n200, but the imagenet_vit_l + transformer combination has been among the cheapest (3.6–4.8 GPU hrs), so I estimate ~5–8 GPU hours, comparable to or slightly above config_020.

The current best (config_020: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted → 0.7250) has been built up through a clear progression where each component change improved accuracy. The only untested variant in this exact neighborhood is config_039, which swaps weighted fusion for concat while keeping transformer aggregation, imagenet_vit_l, scvi_n200, and multiprofile. This directly tests whether the transformer aggregation can compensate for the weaker concat fusion (which has been ~0.04–0.05 worse in avgpool settings) or whether weighted fusion remains essential even with transformer. If config_039 matches or approaches config_020, it confirms the current best is robust and we can lock in the configuration; if it is clearly worse, it validates that weighted fusion is a critical component. This is the most informative single experiment remaining in the best-configuration neighborhood, and it is cheap (expected ~3–4 GPU hours, similar to config_020's 3.60), preserving budget for the final 3 experiments to explore any remaining upside.

The current best (config_020: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc=0.725) has strong evidence supporting each component choice: imagenet_vit_l > resnet50, transformer > avgpool, and scvi_n200 > scgpt. The remaining uncertainty is whether the RNA encoder choice (scvi_n200 vs pca_n2000) still matters when paired with the strongest image encoder and aggregation. config_001 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) directly tests this: if PCA performs within ~1-2% of scvi_n200, it would offer a cheaper RNA pathway; if it drops significantly, it confirms scvi_n200 is essential and locks in the current best. This is the highest-information experiment remaining because it isolates the last untested variable in the top-performing architecture. Expected cost is moderate (~3-4 GPU hours), comparable to config_020, since PCA encoding is cheaper than scvi but the ViT-L image encoder and transformer aggregation dominate training time.

The current best is config_020 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, 0.7250). The evidence strongly supports scvi_n200 and imagenet_vit_l as the optimal encoders, and transformer > avgpool for aggregation (0.7250 vs 0.7062). The only untested combination with these best encoders is avgpool + concat (config_017). While it is unlikely to surpass 0.7250 (expected ~0.70–0.71 based on config_010's 0.7062 with avgpool+weighted), it completes the 2×2 aggregation×fusion matrix for the proven-best encoder pair, reducing residual uncertainty about whether the small weighted-vs-concat gap (0.7250 vs 0.7207) is systematic or noise. With only 1 experiment remaining after this, confirming the design-space boundary around the best configuration is the most informative use of the slot. Expected cost is moderate (~4–5 GPU hours, comparable to config_010's 4.82), well within budget.

The best configuration found is config_020 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, multiprofile) at 0.725 accuracy. All evidence strongly supports scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder, imagenet_vit_l as the image encoder, and weighted fusion. The only untested architectural variant using these optimal encoders is the singleprofile setting (no aggregation step), which tests whether a simpler single-profile architecture with direct fusion can match or exceed the multiprofile transformer aggregation. This is the last experiment, so I select config_023 (singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted) to test this alternative paradigm. It is expected to be relatively cheap (~3-4 GPU hours) since it omits the multiprofile aggregation step while retaining the strong ViT-L and scvi_n200 encoders. While the multiprofile transformer setup is unlikely to be beaten, this experiment provides a final check on whether a simpler architecture could close the gap, and it is the highest-expected-accuracy untested option given the encoder evidence.

With no prior evidence, the goal is to establish a strong, informative baseline in the most promising region of the design space. config_003 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, transformer, weighted) sits at the intersection of several key design choices: it tests whether combining image and RNA modalities with multiprofile transformer aggregation yields a competitive accuracy, while using relatively cheap encoders (pca_n2000 for RNA, resnet50 for image) to keep cost moderate.
